Game is great for a nostalgia kick where you can remember the times you played similar racing games at the arcade, but it doesn't go much beyond that. The levels are all kinda samey, there isn't a large variety of modes, and the car customization is nice, but a little lackluster, but if you don't expect a really in depth arcade driving game going in, the experience is still a lot of fun. A lot of others talk about the rubber-banding being kinda bad. I personally think it's somewhat realistic seeing as drafting gives you such a massive speed boost in this game. Staying just behind the leader for most of the race is actually a tactic at higher difficulties, and it just doesn't feel right to play it that way. The music is great, absolutely nails that arcade feel, but just like at an arcade, the time enjoyed is short. Playing with your friends (which I unfortunately haven't had the opportunity to do) is another great way to expereince this game. A few things this game could really benefit from is vertical track design (giant jumps and ramps etc.) and a destruction/crash system. These would make the game feel a bit more "arcady" and fun. Definitely a fun game to spend a few hours on every so often, but probably not worth 20 bucks. Wait for a sale though and then your money is worth it.

Hotshot Racing is a fun little arcade racer that takes me back to the days of my childhood. Hotshot Racing's visual style is low-poly, obviously inspired by arcade racers like Ridge Racer and Virtua Racer. It's hyper-fast and it has a bangin' soundtrack that sounds like it would fits perfectly on any SEGA racer from the 90s. Each track has it's own theme, and while they aren't wildly different in feel, they are vibrant and have a fun charm with animated background props that you'll notice as you race, such as dolphins jumping over the track or a dinosaur roaring at you as you drift around a corner. There's a simple Grand Prix mode, with various difficulties to play through as you go for the gold in 16 different tracks that are split up between four cups. There's also 'Single Race', 'Time Trial', and a couple other modes "Cops & Robbers" and "Drive Or Explode", both which seem to boil down to the same goal 'drive fast, don't crash'. There's also multiplayer (offline and online) for these modes, though I don't have anyone to try the offline multiplayer with so I can't speak for how well these run. Online seemed to work great, when I was able to find a match. You can customize the handful of drivers you can play as (each with their own personalities and phrases you'll hear during the races) and each racer has their own set of cars to pick from, each with their own stats. As you play, you'll be unlocking more cosmetics as you make progress on achievements that are specific to each car. I'm kind of on the fence about this one. I'd rather do mixed but since I have to choose between thumbs up and thumbs down, I'm going to go with thumbs down. It's fine if you catch it on sale for cheap for hour or so of fun but it's certainly not worth the full price tag.Hotshot Racing simulates the classic days of arcade racing. I'm talking about when 3D racing games first became a thing and it does a fine job at it. Everything is low poly to fit into the aesthetic. The driving mechanics feel pretty good.My main complaint about this game is the content. There are 20 tracks all of which a lap time will not surpass a minute. Most races are 3 laps with only the last cup having 4 laps each. You'll complete the entire career mode in about an hour. There are some interesting arcade modes if you want to jump on for a race to kill a few minutes.My main complaint is the AI. They're very rubberband-y. It does make races a bit more interesting but you find yourself just sticking with the pack, saving your boosts, to use them all on the last half of the final lap to pull away and make sure you cross the finish line first. Furthermore, it's like the AI are driving concrete blocks on wheels that are just as fast as you. You can slam into them and it won't do anything but they'll be able to spin you out with ease and it gets very frustrating when they actually get you to crash to a dead stop. Overall, there's not much content and the AI can be very frustrating. If you're looking for a game like this, wait for a sale or look for something

review: For fans of the original Tomb Raider trilogy, this remaster is good. It gives you that nostalgic feeling from your first play through, which was for some of us 26 years ago (holy sh*t). Alone for that, it is worth the price.Objectively, the graphics are like a 1000% improvement from the original, but nowhere near a modern game. The controls are exactly like you remember them, which is a good thing in my opinion. However, if you have not played the original trilogy, the controls will be a pain in the a**, since 90s gaming was not even remotely as convenient as it is today. Likewise, the sounds are basically the same as in the original, which heavily contributes to that nostalgic feeling. From nowadays perspective, the sound simply s***s. Therefore, this game will be great for 35+ gamers who played the original. For new players, it may be not worth it. All in all, a fun remaster. I would give it a B on A to F scale. The only true point of criticism for me is that they did not remake the cut scences. There are not that many, this should have been possible for a 30€ game.

game_name: Tomb Raider I-III Remastered Starring Lara Croft
review: Honestly, this is probably the best remastering of a classic series we could have gotten.Controls are generally fine, camera is as wonky as I remember lol. I tried the modern control scheme and I didn't like it so I went back to the original controls and have had no issues on my xb1 controller.I really like how you can toggle between the new and original graphics on the fly with one button.Some areas are really dark in the remastered graphics but I suppose that is to add contrast in the lighting. By design, enclosed rooms that would have no "natural" lighting in the classic game have been altered cosmetically by opening some ceilings and adding a sky backdrop to allow shadows and light beams/reflections to appear more natural.For those that didn't play the original titles, be warned that these games don't really hold your hand like a lot of modern games. Drop 40 feet? Dead. Miss a jump by an inch and fall into a spike pit? Dead. Run out of meds and special ammo? Tough ♥♥♥♥. I wouldn't say it's as brutal as Souls-like games but there is definitely a learning curve to the platforming, combat, and general puzzle strategies. The only saving grace for newer players is that you can save and load without having to use fixed floating save crystals like in the original. This saves A LOT of time so you're not repeating the same 5 jumps, killing the same 4 dudes, and retrieving the same key to a door just to get back to where you screwed up a jump.Overall, I think $30 is a fair price (a little less if you preordered) for this game considering the minor quality of life changes Aspyr has made. It's not a perfect game but it's good entertainment

The dialogue in "infant-talk" is an irritating contrast to the bleak and gruesome worldbuilding, which is quite unique.Definetly check this out if you like good pixel art and/or quirky roguelikes.

Five Nights at Floppa is an absolute masterpiece in horror gaming, delivering an experience that will make your skin crawl and your heart race. The game's horror elements are executed flawlessly, with every knock and painting serving to heighten the tension and keep you on edge. The cats themselves are the stuff of nightmares, with their lifelike movements and sinister designs making them truly terrifying adversaries. Whether you're being stalked by the menacing Floppa or cornered by the relentless Pop Cat, each encounter is guaranteed to send shivers down your spine. What sets Five Nights at Floppa apart from other horror games is its clever gameplay mechanics, which require you to think on your feet and use your wits to survive like turning off the lamp. Every decision you make feels crucial and adds to the intensity of the experience. But perhaps the most impressive aspect of Five Nights at Floppa is its ability to immerse you in its world and keep you engaged from start to finish. The haunting atmosphere, chilling sound design, and gripping storyline combine to create an experience that will stay with you long after you've turned off the game.Five Nights at Floppa is a must-play for any horror fan looking for a truly terrifying experience. With its expertly crafted scares, innovative gameplay, and immersive atmosphere, it sets a new standard for horror gaming and proves that indie developers are capable of delivering unforgettable experiences. If you're brave enough to face the horrors that await you in the game, then dive in and prepare for a journey into madness like no other.

I want to start off by saying this game is absolutely fantastic. Anyone looking for a fun, challenging platformer should absolutely check it out. It takes virtually no space and its free, so there's no reason not to give it a try.The game has Foddian elements with a rare yet welcomed twist: the player's movement is completely unrestricted. While in many other Foddian games, it is easy to blame the game's physics, janky movement, etc, in Sir Fallen, you have no one to blame but yourself while you fall from the top.This game is also extremely replayable. Once you beat the game, you are already highly skilled at it. There is a built-in timer and leaderboard, which has created a community of speedrunners chasing after new techs, skips and more. As of writing this review, I am placed 3rd on the leaderboard, but that is sure to change soon. This speedrunning community is amazing.If you're considering giving Sir Fallen a try, I highly recommend it. The game is a perfect combination of fun, challenging, and rewarding once you finally reach the top.

game_name: Night At the Gates of Hell
review: Really enjoyed this game. A very interesting take on the survival horror genre. It captures that late night B-movie zombie horror pulp to great effect. The games levels and environments are surprisingly detailed and very atmospheric. From corpse infested run down apartments to to grimy island dungeons and everything in between. You will battle your way through level after level blasting zombies, cultists and demons. The story itself is very basic, You play as a survivor of the apocalypse making his way from his home to the monster filled streets of his city and beyond. Whilst the game captures the elements of suspense and horror very well it also exceeds in making the player laugh, mostly through hilarious dialogue with the weirdo cast of characters you meet on your journey. If you like B-Movies, 80s Horror, Survival horror, Retro style graphics and crudely animated dongs I highly recommend this game. Well worth the price of admission. I am personally really enjoying this trend of PSX / retro style horror games and this one might be the best I've ever played.

game_name: Night At the Gates of Hell
review: A PSX/CRT visual styled action horror game with tropes and scenes inspired from Italian zombie films from people like Lucio Fulci and Bruno Mattei.The portals to hell have been opened and you have seven chapters set in various locations to play through as your main character and a group of mostly weirdos and a terrifying maybe child try to survive. You are armed with a revolver and shotgun that you load and aim slowly, can't aim while moving, and need to land hotshots to kill your enemies, whose heads might not always be in the normal place anymore. Knives can be found and act as a defensive item when you are grabbed by an enemy. The combat is slow and weighty and works and feels good enough in a game with this atmosphere. To interact with or pick up objects or open locked doors you need to unequip your weapon, but open doors can often be nudged up as you move into them.There are some strong creepy moments, though they often don't lead to much when you might have been thinking you were going to get into a situation that might change up the mechanics in an interesting way. Good sound design and some nice haunting visuals in the quiet moments.Each of the seven chapters is set in a different area and has their own style and feel to them, some better than others from an atmosphere or combat perspective. Its a short entertaining time. Finishing the game unlocks the more comedic focused Booty Creek Cheek Freak episode and a quick and fairly dull oriented episode that opens with a few elements similar to Call of Duty's zombie game mode.Screenshots:

And I frequently missed point-blank attacks that left me completely open to getting shot.This was one of my most anticipated games of the holiday season. If it was a little more polished, if a few annoying mechanics were tweaked a bit, if the developers just took a little longer to really make the game shine, this could have been a masterpiece. This game is basically Hyper Light Drifter as a boss rush. The controls are smooth and each boss has a distinct flavor in design and attack patterns. It's not Circle Left Against Dude In Armor Simulator. It's different from Furi, in that there's some concrete power progression. Completing objectives while attempting bosses (e.g., reach phase 2 6 times) or doing bonus stages gives skill points that you can spend on accessories that change your fighting style. Stacking badges of the same type gives you passive stat bonuses. E.g., you can find a combo that reduces your damage taken by 25% and adds a flat damage boost to your normal attack. As you beat more bosses, you can stack more badges for more stat boosts. As a result of the progression system, the difficulty feels heavily frontloaded. It feels like I spent more time on the second boss than I did on 3-6 combined. At that point I started stacking more badges that let me get away with mistakes. I also got a better handle on how exactly the Absorb mechanic works. The game runs beautifully on Steam Deck, but the starting resolution was Potato Mode when I launched it. Make sure to increase the resolution and you're all set. Also, the game sometimes displays keyboard prompts during story scenes, instead of my controller. The game delivers what it offers, a pretty smooth gameplay with tight controls and astonishing visuals. The movement is highly polished and moving Jacktus, the main character, is very fun. Along the adventure, you’ll be introduced with new mechanics and enemies, which will make the odyssey of rescuing Cattus more challenging as the game progresses. Regarding the look of the game, it looks great. Even though all the game happens in the desert, each of the different zones has a unique feel to it. Furthermore, the game feels alive thanks to all the individual details it has in each of the areas, such as the villagers interacting with the player, the animals and indirect narrative which can be seen all along the adventure. As for the characters, all of them are charismatic, entertaining and fulfill their role perfectly.In conclusion, the game offers a compact experience which is enjoyable from the beginning and keeps you engaged until the very end. Besides, it's free! So don’t hesitate and try it for yourself!

The dev was inspired by Refunct and I think it shows in a lot of ways. Some could argue to it's detriment. Gameplay: It's very similar to Refunct except you're collecting the cubes as the main thing to change the world instead of pressing buttons and coloring the world as you go.Neave also does something different in that you're not slowly bringing up the world around you. You're changing it as you collect the cubes and is also different in the fact that you finish and are done you can't explore a completed world like in Refunct.Controls: Refunct has really tight controls and feels very responsive in how you can string things together. Neave does not and feels very floaty and too snappy. I was forced into wall runs into walls I wasn't aiming for when I wasn't that close to them. They're fine enough I'd say but they could use a bit tweaking if there's any plans for a sequelMusic: I really like the music. I like Refunct's better overall but the music in this was pretty good.World: Talking about the world feels a bit important since I brought it up earlier. It feels pretty barren because they're just basic blocks with there only being like two different colors. Refunct got around this issue by having your color the blocks in making them look like land and also having elevators and bounce pads to change movement even a tiny bit. Neave's world changes but it doesn't feel as satisfying or as organic.Would be really hard to give this a score out of 10 and while I may have ragged on the game throughout this review I think the most important thing to take away is that Neave was still fun to play. I look forward to any more games

'NEAVE' is obviously inspired from 'Refunct,' both operate in a similar matter while still being different.In Refunct you go through pushing buttons to bring color to platforms and to expand the overall world you're in while in NEAVE you are grabbing cubes to change platform sections of the world. Refunct is also a lot faster when it comes to getting buttons as it's more linear when it expands as NEAVE is slower as it allows you to capture the cubes in any order.Refunct controls better overall being pretty precise, but I notice NEAVE gives you way more acceleration going forward meaning you can and will certainly miss a few jumps. NEAVE has wallrunning which sounds good in theory until you actually play the game where you will just randomly lock on to walls without meaning to and again this also have acceleration launching you sideways again meaning you can and will miss platforms. There is sliding in NEAVE, but it's kinda useless, it gives you a very tiny speed boost, but since you can't immediately jump out of it, well, you're not gonna use it.Also if you're playing a Linux like I am there is a Native port, but I wasn't able to test it as turning on VSYNC will automatically crash the game every time you start it up. It might actually work without this if you don't tick the option, but I had to rely on Proton here.Yes I compared the game to Refunct, it's inspired from it so you obviously got to go head-to-head in areas and while it's not as good, not even matching Refunct, it still is a great little title to run through if you are like me and wanted more Refunct action. I'm hoping that NEAVE 2 fixes some things with just fine

CameraThe camera in this game seems to go in the direction your left joystick is facing and not the direction your character is moving. This means that if you’re trying to slow down (holding the left stick back) while rolling down a hill, the camera will think you’re trying to go uphill so it pans backwards even though you’re technically still moving down the hill. This is especially prevalent in the “Tilted Rings” and “Pachinko” stages.To fix this, they added a free camera that you can change with the right joystick, and I appreciate it. It’s extremely helpful for stages like “Exam” where I need precise angles to move forward. But most of the time, especially with “Tilted Rings”, I’m using it because the camera doesn’t go where I expect it to, so I correct it myself. The default camera settings are a little slow to my liking. Again, if you’re a purist, I’d set the camera sensitivity to +2. It makes turning much more fluid.2. BounceThis feels like the ball is made of rubber. Why do you bounce so much? I can only imagine trying to play “Opera” with the bounciness from this game. Oh wait, you do. It’s called “Stairs”. And you can’t smoothly roll in “Rings” (a different stage from “Tilted Rings”) because you bounce way too much.It’s not just a problem with bouncing on the floor, it also affects your impact with walls. The stage “Ceiling Fan” is a perfect example where the wall is supposed to keep you safe from the wind blowing you off, but more often than not, the wind pushes you into the wall and you bounce off too hard and fall

Amazing monkey ball clone that has great music and fixes A LOT of the problems with monkey ball and other clones. The jarring camera we're used to can be tamed in the options menu. There are no slow/speed up switches in levels, thank god. There are no multiple exit levels. You can't bonk off the side of exits, you can enter them from any direction. There's no levels with insane jumps that rely heavily on lucky physics. They also added a slight horizontal deadzone so that it's possible to move forward in a perfectly straight line. The level design is pretty decent, with the perfect amount of content. No level feels like a grind to get through (except a slight few in the bonus stages, but they're a good challenge.) No gimmick ever overstays its welcome. They also add a few unique mechanics like pushable blocks and teleporters. The pushable objects slightly stick to you so that they're easier to control, which is a really smart addition. The only thing I found finicky is the consistency of the bounce pads, but it's rarely an issue.Definitely recommend if you love Monkey Ball, or even if you're new to the style of game altogether. It's a great representation of the genre with great feeling controls and good pacing and challenge.

PO'ed is a FPS game from 1995 released on the 3DO and later PS1 remastered by the pinnacle of videogame remasters: Nightdive Studios. PO'ed is a strange game that somehow is also a Retro FPS, that's basically how I can describe it briefly as it's outstandingly unique compared to anything else in the vast library of 90s FPS games. Unfortunately that uniqueness comes at the cost of having some agonizingly bad level design choices. It's a game that's fun to look at and admire but not nearly as fun to actually play. Gameplay of PO'ed is fairly simple, find the exit while shooting anything in your way with a variety of weapons. Unlike other FPS games there's no keys or whatnot. Although sometimes you need to fulfill a certain criteria to make the exit spawn in such as a switch or killing a certain type or amount of enemies, the game never tells you. PO'd Chef gets his hands on a variety of weapons mostly being in a category of Melee, Hitscan and Projectile. Despite the variety they're quite ordinary in comparison to other FPS games surrounding it, the exception is a manual missile guiding weapon, and a gun I didn't manage to find that supposedly homes on targets. Yars Rising is a sequel to Yars Revenge (released in 1982 for Atari) and turned into a Metroidvania game.The game's strengths lie in its creative hacking minigames, which offer a unique twist by drawing inspiration from Atari classics like Yars' Revenge, Missile Command, and Centipede. These minigames are engaging and varied but become repetitive over time, which can detract from the overall experience. Players unlock new abilities and upgrades through these hacking challenges, but the limited visual variety and overly familiar environments can make the gameplay feel.Boss fights and power-ups are notable highlights, with some battles showcasing tight, strategic design. However, the early emphasis on stealth mechanics is widely considered the game's weakest point, detracting from the otherwise fun On the positive side, the soundtrack stands out, featuring city pop-inspired tracks that give the game a distinct energy and make even its duller moments more enjoyable. The music, contributed by a variety of artists, has been praised for its catchy tunes that stick with players long after they finish the game​(In summary, Yars Rising brings a nostalgic yet modern take on Atari's legacy, but the lack of variety and underwhelming environments hold it back from reaching its full potential. However, its creative hacking mechanics and strong soundtrack make it an interesting, if not groundbreaking, entry in the Metroidvania genre.

Yars Rising does exactly that by respecting the history while also bringing it to a more contemporary setting. The game is a Metroidvania at its core as you explore the Qotech building with various upgrades you find scattered around. They improve movement and your combat abilities so its very satisfying to find new ones as you get them pretty often. However this game is a little sneaky because it has a 2nd game hidden inside it. The character you play as is a hacker called Emi and you will be hacking almost as much as you will be exploring. The twist being that the hacking games are actually Yars' Revenge levels! Every single one will have you doing mini challenges in a new version of Yar's Revenge and they are such a treat! Some are very challenging and there are even a few other hidden Atari games inside those hacking games as well! The characters are fun and well written, the music by Megan Mcduffee is always a treat, and the expanding on the lore of a 1982 arcade style game is commendable. I really appreciate how Wayforward kept the original games spirit alive with this. I do hope more people try this out as it is one of those games that's just a genuine good time with lots of charm.

The gameplay loop follows others in the genre – Kill > Level > Unlock skills > Die > Repeat. There’s a unique twist, however.When starting a new game, you’ve only one skill slot, with additional slots being unlocked during the run. Thankfully you have a bag to hold purchased skills so you won’t lose anything as you level, additionally, the bag is necessary should you seek to upgrading them. Basically, you need 3 matching skills of the same tier to upgrade it to the next tier (moving from 1 to 2 star), with the final tier (3 star) requiring 3 matching tier 2 skills.The lack of difficulty I experienced in IT caused me to not enjoy it as much as other VS likes. In saying that, I still recommend IT – It’s a good game which nails the loop I’ve grown to love from the genre. Give it a try, you’ll know within the 2 hour refund window if it’s the VS like for you.

That said, for outposts the towers do help a lot, and the tech-tree allows for a bit of customization in the tower defense section.Do note that the tower-defense is more "base defense" than anything else.On the whole, the game feels a bit clunky - I played using mouse and keyboard - and has a bit of the "indie jank" - things feeling not quite polished, your character (mine was Quinn) not quite fast enough in the action part, but on the whole the base building saved it for me, as well as the tech tree.The story is okay, and the objectives are mostly enough to keep you going forward (except for repairing the world heart, dragging and dropping its parts are not really explained well enough).There is multiplayer, which I didn't try, and other characters to play as, each requiring an in-game non-premium currency to get - I had more than enough to get all other characters after one solo play-through. With more players, you can likely build bigger bases, and gathering resources are probably much easier. The replayability of the game is probably OK, particularly if you do it multiplayer after playing solo.I'd highly recommend getting the game if it's on a sale, if not, you should really like its base building / ARPG hybrid style.

is not your typical tower defense game. In fact, calling it a "tower defense" might be a stretch. While you do build and upgrade turrets, the gameplay is more of a frenzied, meme-infused, survival experience. This game fully embraces absurdity, and somehow, it’s all the more addictive because of it. Let’s start with the fact that the entire enemy lineup is the same meme-worthy Kunkun mascot, coming at you in relentless swarms. There’s no variety in design, and yes, it can feel repetitive—but therein lies part of its charm. It’s like the developers thought, "" And oddly enough, it works. There's something absurdly captivating about the chaos as you fend off hundreds of identical foes. At its core, the gameplay loop is simple: That’s it. The tower defense mechanics are stripped down to the essentials—don’t expect a wide array of strategies or a complex defense setup. Instead, you’ll focus on using your weapons and finding ways to manage the increasing chaos as enemies overwhelm your defenses.What sets this apart from other defense games is how the kicks in during later waves. Enemies can you, making survival a nerve-wracking test of endurance. The slow pace of the early waves can lull you into a false sense of security, but the difficulty ramps up quickly, making you wish you’d upgraded just a little faster. Yes, it’s repetitive, and yes, all the enemies look the same. The humor and chaos, however, keep it from feeling entirely stale. It's like a meme-infused experience where instead of grotesque monsters, you're being swarmed by hundreds of Kunkun mascots. The absurdity almost becomes a feature rather than a flaw, and there's a strange satisfaction in outlasting a massive wave of these identical foes.However, the repetitiveness can be a downside if you're looking for variety. "El Paso, Elsewhere" stands out as a remarkable hidden gem of indie gaming experience, boasting stunning visuals, a fascinating narrative, all complemented by an incredible soundtrack. These elements truly shine and make it a game worth exploring firsthand. While other aspects of the game may be passable, it's these standout features that will capture your attention and hold it throughout your journey. Without delving too deep to avoid spoilers, it's safe to say that these are the game's strongest assets.In terms of gameplay, "El Paso, Elsewhere" channels the spirit of classics like Max Payne, but with a supernatural twist featuring mummies, werewolves, and ghouls. The storytelling is poetic, offering a unique and immersive narrative experience. The music adds to the atmosphere, providing a badass backdrop to the action. Surprisingly lengthy with 50 levels, both the gameplay and story captivate from start to finish.One of the game's most commendable aspects is its portrayal of female-on-male abuse, a topic rarely explored in media. The narrative delivers a moving and thought-provoking depiction of this issue, adding depth and emotional resonance to the overall experience. The soundtrack is so exceptional that it warrants standalone listening, and the environments are breathtakingly atmospheric, immersing players in a world that is as beautiful as it is haunting.

The description of this being a rigged carnival game is apt. It's better than other free to play clones of Devil Daggers, but still misses the mark. Focuses way more on movement than shooting (Bullet hell, not FPS) so keep that in mind. Jumping feels very floaty. You can hold jump to go higher, or you can double jump to go higher much quicker, but have no way of getting back down quickly, making certain wave dodging or gap jumping sections feel like you are fighting the controls more than anything. The dash mechanic helps overcome this slightly, but this works in all four cardinal directions, so if you are pressing forwards and sideways at the same time it feels like a coin-flip which way you end up dashing. Just when you start to get the hang of the controls and their limitations, and work out how to combine dash and jump to navigate a section of waves, one of the randomly directed spheres will take you out. Personally, I have no issue with the monetisation model. You can play the entire game completely for free, you only need tokens for the scoreboard. That's entirely reasonable, and is actually pretty thematic for a carnival/arcade game. It's the movement that holds this back, not the tokens.

BLACKOUT, developed by INNERVISION, immerses players in a chilling environment filled with suspense and mystery. As an office worker isolated in a house filled with unsettling occurrences, you must navigate through dark corridors and eerie rooms.The game's use of is commendable, effectively enhancing the mood and immersing players in the terrifying atmosphere. The soundtrack, while decent, complements the overall experience. The jump scares can be effective, providing some genuine fright as you explore.However, the pixelated art style feels disjointed. The combination of high-resolution textures with a pixel filter detracts from the overall visual appeal. It would benefit from a more cohesive design that aligns with the horror genre, avoiding the pitfalls of a mismatched aesthetic.The narrative falls short, lacking world-building elements like notes or dialogues that could provide insight into the protagonist's psyche and the events occurring around them. The abrupt ending leaves many questions unanswered, diminishing the sense of satisfaction upon completion. A good horror experience should balance clarity and mystery, but BLACKOUT leans too heavily on ambiguity.The game incorporates platforming sections that are frustrating and poorly executed. The influence of games like PT is evident, but the overuse of this style feels unoriginal. While the exploration aspect builds tension, it often feels like a walking simulator with limited interaction.BLACKOUT has strong elements, including its atmosphere and some scares, but ultimately falls short in storytelling and gameplay execution. It’s an inexpensive title worth considering, especially for fans of atmospheric horror, but it leaves much to be desired. game_name: Captain Firehawk and the Laser Love Situation
review: This game is unlikely to satisfy fans of bullet hells, and the adult content is unlikely to satisfy anyone looking for a porno game - yet somewhere in the middle of this venn diagram of interests, there is a spark of magic that happens. The artwork and retro-inspired aesthetic is absolutely fantastic, and accompanied by some very catchy music to complete the mood. Though the game was short, it was a very enjoyable three hours. That said, there are a few glaring flaws that I would like to see the developers address. Firstly, there is the potential for a mildly challenging game here - but there needs to be a lives/continue system in place which resets your score (or the level) when you fail. Maybe as a future "Hard Mode" update? Enemy variety could use some expansion, as well as maybe multiple stages for the Giantess fights - which would be a good opportunity to have them change positions for clothing damage - rather than blocking off certain targets until preceding targets are destroyed. The game desperately also needs a proper gallery mode for the Giantess's, perhaps with a series of unique artwork or sex scenarios, maybe some comedy skits, which unlock based on your score in their levels. There also needs to be some form of ship upgrades, which are a staple for bullet-hell shooters. The game has only one basic attack, and could benefit from having different firing patterns, elemental shots, bombs, shields... things like that. You collect coins from defeated enemies, but these really have no function in the game aside from getting "gas money" to make it to the next stage as a minor performance threshold. It would be nice to use the surplus to upgrade the ship or buy special attacks.Still, despite these shortcomings -

Along with this, the speedrunning accounts for the the fastest time to complete the sets of levels or the individual levels, depending on how you choose to play it. It does have cool looking pixel graphics with some nice kind of retro and arcadey music. The levels themselves are fun to play with them being designed well. With obstacles from shooting bolts, floating spikes, rushing enemies, bats holding keys that are required to be taken in order to open to exit to the level etc. There are a few sets of stages with a number of levels within. It is currently in early access, though more frequent updates seems to be coming with more levels added along with a level editor. I got to speak with the incredibly kind and welcoming developer and demo this game at PAX East 2020. I didn't think I'd even bother playing the demo because time limits makes my anxiety run rampant and I'm historically not a huge fan of 2D platformers, but after spending so much time talking with the dev I decided to give it a shot. I did not beat the demo but I was shocked at how much fun I found it and bought a copy immediately after.The most surprising aspect of this game to me was how comfortable it felt. Death and failure are the very nature of the game, so not finishing all the levels doesn't feel like a kick to the ego, It's easy to get caught up in the stress of the clock by trying to complete every level as fast as possible, but when you're stuck on a level, sometimes it's better to use two or three attempts worth of time for one well thought out attempt. The game doesn't allow you to sit on one level and be frustrated with it. Because time is so limited, it forces you to take a step back after running out of time and take a short break from the point you may be stuck on, which for me is very helpful. The soundtrack is also excellent and will be stuck in my head for quite a while. I'm excited to see what gets added to this great game!

My only gripe with the game is that the timer shouldn't start until you start moving. There's a quick animation for your character spawning in and then the timer starts. Sometimes there's a hazard right next to you and it's hard to get the timing down to immediately start and not hit the hazard.

Bashing monsters is fun. This game delivers a nostalgic type of platforming-action experience with a distinctive personality in presentation that perfectly captures what made some of the classics so great in the first place. Tres-Bashers is innovative without re-inventing the wheel, just an interesting mix of gameplay mechanics with a very charming visual style and whimsical premise: You must help Terry Pinkerton rescue his friend from Sasquatch, the King of the Cryptids, by infiltrating your haunted high school and bashing the monsters hiding inside.The progression is 'vania-lite, as you explore the map and find shops to purchase upgrades, abilities, and some cosmetic items, which help you better deal with baddies and overcome obstacles, and look cool. Money nor health recovery is really that much of a problem, for the most part, in that save points are initially plentiful, and while most bashed enemies stay bashed, you can always find something to smash for food or a couple of coins.There are plenty of secret areas and pitfalls to discover, and another use for your flashlight is to reveal hidden objects such as keys which are used Zelda-style to open the doors of your choosing. Yet staking out even a few rooms of explored territory almost certainly involves more than a few surprising encounters from the game's bestiary of 40 or so bizarre monster gags, some of which can really getcha.The inventive challenge of the game is that the cryptids can typically only be made fully visible/vulnerable by spotting them with your flashlight, which recharges but has a limited battery. To complicate matters, you cannot turn around while holding your flashlight, you can still move but you can't aim behind you as long as it's on. The monsters also generally have to attack to get you, that's how they can sneak up

If you've never played Crysis before, I think I would still recommend starting with the original version, but if you're a longtime fan this remaster offers an interesting new lens to play the game through and it never hurts to play Crysis again. I would probably give the game a sideways thumb if I could, since there are aspects both better and worse than the original, but considering owners of the original can get a pretty good discount it's worthwhile if you can get it cheap.There are definitely some visual aspects that look a bit nicer. It's not revelatory but the new reflection effects to make certain things pop a bit better and I've always been of the opinion some of the original game's textures looked a bit over-sharpened, which the new volumetric fog smooths over nicely. The raytracing is pretty tasteful and in-line with the original art direction without being overdone, and there's some cool uses of it, such as being able to see your own reflection when you pick up a CRT Television. Character models seem largely the same but again, the facial textures don't seem as overdone on the sharpness filter and faces are a bit nicer to look at in general. For some reason the original Crysis didn't have anti-aliasing which struck me as odd even at the time given the game's intent of having every graphical technology under the sun. The blues and greens of the island seem to pop more as well, which is very pretty to look at and the water in particular looks great.What is disappointing is that the Godrays seem toned down compared to the original. The scene in the first part where you finally step out onto the beach at sunrise was not only an iconic moment of the game,

Don't know how it compares to the original Crysis, but here's my thoughts.Positives:Looks absolutely astonishing, especially in the hyper-atmospheric and detailed alien structure levels.Fairly small download size for such a good-looking game, and system requirements aren't too bad either. Turns out it can run Crysis!Decision to stick to a relatively manageable and linear progression path in such a large play area, rather than go full-on open world, is to be applauded, so not much unnecessary busywork or meandering.Gameplay is mixed up with armour and cloak abilities engineered into your nano-suit, letting you go stealthier if you want to, or help you out in seemingly impossible situations.Negatives:It's short. The end credits (which are interminable) feel longer than the game. For completionists, there's no excuse for that. I wasn't able to use the mouse to steer the vehicles, like I could with the Halo games. You may have to make do with arrow keys or get a controller.Foliage, no matter how dense, does not seem to hide you from enemies well enough, and yet it's difficult to see them.Feels slightly bland and generic at first, like a typical AAA shooter (but persevere with it and you should have fun). The unimaginative story doesn't help.Overall, it's fine, not life-changing but entertaining enough while it lasts. I wonder how good the rest of the games in the series are.

Recommending this as an impressive game from a small dev that punches above its weight and hits its marks for the most part. I'm looking forward to a more fleshed-out experience in the follow up.The visuals are fantastic, both the graphics on display and overall visual design. The cyberpunk influences are obvious but it has its own distinct twists on the formula. There were quite a few spots I stopped to just rotate the camera and take in the scene, and a couple of eye-popping set pieces in the end. The music was a bit offbeat, as was the English voice acting. The performers were fine (and pro actors) but the directing was maybe a little quirky - if anything it added to the overall charm. Combat is fun but takes some getting used to compared to other hack-and-slash games, to me it feels a lot like Shinobi and Kunoichi on PS2 without the aerial moves (for the most part). Fights can play out pretty differently depending on the powers you have equipped, especially the larger hordes and bosses in the last act. There were a couple of glitches that forced me to reload but the game saves so often they weren't much of a bother.I don't really factor price vs playtime in my purchases but knowing it's a big deal to some, I'll say the game IS pretty short - I saw credits in less than 5 hours and I wasn't exactly rushing. With the power-ups you acquire, initially it seems like a metroidvania but you only use them a few times at most. On the other hand, a time attack mode did unlock after I rolled credits, and there are a few achievements left to hunt.

SWORDCAR is a silly concept that delivers with full seriousness. Rather than making fun of its absurd premise. It genuinely answers the question of "what if car had sword?" In a fun and enjoyable way that has immense potential. It has solid controls that allow for great maneuverability and offers the option of different weapons both ranged and melee which is a nice touch and gives you a reason to replay it. While the game is functionally a demo during the writing of this review, It gives you a taste of something amazing and gets you excited for more. While it needs fine tuning, the core gameplay succeeds impressively. As for feedback, i would add color coding to improve visibility on special enemies and perhaps some more unique models. currently a hoard of enemies can blend together when it includes different types, making it hard to tell them apart. For free, you can't complain at the game, it punches way above its supposed weight as an extra in a AAA action game. The music is average, seems to call back to 16 bit era days with very average composition.As far as gameplay you have access to bombs, 3 weapons (Normal, Homing and Laser), 4 powerups ("P" for power, "S" for speed, "B" for bombs and an Option you can manually redirect) and 7 stages with 7 distinct bosses. I would recommend picking up the speed powerup as a priority ("S") so you don't feel as sluggish and can actually dodge, the hitbox is very small so it's more lenient that it initially appears to be. The "freezing enemies to then blow them up in chain as a bomb" concept is very interesting from both a scoring and gameplay perspective. It takes a while to click with it but once you do you'll figure out the game is meant to be played in a more tactical way than most shmups that come out nowadays. You'll begin to think tactically as to -where- you want to kill enemies to use them as bombs and create chain explosions with upcoming enemy spawns, -when- to stop holding the shot button to maximize the effect of enemies blowing up, -what- weapon to use, upgrade to pick and direction to have your options facing at. However, there are times where the pacing will grind down to a halt where you are forced to proceed with a specific mechanic or you are just forced to wait in general. Some minor issues with scalability and interaction mechanics are present but don't overshadow the game's strengths.Customizable difficulty settings cater to a broad range of players. The variety of characters and unlockables, along with challenging Providence trials, ensures high replayability.Despite the absence of crossplay, the multiplayer aspect is engaging and well-executed, turning brief gaming sessions into hours of fun."Risk of Rain Returns" is an exemplary modernization of a beloved series. It's a game that will delight both long-time fans and newcomers with its engaging gameplay, stunning visuals, and captivating soundtrack. Gunvein is a bullet hell game, developed by NGDEV. They reportedly make highly acclaimed games, yet apparently have an allergy when it comes to PC, almost never releasing their games for this platform. And I say "almost" because Gunvein is the only exception.This is a damn shame, because if their other games are as half as good as Gunvein, we're really missing out on them.This is not a weak point of the game, just something that feels pretty weird on first launch and I have to address first.Usually, shmup/bullet hell games offer you a story to put the events into context. They either start with a brief cutscene (Devil Engine, Infinos Gaiden), have the characters talk mid-game (Touhou) or talk about what's happening in the manual (The Tale of ALLTYNEX Trilogy) or on the store page. Often times, the games also feature ending cutscenes explaining the events that happen after the game. That is not to say pure, gameplay-focused shmups don't exist. There are numerous games like this out there (Raiden IV, Crimzon Clover) but the thing is, they never do something that gives you the impression of a story being present.Gunvein is a game that falls between these titles, and that makes its presentation very weird. It presents brilliantly drawn characters as playable pilots and even features them on the store page, on the soundtrack's album art and in the tutorials, giving you the impression of a story-based game. However, it doesn't offer you any story context in the game and doesn't even give you an ending either. Quite confusing at first if you ask me.The first and the most important thing that Gunvein does right, is allowing the player to tailor their visual experience. You can decrease the background brightness, turn off the optional HUD on your ship

While the production of this game is very good, and surely the contemporary philosophical discussions will be interesting to some, I felt the game play tried to awkwardly straddle its clear story-driven design with faux world exploration player interactions. It felt stifling, bothersome, and slow to have to personally traverse the world to progress the story, when there is no particular reward for spending any time in the world. I would not recommend this game to people who aren't the type to find themselves deeply immersed in a game's story and setting.For those who are likely to be immersed, you will hopefully be able to indulge in the story, the character choices (which are somewhat unclear as to what effect they actually have on the direction the story takes, except clearly the endings), and the setting on a strange alien world.For people like me, who are not easily immersed, you will probably find some frustration in the pacing, the tedious world traversal, and the feeling that most choices only affect voice prompts. I would rather this have been made in the story telling style of a Telltale game, than one where I'm expected to move the character from a first-person perspective. That style would allow me to fully focus on the story, the choices I'm making, and view the world from a cinematic perspective.Scrambling over terrain obstacles is not interesting. Quickly running out of stamina in any effort to move the character faster is not interesting. Attempting to explore the world map to - at best, get a little extra lore - is not rewarding for the time sink that it is. Driving through the map doesn't even let one enjoy the passing view, because between the helmet cover and tiny rover windows you can't see much of the world

This game is incredible to look at. The story is simple but works to its advantage, telling a short and sweet tale. The game also runs extremely well on Steam Deck.Unfortunately, that is where the good ends and the bad begins. There are so many questionable design decisions in this game that I can't help but feel frustrated at the waste of time it all adds up to.Needing to gather purple energy to use the haunted objects' special actions feels like such a tacked on aspect. You never needed to collect anything special for Cappy to do its thing in Mario Odyssey; and running out of energy during a crucial moment just destroys whatever semblance of progress you've made.The feedback design on controls are also pretty poor. It's impossible to tell where your sandwhale is going to steer/jump during the Vortex battle of the game, for instance, and the cowboy shootout portions doesn't give any sort of aiming reticule, so you have to "best guess" it for a precision shooting activity and end up missing most of the time.Other incredulous pieces of bad design include the coaster battle in Wickland, where it's impossible to see where the first bombs are on the track until a split second before you collide into them (the camera is shifted far too much behind you rather than showing what's ahead), and i ended up having to just not use the boost at all to be even able to make it through the section, which is a pretty anticlimactic end to what is
Truly a work of art, the devs should be very proud.(Also for anyone wondering, it works perfectly on Steam Deck)

I'd just like to interject for a moment. What you're refering to as Linux, is in fact, GNU/Linux, or as I've recently taken to calling it, GNU plus Linux. Linux is not an operating system unto itself, but rather another free component of a fully functioning GNU system made useful by the GNU corelibs, shell utilities and vital system components comprising a full OS as defined by POSIX.Many computer users run a modified version of the GNU system every day, without realizing it. Through a peculiar turn of events, the version of GNU which is widely used today is often called Linux, and many of its users are not aware that it is basically the GNU system, developed by the GNU Project.There really is a Linux, and these people are using it, but it is just a part of the system they use. Linux is the kernel: the program in the system that allocates the machine's resources to the other programs that you run. The kernel is an essential part of an operating system, but useless by itself; it can only function in the context of a complete operating system. Linux is normally used in combination with the GNU operating system: the whole system is basically GNU with Linux added, or GNU/Linux. All the so-called Linux distributions are really distributions of GNU/Linux!

A great old-school style ninja action platformer. Very reminiscent of Ninja Spirit by Irem, you have a sword main weapon and 6 subweapons that have their own strategic advantages and disadvantages. Each stage is comprised of 4 sub-segments, with short sidescrolling platforming sections, and 1 boss for each segment. Three are mid-bosses, with a bigger, more difficult end stage boss. The abundance of bosses has a Treasure feel to it, which makes it stand out from the game it's based on.If you enjoy simple but challenging oldschool feeling games, with nice weapon variety and mobility, this is a good pick for you.

This is a boss rush game in the vein of Alien Soldier inspired by Strider (you can swing your sword in 8 dierctions), Shinobi (screen clearing ninja magic) and classic Ninja Gaiden (a powerup summons two clones that mimic you).You have access to a dodge, a double jump, a fast fall (press dodge in the air) & 6 sub weapons. The game gives you all 6 sub weapons at once and you can freely switch between them. For example; shuriken are fast and cover a wide arc but deal low damage, meanwhile the canon is slow but has solid range and deals tons of damage. The catch is that they all share the same resource (magic) but have different cost, with shuriken costing very little and weapons like lightning costing a lot more. You can recover magic by killing enemies or opening chest.This is a very focused game, so you won't really do any exploring and the areas between bosses are pretty short and mainly exist to refill your magic meter with the enemies they throw at you and you health with the chest they put in your way, all to prepare you for the bosses. The boss fights are varied and pretty good, normally I hate it when games throw enemies at you during boss fights, but here it makes sense because you have to kill an enemy to get magic from them, so they're essentially there to keep your magic up. I also like how the dodge isn't overpowered, it's invincible, but it has recovery frames and if the attack last long enough you will get damaged. The last boss of Chapter 1 actually test you with this, he has a ground attack that will hit you if you try to dodge it early and a wave attack

There are 4 or 5 in each of the game's 5 stages, and they're all incredibly well thought out. But they will mostly require a few practice rounds to beat, and accordingly the game gives you infinite continues. So higher level gamers will probably want to practice until you can beat the game without continuing to keep your score until the end, which is no small feat.I would say this is one of the best linear platformers to come out in a long time, probably on par with the first Curse of the Moon. So just enjoy what's here and if you want more, see how far you can get on one life.

My impressions video: HOP TOP at its core is a combination of Doodle Jump (I said Bubble Bobble in the video because I never played Doodle Jump) and Galaga, packaged together with some very accurate 16-bit arcade vibes (or 8-bit vibes if you play the arcade mode).Your goal is simple: Ascend the tower as far as you can while taking out waves of enemies while perpetually hopping upwards. You'll have to deal with changes in the platforms such as ones that crumble under you, rotating spikes or platforms you have to jump onto in a certain order while not taking too long to clear a wave of enemies, lest a large invincible enemy spawn that will try to block your progress. In the campaign mode, every 10 levels will move you forward into a new environment, while the arcade and endless modes are more of a traditional score attack.Like the arcade games it emulates, this one doesn't pull any punches, has a high skill ceiling and demands practice and persistance to best its challenges. You will unfortunately be comparing your performance to yourself as its leaderboards are local only and it currently lacks achievements, but it nonetheless provides a challenge that's satisfying to overcome.There have been more and more of these "modern retro" arcade titles coming out lately and I'm happy to see it. I hope we get more like this soon and the price is right to boot.

The game is a 2D platformer in which we control a cake named Cakeboy as he fights against the evil cooks polluting Cakeland. The game has nine levels, each with different enemies, obstacles and environments. At the end of the game, I face Dark Cake, Cakeboy's arch-rival.Here's what I like about the game:The graphics are very cute and colorful. It's fun to navigate a world full of cakes, cupcakes, cookies and other sweets.The music and sound effects are also very nice. Each level has its own unique soundtrack and the sounds Cakeboy makes when he hits his enemies are very funny.The controls are very simple and fluid. I can control Cakeboy with the keyboard or gamepad. Cakeboy has various moves like jumping, running, punching and throwing.The game's weapons are very creative. I can attack my enemies using bakery-themed items such as Croissant Boomerang, Cupcake Bomb, Super Donut, etc. Each weapon has a different feature and usage.The difficulty level of the game is very well adjusted. The game is easy at first but gets harder as you progress. There are some levels that require timing, reflexes and strategy. It takes some effort to finish the game.Here are the things I didn't like about the game:The story is very simple and uninteresting. I don't know why Cakeboy is protecting Cakeland or why Dark Cake is his enemy. There is a short video at the beginning and end of the game but it doesn't make much sense.The game is very short. I can finish the game in about 20 minutes. I wish the game had more levels, enemies and weapons.The replayability of the game is very low. The only thing I can do after finishing the game is to find hidden materials, achievements and other secrets. But that doesn't change the game much.

Exploration means treasure, treasure means more time, more time means more exploration...This is quite an enjoyable game with fluent free-running and quite some things to discover. I never encountered any serious bugs (although I found some dinosaur bones) and apart from some slightly repetitive elements towards the end experiencing the generally same time over and over again feels fresh every time when you unveil more and more of the map, find more clues about the prophecy intertwined with the events at hand and unlock the mechanism hidden on the treasure island you ultimately want to get away from (getting away rich, of course).There are some quality of life issues, e.g. you have to tap through the story sequence at loop start to save and exit. And as far as I understood, you cannot pause your progress but have to end the current loop, so some time management ahead makes it a bit more stressful than necessary.The puzzles seem fair, but I recommend to take notes as soon as you find something that seems important. Which brings me to my biggest complaint. Taking notes breaks the flow of an otherwise smooth run over the island. It is okay, but at some points I wished it was a run & collect game. Anyway, nothing that kept me from 100% completion and I definitely recommend this game!

I think a better approach would be to have the ability to dismantle them and receive a percentage of the fab tokens to re-invest elsewhere.I will admit I did get stuck in one place and in the end I took the option to use the assist mode which I thought was excellently incorporated, allowing you to set the amount of assistance at an extremely granular level. Barold is yet another of literally thousands of 2D retro platformers infesting Steam and lowering the average quality of all video games everywhere. This one is particularly badly made, and while there's no pixel "art", it's badly drawn. Controls are a bit sloppy, you can fall off platforms if you're near the edge... not a lot of testing was done here. Gameplay is equally poor and uninspired, with precision platforming and a bit of projectile dodging, although the best projectile you could ever dodge is by not buying this game. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The artwork here is terrible, it's all just amateurish "My First Wacom Tablet" style drawings used instead professional looking game assets. It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget to arrange someone who can create graphical assets properly, or lack of talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low, enough on its own to deter gamers.There's no option to change the resolution and no useful graphics tweaks. There's no way to ensure this is running at the native resolution of your display. There's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision.The game only displays in a completely bizarre 3:4 ultra pillarboxed aspect ratio. It's possible they developed this using an old CRT they found in a dumpster, and because they never saw a computer before making this, developed the game with the monitor on the side. That's the best reasonable explaination for this otherwise inexplicable defect... either way, this isn't really acceptable in the modern era of PC gaming.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game

Aquarius is a 2D retro pixel twin stick shooter with an underwater theme, as you're a diver shooting various dangerous endangered species underwater to collect gold coins off the corpses of the animals you destroy. The underwater nature of the game influences your movement, but in general movement is not dissimilar to Asteroids or SpaceWar! from 1962.They chose to use obsolete retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics. It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result. While there is a full screen mode, resolution is locked and there's no graphics tweaks that could assist with trying to improve the poor visual quality of the obsolete and outdated lazy retro pixel "art". These flaws push this game far below minimum acceptable standards for PC. The game is completely free. Nothing speaks more to a developers belief in themselves and their product than making their game available for everyone without remuneration. This is certainly a gesture that shows dedication to the gaming industry. It's a shame in this case that the implementation is below the minimum standards a dedicated PC game should offer to enthusiasts. There's no "maybe" option in Steam, unfortunately, but I hope to see more work from this developer, perhaps as part of a professional game development company that can make full use of their talents without needing to make budget/quality compromises.

Some of the later missions start to feel like you really only have 1 true way of completing them due to ammo constraints and the speed at which enemies attack. If you love Hotline Miami, Katana Zero, or Deadbolt, this may be just the game for you.

A big weird messy grab-bag of shmup with a lot of heart. FM synth jams, weirdly lurid art and oddly charming bosses. Despite its apparent weirdness and intensity, it's also pretty accessible due to highly scalable difficulty and many routes to the end credits. It'll take many play-throughs to see everything.Combat-wise, this game has two big gimmicks. For starters, your ship has four weapons, one on each side, and mapped to the face-buttons on most controllers. Each weapon has its own firing pattern and arc and quirks, and its own charge attack, enabled by not firing for a second or two. The other gimmick is that you collect money and regularly open an in-flight store. This gives you a few seconds of invulnerability and the chance to buy health, smart bombs or weapon upgrades, making for interesting combat flow.The other big gimmick of the game is that there are 24 possible stages to play, and a playthrough will take you through 4-7 of them, depending on whether you complete bonus objectives along the way. Scattered through the levels are hidden collectibles with enemy lore descriptions, character art, story vignettes and lots of unlockables. Lots of meat on this one's bones.It's a little intimidating at first but if you crank the speed and rank (bullet intensity) down, it's remarkably accessible. Looking forward to diving in and playing more of this, and uncovering more of its weirder depths.Apropos of nothing, but I'm also pretty sure that the lead developer, HEY, is a big ol' furry. And that's okay.

If you enjoy playing vintage arcade games for score I think this is an easy buy, but it could be fun for casual players and even young children (especially cat lovers!). It's one of those unassuming titles that's so simple on the surface but it unfolds elegantly as you understand more and more how it works. The goal is to cross from left to right, using your slow motion power to dodge raindrops and collect stars for extra score multiplier. The level increases quickly over time until level 29, where you can apparently see an ending if you cross 5 times after that (so far I've only managed 3 crossings at that maximum level).There's also a mysterious badge system that confers special bonuses and power-ups. Suffice to say, figuring out that system is a big part of the fun and there are a surprising number of scoring strategies that develop around it. The first time you reach one million points is very satisfying but it's only the first step toward mastering this game!To top it off, the delightful presentation and theme make it feel cozy despite the frantic action. Combined with the short sessions, it's easy to hit "Replay" over and over again. And although the Standard Mode is my favorite, the other unlockable modes offer some unique takes on the default experience. I’d like to highlight Customize Mode as a charming way to change the basic difficulty of the game - it has its own separate leaderboard.

I have a soft spot for arcade-style throwbacks, and I think this is a good one. Raindrop Sprinters feels like a more fleshed-out interpretation of Helmet, an old Game & Watch LCD game where you earn points by running from one building another while avoiding falling objects (or raindrops, in this case). This game adds enough mechanics to that formula to keep the game interesting for more than 5 minutes (in the way most G&W games feel to play nowadays, to be honest). Such mechanics include the ability to slow the falling objects down, badges that give you extra bonuses and abilities after you unlock them by doing specific tasks within each run, and a 50% point bonus for reaching the goal without stopping once you cross the starting line. That last one seems small, but it significantly affects the way you end up playing the game, especially early on when raindrops are easier to avoid. There are also multiple modes to unlock over time that can massively change the way the game works, so there's a good amount to do for a game where the average run is probably about 90 seconds.For me, this is a very good "Thing To Do With My Hands" kind of game. It's just a nice little game to mess around with while watching videos or streams, or when listening to music or a podcast. It's a type of game that lends itself well to this since there is little going on to distract me beyond the act of playing the game. A lot of old arcade games and puzzle games (in the Tetris sense, not so much the Myst sense) fit this bill for me as well. It's good to have a new one of these to throw into the rotation.

Having played 7-8 hours of the , I can very much say that this game is worth your money. If you are the type of person who loves chasing hi-scores, old arcade games, or shmups(?), I think you will click with this and it's definitely worth checking out.You play as a cat running from building to building, dodging raindrops. They start out very slow, but pick up in speed and density very fast. Everything you do related to this gets you score- you get score for making it across, you get score for collecting star pickups along the way, and you get score for grazing the raindrops. You also get medals by doing certain hidden achievements that give you upgrades for your current run; not only are you trying to score as much as possible, but also trying to complete every goal as fast as possible. This leads to some very interesting routing you can potentially do, and over the course of playing the original Raindrop I changed my strategy multiple times. To help with all this, you also have the use of a slowdown button, where your cat uses psychic powers to make the raindrops move at half speed (at the cost of your ESP gauge, of course).It might sound silly considering how basic the game looks, but I consider everything else beyond this information a "spoiler". Shuhei has gone on record saying the game was inspired off of Namco classics such as "The Tower of Druaga"- while not nearly as complicated (and sometimes obtuse) as that game, it certainly has a similar energy with figuring out how the medals are obtained and weird scoring quirks. After getting far enough in the game you "unlock" more detailed information laying out the medals, which helps figuring out ones you missed.

I have 20+ hours in the Switch version. I see other reviews talking about the deep scoring systems and addicting gameplay, so I want to talk about why I love the game's unique atmosphere.Nostalgia is a pillar of many indie games, but in Raindrop, the actual feeling of nostalgia pervades the entire setting. The achingly familiar school backdrop with the classic Japanese school bell chime, the pitter-patter of a rainy day, and the bold, hot colors and sounds of an arcade machine. Yet, for all the comfort the game offers, it is also rich with mystery and curiosity. Why do I have ESP powers? Are the cats in the window my friends? Why are stars falling through the roof? Is that a UFO???The cute and comfortable is juxtaposed with the cool and curious in a way that really activates my imagination while I play. This is also reflected in the game's mechanics, like mysterious badges and special events. As a result, it captures the feelings many retro games do, by inviting you to imagine and experiment while you play. Congratulations to Miyazawa-san for achieving such elusive feelings in his game.P.S. Game works perfect on Steam Deck. Online leaderboards, extra modes, achievements, and options for TATE and backgrounds makes this a really excellent package.

The first 3 modes use the same sort of game play loop with a few different changes here and there while the last mode is doing the complete opposite of the main objective of avoiding the rain, which makes it a very fun little addition. The game only being 4 buttons ( 4th being the start button which allows you to quit and restart ) makes it a very accessible title in my opinion. The inclusion of a online leader board is very cute addition which should give you an incentive to keep going and achieve more.The music and sound effects are stellar in this game with the creator ( room_909 ) using a software that has damn near perfect NAMCO wave generation, making it feel closer to a real arcade experience than most.The graphics in this game also look pretty yet simple, fitting within the middle period of arcade games.At the end of this ramble, yes I would recommend this game to all arcade fans and would even go as far as saying that most casual players would like it too.

This game is simply amazing. The graphics are the perfect blend of simplistic and detailed, culminating in a superbly minimalist style that really tells a story. The UI is concise and out of the way, exactly how I like it. The smooth, gray inventory is pleasing to the eyes and contrasts well with the sunny world that you inhabit, highlighting the disparity between how the world is on the outside versus how Combat Cat feels on the inside. Speaking of, Combat Cat themselves is a complex and well written protagonist, really exemplifying the extremely deep emotion journey they go through while slaying slimes (I was able to relate to Combat Cat's struggle during the story, it felt like I was really there). Gameplay wise, the balancing is superb. Any build is viable with any combination and rewards balancing out you stats with the variety of unique items. The enemies are unique and variable, with the runs becoming more hectic as you go on. Their attack patterns are tough enough to feel like you truly earned the next level. Bosses are engaging challenges that push your builds to their limit and make you switch up your movement and strategy to shine.TLDR: Combat Cat is a masterpiece.buff big shot

As soon as you start Zero Protocol, you know you have something special on your hands. The main menu is lo-fi but oozes character--much like the rest of the game.Zero protocol is a first-person sci-fi survival horror game with a strong character and impressive direction. The environment and level design is phenomenal, giving the sense of a real place where people actually lived and did work.The game is level-based--you spend your time exploring the current facility floor, unlocking as many of its secrets as you want before advancing to the next floor. Every floor is self-contained puzzle; you can fully explore it without relying on information or items from previous floors. Your goal is typically to figure out what's going on, how to restore power and/or unlock the elevator to go on to the next floor.There is one story fork where you have a choice of which floor to travel to, although it is rather subtle and easy to miss; each path from the fork takes you to a different story path with 2 out of the 4 possible endings. To reach the other two endings, you'll have to delete the saves (through the menu) and replay the game. This is not a problem since you can go much faster in subsequent playthroughs. Expect ~4 hours for the first run, then maybe 1-2 hours for subsequent runs.You have both health and sanity meters, reminiscent of Amnesia: The Dark Descent. As spooky things happen, and as you walk dark spaces, or fight enemies, your sanity drops. You start seeing hallucinations that may cause you to waste ammo or dismiss real enemies for hallucinations, so managing sanity becomes important. But that's not all--some things you can only read or notice when you're sane, while other things you can only see and interact

It's not hard to see where Biomorph draws its inspiration from, mostly Hollow Knight and Ender Lilies. The game puts all the familiar ideas together and on top of that, adding a little twist into formula. You can become the enemy you just defeat. While the mechanic certainly makes the experience solid and bends the rule of gating-abilities, the execution feels off for me. Biomorphing doesn't streamline your combo and the overall combat. And a lot of monster forms are treated as one-trick ponies, a one-and-done deal. That being said, I cannot just down vote the game and move on. Despite my negativity, I still have fun exploring the big alien worlds the developers created. Tons of secrets and scavenge hunts encourage you to use all of your abilities to the fullest. Overall, Biomorph is a solid metroidvania to playthrough. It's just that I think the mechanic could've been better or at least well-used.→I like the western cartoon art style.→Quite a few interesting NPCs and side quests.→Exploration is often rewarding despite the terrible map system.→All 39 Scargatoes have their own cute description.→: There are actually two types of gating-abilities: first type is the usual reward that players can find at the end of the level or after the boss fight, and the other type is related to the biomorphing. For the first type, I am glad and actually surprised to find out Biomorph doesn't just hand out the regular gating-abilities like Double Jump right away. The design choice immediately sets the game apart from other metroidvania. Of course making your protagonist less mobile means the level design cannot be too difficult to navigate, but Biomorph circumvents this issue by introducing biomorphing, in other words, a second set of gating abilities. Each monster forms have their unique attacks and special quirks
