The general premise of KOP Killer 22XX is that you've been arrested and operated on in order to convert you into a KOP (Kapital Operative - basically a paramilitary force working for a ruling class of oligarchs). In the middle of reprogramming (which also serves as the game's tutorial), some unknown incident interrupts the process and you're able to break free. Now you just need to bust out of prison and try to take down your fascist oppressors.While Story Mode isn't available at the time of this review (I played a preview build), there's some hefty references to real-life events even in the intro - whether it be scrip for miners and its uselessness outside of the company's services, the ridiculous cost of life-saving medicine, a ruling class of oligarchs, a long history of systemic racism, private prisons, and police brutality. This game probably won't be pulling any punches when story mode is revealed.The tutorial is actually a bit unsettling - you're being released from prison early, but the caveat is that you're being brainwashed and turned into another cyborg officer. The simulation of course represents the prejudiced, out of touch perspective held by the KOPs and their fascist masters, and a lot of the brainwashing process involves dehumanizing suspects and teaching a brutal, biased approach to conflict resolution.Of course, the further you go, it becomes clear that you're resisting the brainwashing and the character you control starts to flicker out of the fake body and uniform and into their real form. The tutorial continues a bit and you're encouraged to get uncomfortably brutal as you unlock more of your toolkit. You eventually break out at the end (wouldn't be much game if you ended up as a mindless police drone), but not before a tense and yet not unexpected

Time to get in early for cheap price for this modern 8-bit, 2D platformer, beat em up! I have no doubts in the love and attention that was provided to A Robot Named Fight will equally (if not more with additional help!) occur with Kop Killer 22XX. Support indie developers! The game starts with a taste of the story mode which left me excited for future updates. The arcade is great run through the core mechanics of close combat and run 'n gun action. Achievements lead to partner unlocks, upgrades, and higher leader board scores which pulls you into just one more run loop! Every few area clears, you earn partner with clutch powers and each area clear you get a choice of 3 random upgrades; all the while you are jamming to a chip tune soundtrack. Look forward to more!

Every combat encounter whittles away at the durability of every attached module. If you have a fully wooden or metal hull, the majority of your time will be spent scavenging wood and metal trash to recycle for scraps to repair your ship. Weapons require weapon parts for repair, on top of wood and metal.Beyond the resource balance issues, Age of Water feels like a mix of Sea of Thieves and Crossout. Even ignoring the length of time most players will likely spend with this (not very many), you might be asking how said hours are spent. How's that part? Thankfully, the game is pretty darn fun! The game, also, conceptually, might not be, at all, creative to the extent that it is a roguelite with a couple playable characters, some loot to find (with fixed stats, mind you), bats, orcs, potion boosts, etc. To put it another way, its ambitions are extremely meddling. A real palette cleanser!In Crumble, you're a slimeball that mysteriously arrives on a unknown land, and you have to get on the Spaceship headed back to your home planet. You tongue your way through all sorts of objects and textures, and then fly away in a rocket ship.There's no story or dialogue from any of the characters, not even in fake language like there was in Tunic. It contrasts sharply with something like a JRPG - in a good way. You don't have to think hard to play this game. It's incredibly fair with progression and there is no true failure - if you fall in the fog, you rise anew, ready to ball.A "main levels" playthrough is a under three hours, but it belies additional optional levels, a snow world added post-release, and unlockable and content. The variety of objects and how Crumble sticks to them mean there's a wealth to learn and will have you head-scratching how everyone got those fast times.A controller is recommended by the game, but it's completely optional. Admittedly my keyboard switches started popping off because I was holding W for so long on certain sections.I was one of the people who showcased Crumble's earliest builds, back in 2020 when it was known under its codename, "Brumcle". It's made me really sentimental about how far it has come from where it started.BUY THIS GAME!

Our bodies are given life from the midst of nothingness. Existing where there is nothing is the meaning of the phrase, "form is emptiness." That all things are provided for by nothingness is the meaning of the phrase, "Emptiness is form." One should not think that these are two separate things.------So I was a huge fan of the original Samurai Gunn, it was in many ways the ultimate party game. Easy to pick up, difficult to master, all in the reflexes, coming back from behind to become the champ, playing dead, the original had a lot to love about it. Sometimes a sequel takes things too far (cough cough, Spelunky 2) but I really dig the balance they've struck on this sequel. It's a little content light, in that there are many fewer maps than the original (I say one day after launch), and the adventure mode runs out of road pretty quick too, but what is here is super solid, a perfect foundation to build toward a 10/10 1.0 release. Level hazards are largely removed, the Spelunky map can give you infinite procedural maps, and I think the different character abilities are well balanced. I loved that in the original, every character was identical, only skill separated players. Well, it's still that way, except the different character abilities mix things up just enough to keep fights feeling fresh. Losing against cleaver man? Switch to another weapon and punish their long windup, slow recovery and momentum. Honestly it's very exciting to see a game I love and adore given the long overdue update it deserves.

An unsettling and bitesized Slavic walking sim nightmare with "boy who cried wolf" themes. Exaggerated facial expressions, comically excessive bad language, and "pranks" of ever-escalating severity make the characters feel inhuman and the atmosphere utterly unhinged. It's somehow incredibly dark while maintaining an oddly humorous feel too. The cheerfulness with which animals and people are casually abused is very effective at making you feel uneasy and often the bullying and harassment in the foreground hides deeper abuse and neglect occurring offscreen. The most attentive adult in the game just posts cereal under your door each day; indifference is the best most of the characters can hope for and there's a sense that involving parents or teachers will just make everything worse if you could even make them care at all. The highlights for me were the two anxiety-inducing night-time walks - all you have to do is get from the school to your mother's house around the corner but both had more tension than most AAA horror I've played recently. It's less than an hour long but sometimes that's exactly what you need to get your uncanniness fix.

This game is, without a doubt, an absolute masterpiece. I’ve never felt compelled to leave a review for any video game before, but this one demands recognition. CAPTURED isn’t just another anomaly horror game, it’s a pulse pounding, nerve shredding anomaly horror experience that grips you from the very beginning. The realism of the graphics is almost unsettling; it’s as if you’re no longer playing a game but walking through a haunting, P.T.-inspired nightmare.The flashlight? Absolutely genius. I love the way it behaves as it makes the experience extremely immersive. Every door you open is a gamble. Will you find the anomaly, or will you encounter something…else? There’s a constant tension that keeps you on edge, never allowing you a moment of peace. Then there’s Nightmare Mode. It’s normal mode on steroids. It’s brutal, it’s relentless, and yet, you still find yourself playing.There are no complaints other than the wait for CAPTURED 2. 10/10, hands down, the best horror experience I’ve had in years.If you’ve made it this far through myreview and it seems familiar, you might be stuck in a loop. Samurai Warriors 5 has all the makings of a great game, but can't manage to stop shooting itself in the shoot, getting stunlocked and shooting itself in the foot again. The devs are lucky musou players go in expecting the comforting jank, boneheaded decisions, and mindless button mashing.The core game here really is fantastic. Beat up thousands of enemy soldiers, hunt down enemy generals, capture enemy bases to stop spawns, and deal with the ever changing situations of totally realistic historical combats. New to me, was Samurai Warriors unique troop types like "Drum Captains", "Supply Captains", and "Spy Captains" that have particular buffs or abilities that make even weak mobs matter. It's a nice new layer for me and despite minor complaints I enjoyed the core game loop as much as any other Musou game.But everything around this core is a stew of conflicting ideas that each undercut one another. For example, imagine a scoring system that rewards long combos. - Imagine 45 second long cutscenes that break your combo unless you juggle a dead body on your spear. - Imagine certain moves having animation delays that automatically miss that combo time.- Imagine getting an objective "Defeat 200 enemy" immediately AFTER you cleared out all the enemy in a zone so that you can only watch for two minutes while it fails.This constant conflicting design carries into the games two major game modes Musou (story) and Citadel (Grind-For-Upgrades). The idea is fine and it's worked in other games before... But the progression is so unbalanced that neither mode actually feels good. I've had to run 15-20 story missions to unlock the next battle in Citadel so that I can unlock a higher level weapon to make story missions feel better. But by the time I get my new citadel level...

I don’t think I like Akka Ahrr, but I do recommend it.I came into Llamasoft’s work as very much a twenty-first century American human slightly afraid to get spat upon by the beasties, but also enough of an animal lover and video game fan that I brought a towel. I started extremely intrigued by Christian Donlan’s Eurogamer review that compared Jeff Minter’s creativity style to an oil painting and gave Akka Ahrr five gold stars. Thus christening it Essential, I simply couldn’t ignore the entire Jeff Minter / Llamasoft journey.So I set out to undo my ignorance and start in 1982 with Digital Eclipses collection, Llamasoft: The Jeff Minter Story. Boy, has it been an enjoyable education, even if all of the games aren’t my jam. Thus, the journey is very recommended: especially pairing both Akka Ahrr and the Jeff Minter Story as a complete experience.I should say what works and doesn’t work for Akka Ahrr before I sign off. My favorite thing is when I get perfect clarity: know what I need to do and that execution is the only gap needed to cross. Akka Ahrr constantly divides you between an assortment of priorities where the joy comes from discerning the order of importance correctly. With time, I could develop this skill, have my enemy particles driven before me and hear the lamentations of their fragmented pixels. Unfortunately my motivation just isn’t high enough to do so. For the ones who that perfectly scratches their brain itch, I see how it lights up like rainbow gold.So again, not for me; but I recommend the ride.

Ginseng Hero is a short one shot game where your main goal is to gather tea to cure your loved one's sickness. The story is simple and silly but gets a pass as the exploration is the main priority of this game. The one shot aspect comes in the form of having only one life to complete everything needed to win the game, each death resetting your character all the way from the start. It's interesting playing this game now as it feels like a very early rendition of the rougelite genre that is all so popular currently in gaming. Although you aren't gaining anything physical whenever you die, what you gain is knowledge on how to tackle certain enemies and where specific items are. Certain areas on a first visit will seem daunting and absurdly hard, instantly overwhelming you and leading to your death, however this game has been designed with an open nature in mind so they're multiple pathways to take for you to experiment on what route you want to finally settle on. You'll start to realize certain enemies have little weaknesses you can take advantage of and one path might be better than another. It all culminates into your final run where you put all the pieces of the puzzle together and flawlessly execute your run and complete the challenge. That main loop is what keeps you going, along with the beautifully crafted world. This game's art style oozes creativity and every scene is perfectly realized, partially due to the fixed camera angles. Each new environment is a treat to explore and experience and it's always fun to see how the developers transformed this tiny insect world into something that could be explorable. I can't believe the ratings for this game. This is a really great game! And that's coming from a beat-em-up expert. I've been playing beat-em-ups since Double Dragon I for NES. I have every major beat-em-up released on Steam (that I know of, suggest them if I'm missing any important ones). People seem to be fixating on the lack of Options and deadpanning the game because of it. Would it have been nice to have the option to change resolution, controls, and audio? Yes, of course. Is it a flaw in the game that they are missing? Yes, of course. Does it ruin this otherwise excellent beat-em-up? No, of course not! This game is super fun, well-balanced, has some of the best (if not THE best) artwork I've ever seen in this type of game, and it avoids all of the most annoying pitfalls that beat-em-ups typically suffer from. Let me give you some examples. You know what this game doesn't do? This game doesn't do player stun-locks, it doesn't let you get hit from enemies off screen, it almost never gives enemies invincible frames in their attacks, it doesn't make bosses into bullet sponges, it doesn't make levels last so long you start wishing they'd just be over. The combat system is well designed, giving both playable characters their own unique feel and move set and making both equally fun to play with. My girlfriend and I were able to casually play through Act I and II and part of III on medium difficulty in just around 3 hours. One level we had to retry a couple times, and several we only scraped by with a little health, telling us that the difficulty level was extremely well balanced. A small package that pleasantly surprised me. Lithium City mixes high octane action with a 3D isometric view, set in a cyberpunk style world with a modest variety in mood and tone of the environment throughout the game. What strikes me as a pleasant surprise is how creative and artistic this game gets overtime. Being only 2 hours long, Lithium City managed to use its presentation as a strength without dragging it out longer than it has to. Each level has a core concept, gimmick, and gameplay intensity curve that got smoothed out very well, from a fight in a cramped train to a floor-by-floor battle to climb a beautiful skyscraper, the whole 2 hour session felt fresh and exciting all the way through. Designs in weapons and enemies also get better. Starting with generic bad guys in suits carrying pistols, when you start to think the enemies are predictable, the game introduces literal fencer and javelin thrower glass mannequins that will mess you up. And weapons that start off with the generics, like pistols, shotguns and grenades, and later you get introduced to more interesting ones like sharp throwing disks that bounce off walls and enemies - utilizing the isometric nature of the game as its strength as a weapon, it’s brilliant.The combat in Lithium City in itself isn’t something to write home about. It gets the job done. The main protagonist has a substantial health pool to tank hits more than most other games in this genre. She also has regenerating health to help her in prolonged fights, and makes the game feel less like a trial-and-error. But not to be mistaken, you still die really fast. So, think fast and kill them before they kill you.Something I always unexpectedly get impressed by games is the soundtracks. Music

You play a little potato guy who for some reason enters the arena without any weapons. That's OK there will be something in the arena to help you out. It's unique! Like floor spikes or a spike ball and your goal is to knock all the enemies into whatever you got. The starting trap is randomized which can be a little annoying if you have a favorite but the rounds only last three to five minutes so I end up playing it out anyway.Lost Potato turns into a combat puzzle. Trying to stay out of harm's way but line up enemies to be destroyed on the traps. There are also many different ways to play. For example, if you end up with a lot of floor spikes many of the enemies will be destroyed on their own but you'll likely have to push a few them to their death. Which can be a little more dangerous. It's also more passive than playing with the ball shooter traps. Those will only hit an enemy if you hit the ball into them. The strategy changes to playing at more of a distance. I prefer to have a mix of traps since there are far too many situations where one is better than the other.While you start with only one trap you will be able to add more as you go. About every three levels you can choose an upgrade. They're completely random so sometimes you get a potato upgrade or trap upgrade and other times you get a new trap added to the arena. Managing the upgrade is important because selecting between them is a balancing act. More traps vs powering up the potato. I've tried waiting too deep into a run to get more traps, it was a terrible mistake.✅ Unique

It's very rare that I find a roguelike game truly scratches that "just one more run" itch, but Lost Potato truly gets there.Runs are fast, death is quick, and there's a surprising variance in strategies given the few options for items.

It all starts with an archeologist who becomes trapped inside a pyramid. He yells a few explicit cuss words and then starts exploring. He soon discovers a friendly scarab that starts following him around… Plot’s not important anyway. Because of the sparse colors, the game's graphics are reminiscent of an old Commodore or Spectrum. It's a fascinating idea. The source of light is the torch held by the main character. Around the hero, a small circle with increasingly diminishing vision displays how far the light can travel. It almost appears like a rainbow of colors.The torch can be tossed to light the path ahead or other torches mounted on pedestals. You won't lose it since the scarab will go after it, even if you throw it in a dangerous hole or forget it a few screens back.In your other hand, you have a second source of light, though it isn't as effective. Your trusty gun can fire single bullets or a full burst if you hold the button for a few seconds. Charging takes only a few seconds and is signaled by a flash and smoke emerging from the gun. Parts where you have to move forward without the torch while shooting little lights into the dark are both terrifying and incredible. The bullet flash barely lasts a second, but you can see something lurking in the shadows.The objective of the game is to proceed through each floor until you reach the top. Each floor features a respawn location in case you die, as well as keys that must be found in order to unlock the exit door. Mummies, bats, and other things stand in your way, all of which may be easily dispatched with your gun. The best thing about them is that they explode in a gruesome blast

At heart, Lulu's Temple is a basic platformer - run through a pyramid, collecting keys to unlock doors while avoiding monsters and traps. The central gimmick is light and the lack thereof. The player carries a torch and can light torches in the pyramid for more light, but it will never be enough - use only that light, and you will blunder into hazards in the dark. Fortunately, your little explorer can hurl his torch ahead to light the path before him, and he even has a little scarab helper to fetch it for him.Mastering the torch is key to finishing Lulu's Temple. Aside from flinging the torch to ignite distant light sources, you'll also use it to trigger traps and solve certain puzzles. But being apart from your torch carries risks - some monsters will exploit your vulnerability and only attack you in the dark, while others can grab your dropped torch and run away with it.The most remarkable part about Lulu's Temple might be how creepy the game is, despite - maybe even because of - its MSX throwback graphics. The slightly dissonant music and sound effects are properly ominous, and the monster designs are properly weird. Whether it's the glow of red eyes in the darkness above you or the guttural battle cry of a giant scorpion bearing down on you, there are plenty of memorably spooky moments.

Punkcake offers yet another innovative little gem, full of game modes and challenges.Stray Shot focuses on managing counts of enemies both with accuracy or a deliberate lack thereof. Every time a shot hits a wall an enemy will spawn on the opposite side of the arena. The number of enemies present at one time determines the score they will generate upon death. So this leaves you with one question: Do I purposefully spawn enemies so each kill nets me more points, or do I methodically look to hit every shot and dwindle the enemy count down to something more manageable.The game offers 8 survival arenas with a variety of different enemy types and groupings, as well as various other modes (I've only tried the Contracts mode, where specific counts of certain enemy types spawn together, not matching the standard Arena groupings). If you enjoy the core gameplay mechanic there is a lot of bang for your buck with the custom game modes and various levels.

In Stray Shot you won’t be collecting points that are dropped from defeated enemies and enemies don’t have a fixed point value for being defeated. Instead, each Arena has 5 enemy ranks that indicate both their rarity (think common to legendary) and their multiplier.A blue enemy is the most common and worth N(1) points. N being the population of enemies in the arena. If that blue enemy is the only one in the arena it’s worth 1 point. If there are a hundred enemies in the arena that same enemy is now worth 100 points!With every shot you fire at the arena wall being converted into a new enemy, you’ll have to balance being super accurate while intentionally adding in enemies to keep the population high so you can score more points. Since you are both the person shooting, dodging, and adding enemies you’ll only have yourself to blame when the game over lights flash. Good Luck, you’ll need it

Asset flips are an insult to both PC gamers and to professional game developers who create genuine, high quality PC games. Anyway, Portal clone, that's fine, but then add the caveat, "when it works".Fullscreen or borderless fullscreen doesn't work, you can't access the menu in these display modes. Windowed mode is the only option, with glaring performance issues (RX 6800 and Ryzen 5900X), and obviously things like FreeSync or G-Sync won't work on those modes, so your spendy GPUs and monitors are useless. This probably is too early even for early access - I understand you can't build for every piece of hardware, but making sure your display modes work should be one of the very basic things you're looking to get right. Maybe get someone with other hardware to do more testing for you, a closed beta, something, anything.There's plenty of other Portal type games out there so you don't need a broken clone - for instance, Portal, Portal 2, Portal Reloaded, Lightmatter, QUBE and QUBE 2, The Turing Test, etc. etc.Then again, there's always room in my life for first person puzzle games - so even if there is a point where changing display settings doesn't break the game, maybe just don't let the first impression be that I'm playing a dollar store Portal.

Conflict Area is an abandoned Early Access asset-flip tier Unreal based PvP FPS, essentially a weak Counter-Strike ripoff. The focus seems to be on PvP (PvE is simply botmatching) which is unfortunate as SteamDB shows the game only collected 9 concurrent players at the very peak, which is a pitiful number not even enough to fill a server. It's impossible to play PvP now as there are no players (for obvious reasons). The game was abandoned roughly 6 months after launch and hasn't been updated in almost 2 years. There's no reliable indication the game will ever be completed, which is a reason for gamers to avoid this.The game looks deceptively decent thanks to Unreal, but I wouldn't be surprised if the game was entirely asset flipped. Unethically, the developer sold keys to this abandoned Early Access game into cheap, nasty game bundles, where they knew it would be advertised and sold as a complete game. This seems to have been done in an attempt to mislead gamers into buying a knowingly faulty, defective and incomplete product. When a developer does this for a game they have zero practical intention of completing, this is essentially a scam, an intention to get paid for a broken/unfinished product. Often this is done as an exit strategy, as the developer takes the money and runs. No refunds have been given, the developer kept all the money they took from gamers.Given CS:GO is free, and a complete game, and without the ethical problems associated with dumping incomplete trash into game bundles as a cash grab, it's impossible to recommend this failure.

I picked this up a while ago to play with a friend using Steam's Remote Play Together feature. We found the concept of the game to be amusing and appreciated it's visual style. After we got started, we were treated to a narrator doing a half-decent Morgan Freeman and a drill sergeant doing his best R. Lee Ermey.The way that plays is as follows: you'll first pick a mission, and then you're given the opportunity to purchase a number of uses of each of the characters you have unlocked. More powerful characters cost more of your mission budget. For instance, at the beginning of the game you only have access to the carrot character. For one of the first missions, you have enough mission budget to perhaps purchase three uses of the carrot character. You'll deploy with your first carrot and do as many of the mission objectives as you can before it is killed. Upon death, you'll spawn in as the second carrot you purchased. If you haven't completed the mission by the time your third carrot perishes, you'll fail. The second character I recall unlocking was the pea character. You can then alternate with your selections if you wish. For instance, first spawning in as a carrot, then a pea, then a carrot again.There are a few complicating factors here. First of all, you'll sometimes need to activate an ability that kills your character (usually creating an explosion) to progress in a level. This cuts down on how much leeway you have with your character lives in each level. However, in my experience, no matter what character you pick you're going to be relatively ineffective at dealing with the game's enemies. This means that you'll need to rely on stealth, and this system is not very good. Enemies

Visual Novels usually don't tend to leave much to talk about, doubly so when you get just a taste of the real deal. I can't say that really improves my overall opinion on Deep Lake Prologue, though.Primary problem persisting throughout and clouding my experience is a straightforward one - dubious translation. This happens to be a big deal in a game so centered on the written word. Even more so when even I notice it and I'm no native English speaker as my other reviews clearly demonstrate. Game is inconsistent even when it comes to our protagonist's name which doesn't match the one given in Steam store's blurb. I'll call him Sally. Former forensic photographer and fan of horses finds himself manifesting a vague esoteric power and getting embroiled in meeting a stranger to whom he gives eggs marked with runes. This idea of mysteries forces at play ended up being WAY more interesting than a random ghost girl and figuring out why staying at the local mansion might be the best way to stay alive as said girl is after him now.Prologue did not hook me and this does appear to be a very linear VN with no choices on display. At least none that were demonstrated in this brief offering. Game does have dense and foreboding atmosphere I'll give it that, but it's totally on-rails with no branching dialogs or points of interest to explore so what you see is what you get. Pretty nice visuals help on the presentation side. I would suggest reviewing and revising the translated script to tighten up peculiar word choices and straight up errors.

In both sound & vision this game is superb, with writing that seemingly has taken to many people. However, there seems to be a common denominator between those people; their gaming history. For those with the childhood muscle memory of Silent Hill 2/3, or nostalgia for Neon Genesis Evangelion, this game is a love letter. But for those of us who discovered SH2 and Eva later in their lives, or never at all, the homage feels more like fanaticism than love.The gameplay is infuriating; with the repetitive screech of the main enemy type dulling the horrific atmosphere, and retro qualities like the limited inventory stalling the pacing. Its hard to engage with such an unconventional plot when the medium is so hard to parse without nostalgia for PS1 horror. (Even considering the settings in gameplay to bandaid this problem).Regardless of the gameplay, I can only praise the visuals and story for their quality of homage. Again, suffering from the intent to serve a particular audience who hunger for more of their favourite properties. As someone who appreciates Eva, SH, and the King in Yellow, I can enjoy these qualities; but other than that I don't get much more out of Signalis than I did those original works. Really, I must reccomend those original works to those who have not enjoyed them, and can ONLY reccomend Signalis to those who not only love but are in-love-with Silent Hill.

They scream They scream loudly, and they respawn. To the point that when I looked up how people recommend you play the game to manage the enemies, the advised method is that you don't. Just run past them.What?By the time anyone sees this review, you'll probably have already seen other people describe the inventory system, or the backtracking, or how cluttered everything is. Those are real problems, but honestly, I could have dealt with them. It's the enemies that make everything painful. Backtracking on its own isn't fun, but it becomes tedious as hell when I need to listen to the incredibly loud screeching of enemies that you can just walk past. I want to enjoy this game. I like the idea behind the sword/bow mechanics, and I like the artstyle.But the enemy design simply does not support what the combat is apparently supposed to be. You're expected to fire off 5 arrows in quick succession, and then dive in with the sword to "reload"--but enemies are slightly faster than you, so it's not possible to kite them in any meaningful way. Instead of weaving in and out of melee, I find myself simply being trapped in melee whether I like it or not. The dash is supposed to help, but--since enemies outspeed me, and my dash has a cooldown--I find myself simply not bothering with it, as it doesn't keep me out of trouble for more than a second at a time, and most foes simply close the gap again.On top of that, many enemies have projectiles or dashes on top of a high base movement speed--which leads to me eating 1-3 points of damage when I inevitably enter a room with only my sword. Energy is limited, as well--and it's an incredibly valuable resource, because it's the only reliable way to recover from the seemingly mandatory damage that I take in every combat. It would be one thing if I could reliably *avoid* damage using Traps and Arrows, but traps just feel like a waste of space, because enemies are simultaneously too fast to safely kite into a trap and too tunnel-visioned for me to hope for them to wander into one. Arrow effectiveness varies wildly, too--the Shadow Arrow has an impressive amount of crowd control and damage, but the Poison Arrow isn't worth the energy cost because it just doesn't kill fast enough.So, I am left with an experience that simply doesn't feel right. NEON STRUCT: Carrion Carrier is a demo/quick game developed in a very short space of time for a game jam. It's a very simple cut down ripoff of games like Mirror's Edge as you do basic third person platforming to beat the clock on a series of deliveries while running through esoteric, low poly minimalist environments.Because the game was slapped together in a game jam instead of developed as a serious product intended for gamers, a lot of corners have been cut. Game jams are fine and well for evangelising game development and trying to convince people game development isn't a job but a hobby, but the products produced in game jams obviously aren't of the same high standard as professionally developed games intended for gamers. While this looks pretty good for a game jam demo (at least it has 3D graphics), the minimalist/low poly "art" makes this look like a reject from 2003 rather than a contemporary video game. There's not a lot of depth to the game, either. If you're looking for a parkour/3D runner game I suggest looking at the excellent Mirror's Edge series. The problem with game jam games is that they're typical of the effort that's put in. If this was an aircraft, would you want to ride in the plane that was designed over a period of years by teams of professional aeronautical engineers, or the plane that was built in a weekend by a guy in his backyard out of old nails and bits of wood, just to prove it can be done?Yeah, not many people are climbing aboard the airplane-jam plane. At least they've made this free and aren't trying to make this into a cash grab.

This is a game where the environment and attention to detail through graphics comes first and game design comes at a much significantly less priority. The creepy ambiance and atmosphere is there. However, as the player progresses in this game there is a lack of developing horror through theatrical game design. There are no cut scenes, no jump scares, and no immediate fear inducing consequences. It is run, swing, and gun away in dark creepy rooms. The boss fights are acceptable but not compelling or outstanding. There was a lot of room for improvement there.The biggest issue is the player is left with too much control and not enough threat. This is where this game falls flat. Great horror games do not rely on good graphics. They rely on designed delivery and control against the player. In this game there are times the player will be left backtracking in previous rooms or an entire level because they missed a plot advancing item or have no idea what to do next. All because of bad item placement or poor game design in luring the player. These flaws alone are immersion breaking and completely ruins the horror element.Recommend to get this game on discount.

What could have been a sharp, satirical romp ends up an exercise in tedium, bogged down by too much Hitler and far too little of anything resembling the "sex" the title implies.The Premise: Bold but MisguidedAt its core, Sex with Hitler presents a premise so absurd it might have worked in the hands of skilled satirists. The title suggests a game that could explore dark humor, absurdist romance, or even a biting critique of historical narratives. Instead, what players receive is a game unsure of its identity, lurching between gritty depictions of wartime atrocities and clumsy attempts at risqué interactions. The narrative fails to establish a consistent tone, making it difficult to discern whether the developers intended parody, provocation, or something entirely different. What could have been a sharply irreverent take on history ends up a confused mishmash that tries to do too much and accomplishes very little.Gameplay: A Tedious March Through the PastThe gameplay in Sex with Hitler is perhaps its most glaring misstep. For a game ostensibly about intimacy or relationships with a historical figure, the majority of the experience revolves around repetitive, uninspired wartime missions. The game is fun, and there's a good variety of songs available within the base game and through 3rd party sources. These are qualities I'd say are key to any rhythm game, especially ones that a player might expect to play for hundreds or thousands of hours.However, I feel the health system needs to be changed. Other rhythm games heal you for hitting a note but damage you when you miss. This game chooses to not heal you when hitting a note, instead choosing to give a flat heal that heals you very slowly over time. Essentially, the only feasible way to regain health is to 'not miss' for an extended period of time.The problem with this is that as you start upping the difficulty, the rate at which you can lose health vastly outpaces the rate at which you can regain health. This flat heal is balanced at the lower stages of the game, but becomes increasingly punishing as difficulty increases - something you will no doubt become painfully aware of when starting to play customs, where patterns become more dense and difficult to read. When describing the health systems in other rhythm games, they can normally be described as "punishing but fair". If you take your hands of the keyboard or controller for 2 seconds or less, death is almost certain. But as long as you can perform 'well', your chances of surviving the song are greatly increased. The health system in this game, however, can only be described as "punishing". No matter how well you're playing, missing one note will take a chunk out of your health that will take a very long time to recover. In the time taken to recover that health you lost from missing a single note, you've likely missed another note. Rinse

It's not a satire, they're trying to be serious, so hopefully CW will step in and legally annihilate these guys. VD Games, by the way, are your usual typical Russian asset flipper with all the toxic and unethical behaviour you'd expect. Which of course results in disastrous, unplayable asset flip trash like this. It has no value or merit as a real game.Taking this shovelware seriously as if it was a genuine attempt to make a game, it doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The mismatched game assets are fairly mediocre/low quality, it's a wonder why they couldn't be bothered "borrowing" higher quality assets for this asset flip. This is a lot like going on a shoplifting spree but only stealing the cut price store brand goods. Regardless, the poor quality assets alone should be enough to deter gamers from bothering with this.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.The poor quality of this game is reflected by how many people spent time with it.

TLDR: Generally speaking, I don't think this is a $60 game.The singleplayer aspect game is just a walk-through of the main story in Jujutsu Kaisen, specifically season 1 and the movie Jujutsu Kaisen 0. There are combat sequences included, but unless you're going for their extra challenges for all the loot, (which are useless cosmetics that aren't even particularly appealing) every single level is a piece of cake and almost not enjoyable to even play. There's also the case of some of the challenges being very unnecessarily difficult, or mistranslated from the Japanese so it's ambiguous. Pretty disappointing all around since there's practically 0 original content (other than a couple of useless extra comedy comics only a few panels long that a monkey could write.)The multiplayer aspect of this game is not competitive in the slightest, nor particularly fun to play. While it is fun to explore the unique powersets of the characters (because the writing in the show itself is interesting), actually using those abilities against curses and other players is not particularly enjoyable. The speed of combat is especially slow, so your actions can't match the pace of the decision making and intensity involved in 'realistic' anime combat.This doesn't mean the game is absolutely worthless. It has a few positive qualities. Playing through the singleplayer as a revisit to the first season if it's been a while since you've consumed Jujutsu Kaisen might actually be enjoyable. As well as playing this game with your friends LOCALLY just for fun, or to use it as a way to introduce your friend to the series.However,All in all the game isn't worth $60. It's carried by the IP. I wouldn't recommend buying this unless they put it on sale for $30 or less.

I think this game is so close to being a very good and fun VR game. There's unfortunately, a few things that are holding it back. It has some nice visuals but then a lot suffers on the gameplay side I think, here's a list of some issues.- the game is overly precise with the grabbing mechanics. You'll often find your hands failing to grab and just phasing through objects. This makes playing the game quite frustrating as you'll lose runs to what feels like literal bugs. Imo the grabbing should be much more generous and assisted. Something as a big sphere radius around your hands where it coming in contact with anything while holding grab, SHOULD grab.- It's super easy to miss-judge the amount of velocity you'll get from any given swing, but the swinging also feels a bit inconsistent in this regard, you may be intending to go a certain direction but will end up going in a completely different trajectory and just fall out. Going off purely from the swing angle the player gives is too precise imo and the game should probably have some subtle aim assist in the background assisting you, like pushing you a bit towards where you're looking.- There's an air grab ability... Only problem: you get it 10 worlds into the game. The air grab ability should be a default, available from the start. it makes the game so much more enjoyable as you can course correct or save yourself from the tiniest mistakes that would normally cost you your life. For some reason the game waits 10 worlds of incredibly hard and hell map-ish level design to give you the ability to essentially do an air recovery. Yes this ability would make the game easier, but difficulty doesn't equal fun imo.

Ghost Stories 2 is an asset flip, or what Valve calls a "Fake Game". The "developer" paid for/pirated someone else's Unity house/manor asset and used it to make a short, simple FPS adventure of extremely low quality. At no point did the "developer" of this train wreck properly credit the developers who assets they used/stole. Taking this shovelware seriously as if it was a genuine attempt to make a game, it doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings. There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.The poor quality of this game is reflected in the general public reception. At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 6 players, and they were some of the accounts the developer used for the fake reviews, idling the game to get enough time to dump the paid reviews.This game features a number of fake positive reviews from accounts known to be in the business of review manipulation/paid reviews. They're all written in either Russian or broken English, appear at almost exactly the same time, very shortly after the game launched on Steam, all have a direct Steam purchase of the game, and the accounts are used consistently to write fake reviews for asset flips and other cash grabs/scams. With no where to go you head anywhere where food, water, and shelter is located. Since this all takes place after a nuclear holocaust there's no one around creating a sense of isolation as you jump at every small sound and wonder if something is stalking you.The developers did a great job creating that sense of seclusion but this excitement is quickly overshadowed by tedious collecting. You have to collect supplies to maintain your hunger, thirst, radiation levels, and regulate heat but since most food and water is radiated you'll have to scan everything before it can be used for use or in crafting. The problems surface when you're given little direction of where these key items are located and the constant need to rebuild your camp.The opening level provides arrows to give you direction but once gone you start to notice how poorly things are telegraphed. For example you're told to find the keys to a locked door but given no idea where they are or where to begin your search. This goes for blankets, wood, matches, and so many things that you'll wander around in circles just hoping this this specific wood pile is what you need all while your survival gauges continue to drain. You can make the argument that this is a survival game so locating items in random locations is part of the experience. But when you spend 1 hour looking for blankets for another camp because your character decided to abandon perfectly good supplies at a previous camp

The original Star Fox 64 is perhaps one of my most played games of all time, and it remains one of the best games I've ever had the pleasure of playing even to this day when I return to it on occasion. This game, on the other hand, isn't particularly good, owing to the numerous copycat references to the Star Fox team. The game play is good, decent, and plays well. However, because it feels like a blatant rip rather than a real respect to the game it is trying to recreate in a different way, it fails to impress and instead irritates me especially Kiro. Terrible rip of Starfox 64 would have been pretty solid if it had played the role of a game paying homage to the past while attempting to be more original to itself with the characters and phrases utilized.

I know this was made with a much shorter budget, so I *really* want to cut the game some slack, especially given that the game isn't expensive. The length is what I would expect from the price. It does have a small replayability factor if you're looking to take on higher difficulties and trying for higher scores. I feel like you can make a homage to Star Fox without using such poorly written dialogue. I'm not asking for a complex story, I just don't feel like any of the characters have their own identities. That's just a personal gripe, I don't think that will make it or break it for everyone. I understand it's a nitpick at the end of the day. Despite this nitpick I DO find the character portrait art to be very cute and expressive.The controls are responsive and snappy, however certain sections make it a tad bit difficult to tell the depth on certain things. For example, the fight with the BF-Worm isn't hard, but it can be tedious if you're trying to do a no damage run to optimize your scores. I'm not sure I can personally recommend this game to other people who enjoy things like rail-shooters and star fox. I see they have another game in the works. I will definitely check that out when it does release. I hope it can deliver more of what I wanted when it does come out. I still think if you're looking for a small game to scratch the star fox itch, this is ok and inoffensive. It just wasn't all that for me.

Not recommended at full price unless you really, seriously like Sherlock Holmes or the eponymous franchise. This is the first truly open-world instalment in the Sherlock Holmes series, and expands upon the successful prequels by adding new gameplay features, side quests, and a greater variety of characters and locations.I'll start off by saying that the world is absolutely gorgeous: the graphics are great, the engine is well-optimized, and being set in a British-occupied fictional island that was formerly part of the Ottoman Empire, there are a wide variety of different locations to explore and people to talk to, each with their own unique cultural background and flavour. This makes the world feel much more alive and real than any other in the franchise to date.There are many minor changes in the way investigations are conducted in this game, but perhaps the most stark departure from previous games in the franchise is the fact that almost all cases (bar two, from memory) have no objectively correct conclusions to arrive at - while clues, case notes and deductions function similarly to how they always have done in this franchise, Chapter One removes any semblance of concrete confirmation as to whether you'd done anything right during the investigation at all. The devs attempted to explain this away as Sherlock's relative inexperience during the time period in which the game is set, but if you're like me and want a definitive answer as to whether or not you made the correct deduction then you'll only view this as an irritating design choice.The combat is terrible - combat sequences only serve to break up the monotony of running around and interacting with crime scenes and suspects, as it's awfully implemented, repetitive, unintuitive, and quite frankly feels like an afterthought rather than a facet of gameplay.

"A deviously simple puzzle game"---This game is about dropping down spheres onto matching spheres to make bigger spheres, but that description is a little unfair. The challenge to the game is optimising the limited space you have, and avoiding creating partitions that might frustrate your efforts to make the matching spheres join, especially the large ones. Also, the spheres have physics, which always seem to be active.There are a couple of issues with this:- the game fundamentally doesn't have enough going on for you to exploit. You can try dropping smaller spheres towards the side, bunching together larger ones but not really much more as far as I can tell. Unlike the spheres in the game, the one in your head will not grow from playing this- there's a strong element of randomness. Sometimes you pop a sphere and a bunch of things will just fly off the top of the screen. Sometimes the spheres will shift around for a very long time without interaction, and the optimal thing will be to wait a while and see what happensOn the plus side, RoRo/Lola is the best, and there are a bunch of her songs in the game at a relatively low price. On the other hand, you start with one song and one instrumental, and you have to unlock the rest by playing the game. Also, realistically, opening a game to listen to a song is inconvenient and you probably aren't going to do that.

Forgive the assertion, but I feel Sonar Shock is a good example of what happens when you enjoy something, and have been inspired by it, but you haven't learned *why* it exists the way it does. System Shock 1 is a product of its time that is really only well-accepted in the modern age thanks to mods and hardware improvements, and the cursor-led world interactions style the dev lovingly re-styled for this is entirely because of what Looking Glass had to work with. Nothing wrong with doing this on modern hardware, but you need to understand what the control systems and UI are actually doing in order to recreate those well. For a start, in SS1 you had full movement control to an often boggling extent. You can change how far you're leaning, interrupt and reset it, crawl (and somehow use the jetboots), climb up certain wall tiles and drag things from the world into your inventory in a really organic way. You can even aim wherever you want since you're controlling the mouse cursor, not your viewpoint! In Sonar Shock, you cannot strafe, nor look up or down. You can move crates in the world around, but it isn't all that intuitive at first. The UI leaves a lot from what made SS1's usable behind- 8x8 pixel sprites are meaningless compared to a single word at the bottom of the screen telling me what section of the UI it activates, and having to wait for each panel to appear for some reason would inevitably get on my nerves and make me hate playing the game if I allowed myself to

Sonar shock takes a of inspiration from the original 1994 System Shock, without taking any consideration as to what made the UI semi-bearable for the average player, and genuinely enjoyable for the people like me, but hidden behind the needlessly wonky movement and optimization is an admittedly fun experience that combines System Shock 2's roleplaying mechanics with old DoS game shooting mechanics.Take the movement and aiming, for example. In the original DoS System Shock, you could move in any direction, crouch, jump, and toggle between mouselook or cursor for interaction and combat. In Sonar Shock, you only get to move forward and backward, turn around with A and D, crouch, and cursor only for interacting, and that's literally it. Combat becomes insufferable because of this. For example, when trying to poke out at an enemy to avoid being shot at, you have to go across your cover, turn towards the enemy, look at the enemy, turn towards the cover again, and hope you don't get shot as you spend 75% of the time trying to actually position yourself because of bare-boned movement. Compared to System Shock, you could easily go in and out of cover, and even shoot while behind cover thanks to the option to fire where your cursor is, without even needing to expose yourself.There are a couple other things that otherwise make the game unnecessarily frustrating: lack of health gauge, and saving. For the health, there is next to no way to gauge it reliably. The best there is is "Critical" text when you're at low health, a item that shows your current and max health on using it, and one of four passives that can be picked upon creation. Outside of that, you're out of luck if you actually want a gauge of how much HP

These mechanics felt clunky, largely due to the game's awkward movement system.The story, on the other hand, felt like fragmented pieces of insanity that never came together in a meaningful way. By the end, I had no real understanding of who the characters were, what my objectives had been, or what I had achieved. Much of the dialogue came across as nonsensical, a jumbled mess of words that seemed to lack purpose or coherence.While there are games where a sense of disorientation can enhance the experience, this one fell short for me. The zany and stimulating visuals did add some charm, but they weren’t enough to compensate for the lackluster gameplay or the disjointed narrative. Ultimately, the gameplay wasn’t engaging enough to make the experience enjoyable, and the story wasn’t compelling enough to justify the effort.

This isn't a bad game by any means, and there's a good chance you might enjoy it, but I do think it has some serious problems that will be very frustrating to a lot of players. The biggest issue is just a basic design decision around difficulty and enemy damage. Simply put, it's just impossible to avoid getting hit in this game. By the halfway point, pretty much every encounter will have a moment or two where the screen is just *so* full of projectiles and the action is *so* busy that you're going to take some damage. The game is obviously designed this way, because by the end you can take at least a dozen or so hits before dying; in other words, it's balanced towards "You'll get hit a lot, but you have a lot of health" as opposed to "you can avoid getting hit at all, but if you are hit, it'll really hurt you." I found this extremely unsatisfying - it rewards a sort of tank-y approach where you just run in, take the hits, and heal afterwards that felt really at odds with the finesse and agility that traditional bullet hells rely on. I think it would have been much better to reduce the number of enemies and projectiles, but make them really count. Otherwise, there isn't a ton of variety in your attacks and all of the weapons end up feeling the same. There are tons of them, but much like the enemy attacks, it feels very "quantity over quality" in its approach. There are also some major difficulty spikes and issues with how the world is navigated - I ended up missing two entire sections until the very end, which meant the ones I did beforehand were harder than they should have been

The 'riddles' that the game throws at you can be solved within seconds, and the large body of gameplay involves running back and forth through dimly lit corridors, which - after 15 minutes of doing so - becomes monotonous rather than unnerving.There are upsides, namely:Otherwise, it's way too short and doesn't do anything particularly interesting when it comes to gameplay. If the puzzles had been more thought out, they might have warranted a playthrough, but the retro stylings aren't enough to hold this game up by itself, and that's sadly pretty much all this game has.3/10

This level of quality for the amount of people who worked on it is unacceptably bad. Just as a short list of issues:- Optimisation is absolutely horrific. I don't know if this was bugged or intended, but it meant I could blast down everything without a thought.- Enemies killed stay dead when you respawn, removing any need to take care at all. I don't think most of the reviews try to answer the question: Is LEAP a good game? is it fun to play? That question is what makes me wish Steam had a mixed review option, especially for early access games such as LEAP where the gameplay is actually really fun, but it's riddled with a lot of very valid issues. So, I'm going to be giving this game a negative review, but in the hopes that LEAP gets some very well needed and loving developer support. To quickly summarize the pros for you, the movement in this game is stellar. Graphics are pretty astounding honestly. Gunplay, abilities, and TTK feel different from most other shooters in a way that makes gunfights feel a lot more involved mechanically. The quality of a lot of the gameplay elements feels better than most AAA shooters.However, LEAP has too many current issues that I think stem a lot from releasing too early. While the same could be said for several of Nuk Games' other titles, those also don't make the same claims at being innovative as this one. As both me and my co-op partner dig top-down shooters, we thought this one was worth trying for the cost of "free." Unfortunately, we didn't come away with a positive impression. First off, as other reviewers have noted, the game is very dark. Often, I wouldn't even know that an enemy was near me until I began seeing the little white bite symbol over the top of my character, indicating that I'm already taking damage. On the flip side, this does increase pressure on the player to travel using the main roads, which are illuminated slightly better. It's interesting to feel this pressure through the gameplay, although I'm not entirely convinced that main roads would be safer than side paths in a zombie apocalypse.We found the design of the city to be pretty lackluster, and felt that the procedural generation stripped it of personality. Although we killed the first three bosses, two of the three had the same subtitle (Taste Tester). It was a funny joke the first time...The bosses themselves run around wildly and stop in strange places and corners.However, the biggest issue with the title is likely the pacing. With a lot of zombie-focused games, you'll have an involved defensive or offensive segment and then a slower-paced moment or two to "catch your breath." With , it's just "all go, all the time." When we did die on our run, I think this pacing issue contributed to our reluctance to try another.

I don't think I've ever been more disappointed in a game. Superliminal starts off really promising and then just peters out and keeps going for about an hour. It's one of the few times I really have to point to the devs and ask, "Was this really the best you could do?" The engine is, frankly, bad ass and I want to be clear: the game and its tech is really cool. I originally thought I might dislike it because it's a faintly pathetic Portal rip-off, the latter half of the game relying on portal -based puzzles doing nothing to hide the influence, but it doesn't even manage that. It blatantly borrows some Portal themes and mechanics, but ends on some weak philosophical, "Now you've learned to look at something from every angle, you are better equipped to handle whatever life throws at you."That piece of wisdom does the game no favors because from a narrow point-of-view the game is quite good. The engine is solid and the first half of the game is rather promising, but from a wider angle it fails to capitalize on its own tech and never lives up to its initial premise. Something tells me it's shorter than the developers would've liked given it's inconsistent tone and somewhat sudden devolution into a walking simulator to wrap itself up. The last thirty or forty minutes contains a handful of fairly weak "puzzles" and relies mostly on illogical architecture to pad out your walk to the end. What a letdown. You think it's escalating towards something but it turns out the game already peaked. If you can get it on sale it's an interesting little tech demo, but it's also a thoroughly underwhelming experience.

game_name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden
review: If you want a nice, short RPG with classic and easy to understand systems, this is your game. Great story, fun characters, a world that, while not necessarily unique, gives you the feeling that it's lived it. I love card games. And while this is not a card game (except the side game you can play with friends locally), but rather a game that uses cards to tell its story. $30 USD is maybe a bit steep of a price, but this and the bundle (which I recommend getting if you like the demo for the first game) often go on sale on pretty much every system. While this one is my favorite of the three, they added an RNG mechanic to skills that people will like love or hate. That being said, this was my favorite story among the three with only one character needing more fleshing out, in my opinion.

review: I only tentatively give this a recommendation. Gameplay is fine and the new monster skill mechanic works fairly well, even if the way to obtain them could have been worked out better.The story feels like a much more personal one than a grand one like in the other voice of card games and it cuts off right as the story seems to really pick up speed. It feels like the first episode of a bigger story than a complete one on it's own.The cast is varied, but due to the skill system they don't differ much mechanically. There is some, but the story doesn't really have room for any major character development.I'd put this one a little below forsaken maiden, but not by much. It misses a lot of opportunities and backloads all the story twists and explanations and the story left me feeling more like a visitor in a grander world that I wouldn't get to fully explore. Also the mythical place of legend sure is easy to get to after you party has arrived there ;PI really wish the next game (if there is one) tackles the biggest issue of these games: the status effects. There is just too many of them and they are either too crippling or too inconsequential, the same goes for the item system, vast majority of the items are useless save for very niche situations and only serve to take up your limited item slots.Hey...maybe we could even stay in this same universe and play as a group of monsters next time and add random events to dungeons other than just monster battles, getting one on the overworld was always a breath of fresh air and broke up the tedium.

game_name: Voice of Cards: The Beasts of Burden
review: The Beasts of Burden is the third chapter in the recently released JRPG series Voice of Cards created by Yoko Taro (, ) in which everything is represented by cards. If you haven’t played the previous ones, and , then don’t worry ‘cause each title has a different setting and narrative, despite sharing the same structure. The game follows the story of the Guard, an unnamed girl (we can choose her name later on) living in an underground village that is suddenly threatened by monsters appearing from nowhere. After losing her family and being rescued by a stranger, the Guard leaves the underground in search of revenge, exploring a world that is new to her and in which she discovers the power of controlling monsters. As per Yoko Taro’s tradition, the plot is deeply existential as it investigates the intricate nature of humans and beasts. Storytelling is great thanks to an always present female narrator, who describes characters and events in a very immersive way. There are still few stereotypical parts that are common in most JRPGs (hero losing something, being rescued, meeting new allies and trying to reach a distant place), but the twists and quality of the dialogues are guaranteed by Taro’s unique art direction.While the world and characters are artistically represented by cards, this is not a deck and cards game. It’s a standard JRPG experience with turn-based combat, stats, skills, items and more. review: TLDR: A Touhou Project fangame with barely serviceable gameplay that falls apart once you understand how to break it, a usable cast that seems big on the surface, but only a handful are actually good, a story that is delivered cut and dry, with no sense of urgency, long term consequences, and filled with character assassinations. To top it all off, weird and questionable story elements.I used XUnity auto translator with the Sugoi offline model to translate the story and gameplay mechanics. While not perfect, it allowed me to understand what was going on in the story, items, spells, and equipment.With that out of the way, let's get into the thick of it, starting with the gameplay.It's a slightly different but still familiar take on a turn based RPG. Take a team of 5 ladies (or MC, Rinnosuke, Fortune Teller, they're in there too) Traverse a multi-staged labyrinth, find items, shops, and encounters on the map until you reach the boss stage. Random encounters can have a grid of up to 10 enemies, but the mast majority of the time it is 1-3 illusions that are easily taken care of. Some enemies have UFO's, making them stronger but also dropping that UFO for you to use. Shopkeepers vary, selling a mix of equipment, materials, skills, and gifts for you to use. Certain ones can be invited to join you as a guest, others have a special option that gives you temporary effects for the rest of the dungeon.The gameplay is bearable for the first few hours, but slowly becomes more and more of a chore, the only real change being in enemy levels. It's more A than I, as all they do is choose a random move. You can over level your party to the max story cap of 255

review: A Touhou Project fangame that presents itself as a strange mix of a visual novel and an RPG. Basically, Gensokyo's become a massive labyrinth. There's also weird clones of characters all over the place. You (as an OC), with the help of (among many other characters) Moriya Shrine-namesake Suwako Moriya, must figure out how it happened.Gameplay consists of two distinct modes. The first mode consists of lengthy VN-esque cutscenes where stuff happens. Sometimes you are asked to make a choice (usually in the context of "How do you respond?" to something another character is talking about), and those choices do affect the ultimate outcome of the story. The other distinct mode of the game are tower/dungeon sections, which play somewhat akin to a combo of Pokemon Mystery Dungeon and Touhou Labyrinth, with item pickups and interesting side events sprinkled throughout. The enemies can be seen, and making contact with them sends you into a battle. The battles do not use active time but a speed stat ("agility") does make a difference as to what order your party (and your opponent) fights in. At the end of each "dungeon" you usually fight a boss of some sort, which plays in much the same manner as the random battles - just more difficult.This game does have some mature elements. While this game isn't "Adults Only" and has no explicitly (visible) sexual content, it does have a theme around earthly desires (wealth and lust and all that) and has the odd section that stands out every now and then, depending on your in-game choices. That and the art, of course. So, it's effectively Japanese-only.- I did not enjoy the writing of any of the characters in the cutscenes, and felt that nothing they really said felt like it fit their character. I think at this point calling it "Neko-Ribi" is a meme because it doesn't actually play like Rabi-Ribi; there's no bullet hell or hitstun.The good:The so-so:The bad:

Rabi-Ribi aesthetics and gameplay loop with mostly Hollow Knight combat.It has some of its own ideas as well, such as character and enemy bounding boxes being a core mechanic of both combat and sometimes exploration. Some of the music is really nice, but sometimes is too short or doesn't loop well. There are a few very powerful and memorable tracks to accompany some of the best boss fights and impactful moments in the story, though my favorite was probably in the second Illusion zone and how well the music complimented the area's bleak atmosphere.The game seemed lacking in polish at times. This was felt most in the final zone, and I managed to cause a softlock in what seemed like an obvious oversight in level design (though I only lost maybe a couple minutes in progress due to frequent auto-saves.)The game has some pretty great boss fights, and higher difficulties will even change up some of their mechanics.The game isn't too long for a casual playthrough (13 hours for me on Normal, though I haven't sought out 100% yet.) The extra difficulty levels will add a lot of replayability if you want to master the harder bosses, and this is emphasized more by the post-game adding boss+difficulty selection as well as best record trackers for each.Overall great game and definitely worth a playthrough if you're a fan of the game's inspirations.

I said it at the start the review and I will say it again: this game is a good example why I love video games, a great storytelling medium.I was introduced to Thomas Brush artstyle through the other game of his, Pinstripe, and I really like the way this kind of art works. Simple, yet charming. The art in Neversong is an improvement compared to Pinstripe. The color, however, is a different and proper approach. In contrast to Pinstripe's cold, sombre blue, Neversong utilizes the warm color orange to signify the joy and innocence of childhood memories. The music in both games also does a job working in concert with their corresponding theme. While Pinstripe's OST has a smooth touch, like a winter breeze coursing through a snowy Northern village, Neversong's OST has a quick light tempo of various instructments, making the stages feels more lively,

Tl:dr This game has fantastic dialogue, colorful characters, a truly impactful choice-system and amazing writing.This game provides a truly engaging, action-filled and thought-provoking experience from the very start to the finish line. The characters are all very well fleshed-out even if they only appear for short periods of the game and all of them feel *real* which is impressive from a writing stand point no matter what.This game has a lot of dialogue seeing how it is a choice-based game, however what most choice-based games tend to fail at I find this game does amazingly, that is it doesn't hold your hand throughout the process, you are left to explore the world, notice hidden meanings and motives behind what people are saying and unlock choices by thinking outside the box rather than just following the set path. The dialogues themselves are truly well written, the interactions between characters feel real enough that you could easily see people out on the street having similar interactions, barring the more deadly and threatening ones of course. What really gripped me personally was that the choices you could make always had consequences whether small or big, but not only for you the player, the consequences affected the character and their life in a way most games fail to realize. A lot of the choices really had me questioning my own morality and doing my best to find a middleground between my own wants as a player as well as what I percieved would be the best for the characters themselves. Overall this was an amazing journey that gave me a lot of insight into myself and many hours of enjoyment, I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes choice-based games with heavy moral themes.

According to the developers, many players insist to game is too easy, and it seems a significant number are like me at find it too difficult at normal difficulty.Of course, there is a solution to this - add another difficulty level roughly half way between easy and normal. I understand the developers need to move on, so I'm not asking them to do this. But I do get tired of games where the hardcore players seem to dictate how a game evolves. Why should they care if an extra, slightly easier than normal difficulty is added. I will recommend this game because I did enjoy it on easy difficulty. I also enjoyed it on normal difficulty until I realised I was wasting my time.

Game is relatively simple once you get all the rule entries figured out, and for the most part, you unlock them by moving that respective piece a lot, or losing due to "cheating", because it doesn't move the way you think it does. From a strategy perspective: -Pawn has the biggest changes. You can't promote them, they move/capture similar to a rook but only 1 square at a time. This also implies that you can't "en passant" or move 2 squares/capture diagonally, and you'll want to advance them at least in a "buddy system", where you keep 2 or more close together, no longer forming diagonal rows for protection like in regular chess.-Knight behaves identically to regular chess, except it's severely less flexible due to how pawns move.-Rooks mustn't touch, lest they become a useless piece. Terranova is a charming desktop simulator, where you play an interactive narrative through the UI of a computer desktop. Set in the early 2000s, this game is very much a tribute to the roleplaying scene of Livejournal. When two IRL friends start an online roleplaying community on LimeJournal, they are joined by two additional online RP buddies. As the year progresses, both in and out of character, friendships will bloom...as will rivalries, drama, and of course romance (this is the RP scene of the early aughts after all!).The writing is definitely the centerpiece of the game, as the narrative, and all character development, is done through IMs and LJ posts. All the characters are nuanced and believable, as is the drama, which is in turns funny, heart-warming, frustrating, and gut-wrenching. The creators truly do a fantastic job recreating the joys and sorrows of the high school online experience from this time period. While the roleplaying isn't fully open-ended, the choices you make effect your ending, so take care to save at key moments. You will definitely want to get the good ending ;).

It is to download the patch from the publisher's (Kagura Games) website to access basically the entire game. Don't be like me. Don't waste 3.5 hours doing basically nothing.The meat of the game revolves around NTR (often translated as cuckolding). If getting the main character's girl taken from them is not your jam, only going for the 2 non-NTR endings will make the game a very short experience. If you can stomach it, however, you'll gain access to 6 distinct paths showing, Ryoka—your childhood friend who you plan on confessing your love to—being taken away from you. In addition to her, there's also her sister, Saki, who has a few of her own problems. I'm a weirdo, so I enjoy reading what feels like the "bad ending" of stories that rarely happens in popular media, while others seem to just get their souls crushed.The gameplay getting the stories through is pretty basic, largely just running from one screen to another trying to find Ryoka in order to overhear her, er, predicaments before actually seeing the scene from her perspective using her diary. This game could be good, but this just feels like an asset flipped, pre-alpha proof-of-concept . Most of it is shallow and undercooked, and needs a lot more content than what is currently offered to keep up with the superior games in the genre. Smaller titles like Greedland and Slaycation come to mind. The former is a much better example of horde survival, isometric shooter, in-game upgrades and meta progression grind. The latter is a much better example of incorporating tower defense seamlessly into the mix (read, turret buy-backs) and is overall an extremely polished, over the top fun experience with a ton of personality. The problem here is just that everything feels a little below average. And, as if to make it worse, it feels like the developers just hamstring your power and make you arbitrarily weak as a form of difficulty. You have a very limited stock of each turret, they're not mobile, you can't refund them or even recoup them into your stock. The primary weapons have a very small energy capacity, before they overheat and make you wait a good 2 seconds to recharge. So halfway into any game you're going to have your measely stock of 4 turrets already placed on the other side of the map and a gun that is constantly overheating and unable to be fired. THE TWO MAIN THINGS that you would buy this game for (tower defense and guns) have been prematurely nerfed into the ground. I don't know what it is about game devs that think withholding and/or drip feeding all the fun stuff is going to make the game challenging in a fun way. It doesn't in general, and it doesn't for this game in particular. Skip this one at any price. There are a number of titles
