PixelFade's VNs for a while now achieve absolute hights when it goes to production quality while struggling a bit when it goes to writing. Ethereal Enigma is basically a culmination of that trend, which means you'll likely either love it or hate it, depending on how much substance you want from your story and how much whimsical slice-of-life content can you stomach. For me, EE was ultimately more enjoyable than this studio's previous game, Crystalline, as it didn't try to be anything more than a straightforward waifu game, but it also has its share of issues. Erilynn, the princess from another world, is not a bad character, but her route is very hit-and-miss and lacks a strong theme. The whole story is theoretically about her being stranded in our world and trying to find her way back, but it's a really thin layer on top of fully-generic slice-of-life fluff – and some scenes with her are just awkward and fail to properly build up the romantic tension. The protagonist is the blankest of blank slates, which theoretically gives the player a lot of space to self-insert, but I wished he had something that made him stand out – Ace Academy, studio's debut title, reached a really good balance in this regard, as the lead there had a tragic backstory and a few quirks that defined him to a decent degree, while also leaving a lot of space for player agency. Here, there's simply nothing that makes the protagonist feel like an actual person. Also, there's barely any justification for the story being set in a Japanese high-school – it feels like if the developers were actively trying to make their game look generic and uninspired. And, as the last complaint, the sexual humour in this game is nearly universally awful

Dream Sketcher is an investigation game where you play as an investigator for the agency Dreamland Security. You can play as a single player, or you can play as part of a team with up to three other players. The Mad Dream Crisis has swept humanity where people get lost within their dreams and need help from exiting their dreams otherwise, they’ll be stuck within their weird dreams. Your job is to enter these dreams, investigate, solve puzzles and ultimately save the person stuck within their own head. There are six different stories currently, the first story, Into The Dreamland, is a small story which is a single player story and a tutorial as it will take you over the basics of the game. There are four stories which can be played with one to four players and the last story takes three to four players. Once you have decided which story you will have to create a Room. You do this by clicking on the story and then you can set a few options for the room. You can name the Room, add a Password, choose the Difficulty, number of Players, Act order and Operating Time Limit. Once decided selecting the Create Room button will start the game for you. An investigator will then be assigned for you to play as but you can choose to play as a different investigator. There are six different investigators, each will have different Attributes (Health, Strength, Wisdom, Sanity, Agility and Will), Abilities and Resources. There is also a web chart which shows you how good or not they are in Combat, Difficulty, Investigation, Survive and Support. You can also check out each of the investigators from the main game screen which shows them under Investigator on the left side of the screen.

I never write reviews, but this game was fun from the start and I want to support the dev. Stocking shelves and laying out your store is fun, and it's a pretty good feeling after a flood of customers empties you out and you see your wallet afterwards. Exploring the available region around your shop is nice, the scenery is quite pretty. Also, looting the random dead bodies around is a great way to make some quick cash early on to help stock your shelves and level up. Shooting thieves that steal from your shop with the bow is a little wonky, and the range is pretty awful but little things like that are certain to be fixed with time. Menus need a little work as far as scrolling and accessibility, but again, minor stuff.Overall I definitely recommend picking this up and supporting the dev, the game is very fun, especially if you're a current or former WoW fan, or simply *that* into customer service! =P

This game is a lot of fun and quite immersive but it suffers from a few pitfalls. In the beginning it is very hard to get started, just figuring out what to do is not all that intuitive, I had to rely on another reviewers comments to work out what to do. They've added an in-game tutorial (which is just a bunch of text and screenshots) which helps a bit but could definitely do with an overhaul.The second problem occurs once you actually figure out what to do - and that is the presence of thieves. When you are just beginning to sell things I feel that thieves should spawn a *lot* less often. I had 3 thieves in a row, and only had 3 items for sale, leaving my save-game in a state where I had no money to buy more products. You can shoot the thieves but I found the bow system quite difficult to use, and shutting the shop doors should trap thieves inside, giving you a chance to kill them (it doesn't, they just clip through the doors). Lastly, I would really appreciate the inclusion of multiple save slots, and a manual save button. From what I can determine there is only one save slot and you have to rely on a sometimes unpredictable auto-save system. All in all it's a solid game with massive potential to become amazing, I just hope it gets some more love from the devs. TL/DR: Buy it on sale. 6.5/10

The beautiful art style is accompanied by a growing feeling of sorrow and unease with each step you take towards the resolution of your story. Naughty or nice doesn't matter when you're a zombie. Santa's going to town tonight!Really like the game. Fun vibes, shooting, looting, upgrading and unlocking new skills.Each run has in-game progression: kill zombies, collect gems, and choose skill cards that'll upgrade various shooting mechanics. Each run awards coins which you then can spend on the skill tree to perma-unlock new skills and stat-upgrades for further runs.The upgrades and unlockable skills are really fun and complement each other pretty well. For example, base fire rate for the shotgun is pretty low, well, it's a shotgun. So upgrading fire rate in early runs makes sense. Earn coins and buy permanent fire rate stat upgrades on the meta skill tree to free up an in-game skill slot during the runs and use different skills. Your character is being burned at the stake for some heinous crime and you learn through episodic memory flashbacks what events led up to this point in your character's life. There are a lot of things to praise about AMR. The world building is quite good, offering tidbits about the land that you inhabit in small digestible bites. You get small flashes of information about your character's past through the occasional dream or idle musings that hint at some terrible trauma suffered which has kept you on the move for years. The characters you meet are are all compelling enough, each with their own aspirations and personality which is revealed to you over time.But I am not without criticism. Where AMR falls flat is almost entirely a result of how short it is. Though the world and characters have some interesting charm to them you never really get enough interaction with either. Several proper names are thrown at you throughout the story - noble houses, provinces within the kingdom, important events - but the vast majority of them serve only to sound important without any real context as to why.My biggest gripe by far is the lack of character development. Both the MC and the important NPCs you encounter have only a smattering of interactions with each other that offer the chance to learn much about them. While there are hints of depth, the episodic nature of the story coupled with its short length leaves most of them feeling shallow and tropey. I'm a huge fan of hardcore base building/turret defence games (They Are Billions, Age of Darkness: Final Stand and The Riftbreaker just to name a few). There is a lot of potential here with this game, but first off a few words for people who might not enjoy it:- It's early access. This immediately tells you features are missing. Just like the other games I have mentioned that also fit this genre, these games are built and designed to be difficult. Yes, losing all of your progress on a mission sucks! On top of that, the fact it's early access means you're for certain going to lose (if not on your first attempt at some point) because of balancing issues, possible bugs and just the general learning curve. With the features and mechanics in place at the moment (again, early access) economy is quite the drag. Paying for defences and upgrades is expensive. That's just where we are at the moment.- No multiplayer. Yet...All-in-all, the negative experiences of this game relate to the fact it's still being developed. Devs and players are learning and adjustments are happening. However, the game is very playable and I've not run into any noticeable bugs. So let's talk about the positives:- Polished and playable. For an early access game, this is a huge ticked box!

This game has been coming along nicely since my last review, which I've edited here;While many games do have a habit of not reaching their full potential, so I cannot recommend you purchase it yet, especially given the cost, I can easily see this being a refreshingly modern look at the older Zelda titles. Go Ichinose's songs are fantastic here (he's one of the pokemon composers). A good few songs have been added, but the game still need more of them.The combat is simple and easy, but thoughtful and something that can be approached either by amassing mountains of stats through the zen-garden style progression system, or by taking care to not get hit by larger threats. Currently, enemies are a bit too stupid to be a problem unless they're in packs, but that's at least some of the charm. You feel like a kid lost in the woods with an old game song stuck in your head, pretending to battle monsters and then getting in over your head, then going back home and building with lego or setting up a pillow fort. It's a cheerful, uplifting sort of gameplay loop that bounces around at your pace, and the combat is pretty time-tested to work well. Starting out, you have a dodge, a weak ranged attack, and a strong melee attack, but each can be tweaked and modified through placing furniture and monster-run storefronts on your floating island. Enemies don't do much damage, but you don't start with much HP. Absconding is always an option, though.If the game continues to get worked at and evolve, I think this will be a go-to for me for relaxing, simple gameplay.

At present, Crystarise consists of 5 minutes of gameplay stretched over 10 or so hours of grind. It doesn't evolve past gathering things and expanding the island.The main progress bottleneck for most players will be the Magenta enemies and their biomes. Reducing damage from cold and heat requires 40 levels of resistances per 1 damage, and the enemies require at least 100 combined levels of Sword Attack / Slayer to deal more than 1 damage to them. You can use DPS skills to take them down faster if you're too impatient to grind for the necessary stats, but expect to take at least a minute to kill them one by one. To see the Lava and Snow bosses will probably demand at least 8 hours of your time slowly killing Magenta enemies. If you're lucky with heart spawns and dungeons, it's possible to spend less time than I did.There's a very small range of island customization, consisting of a few palette changes for stores, and biome appearances for plants and rocks. It's possible to make it pretty even with the small item catalogue, but due to the time it takes to expand the island, especially during the Magenta grinding phase, it's very likely your island will consist of a random assortment of rocks, plants, and heart crystals. The "residents" are currently just another accessory for you to increase Enemy Slayer / Absorb levels via shops or walks.It's a very slow-burn game, and with its current content, it's about 4 times more expensive than it's worth. game_name: Kingdom of Atham: Crown of the Champions
review: If you are a fan of old school RPG games, and are looking for one with more elements of survival and crafting on top of the usual questing and exploration, than this game is for you. This game is feels extremely nostalgic even though it has recently come out. Although the combat can feel a little bit janky and unrewarding, the sheer world size and potential of the game is immense. The buildings and survival mechanics are extremely fun, the ability to craft and use multiple different types of spells is amazing, and the vast world feels open to exploration. Collectable mounts are also another fun addition to the game. Another great thing is the large amount of support given by the developers. If you have any questions about the game, chances are that the developers themselves have responded to a steam forum post regarding your question at some point. Furthermore, the official discord server is quite active and has lots of useful information. Overall, I think this game has a lot of potential, but the developer team needs to continue trying to improve the game. Other game likes 7 Days to Die with very small dev teams have dedicated playerbases, looking past the flaws of the game, due to the developers openness and how creative many of the features of the game are. I could see KoA becoming something of the same.

The game started out so well. But over time the design became more sloppy and annoying. Enemies can just turn around mid swing to hit you when you dodge behind them. The Level design just becomes obnoxious with tons of cheap traps and enemy placements like dotting the areas with ranged enemies who's attacks you can't parry.Speaking of Parry: The entire game is (supposed to) revolve around the absorb / parry mechanic, it's also how you absorb the resource to heal. Problem is that later enemies just have very little or no absorbable parts, making healing practically impossible unless you use a consumable to get said resource.You die way too quick / enemies just do way too much damage, pumping exp into HP and Stamina is more of a waste than anything, the increase is so minuscule, you are better off by putting your Hunt points into % increases of your HP and Stamina. Checkpoints are too far apart from each other, and given with how easy you die, it makes backtracking very annoying. There is also besides the Checkpoints a Beacon you have to find to be able to see the map of the area that you explored, without it you are blind. This makes traversing the map / exploring even more a problem, especially due to a lack of a proper fast travel system. If you are looking for a well designed Metroidvania, then look elsewhere, preferably something like Ender Lilies. That game does everything right that this game does wrong.

The majority of the ruin appears to be from destruction or from old age, but a *few* objects are corrupted -- they seem to be glitched out.The overworld plays like an RPGmaker game (but with a more robust engine and graphics), and the combat is a rhythm game. The better you do hitting notes, the better you dodge attacks. (You don't do damage to the foes, you're just trying to survive.) The rhythm game gives you 4 lanes, mapped to D, F, J, and K keys. I think with a few tweaks this game could be amazing, but as it stands I cannot recommend it, as some of the mechanics make it a real slog to get through.Here's where it falls short:- Towards the end, the exploration is stifled by the fights that pop up. Each character has a limited number of actions they can take within a certain round, and these get eaten up quickly (2 action points to unlock a safe, and an additional 3 to then search it, really?!) and then the round resets, and often this means a pointless 10 min battle. The issue is the Action economy used in the fight is the same action economy used in the exploration, so if you use up a character's AP to win the battle, that character can't do anything until you reset the round again, often leading to another battle.- The boss fights, especially in the final chapter are horribly imbalanced. Bosses get multiple actions on their turn, and you have to watch a time consuming cinematic every time they go. You also fight the same boss over and over again and in multiple chapters you won't know when the final battle is, as there is a final series of battles. Battles are long and feel more like wars of attrition than engaging gameplay. - Load out of weapons and equipment cannot be changed mid battleThere's a mechanic of what type

game_name: One More Gate : A Wakfu Legend
review: As easy to play (roguelike) deckbuilders go my first recommendation will always be Slay The Spire. This one might be even more beginner friendly than Spire. If you're like me though and want to play something else for a bit, One More Gate: A Wakfu Legend is solid. I only played through the main story so far. I skipped the story itself though. The game could do with more variety both in terms of enemies as in play styles for your own character. After a while you unlock more cards and this opens up more possibilities but you first have to buy those cards to use them in the game. Buying them and then upgrading is a grindy experience though. Seeing how similar this game is to Slay The Spire and it doesn't really offer anything more or different I can't really recommend this game. It's a solid game, nothing wrong with it but there's no reason to pick this over Spire or other games in the genre. I'll come back to this review after I've played some more in the rift (unlocks after main story). Only really recommended if this is exactly what you're looking for (more of the same in a different package).EDIT: After playing the Rift, the post-story content, it's clear that I reviewed this game too soon. Rift is were the games becomes interesting and slightly diverges from the Spire-like mold. I like how you choose your own starter deck from a selection of randomized cards. I also like how the rift difficulty works. When you successfully play through one rift, you can play again with a higher difficulty. You get to choose between two randomized options of alterations. Alterations for example, monsters start with a certain amount of armor or some cards get less powerful.

Very good game. Your battle commands are limited, so you have to make the most of every command. This makes sure the best tactician wins, instead of the person who can click 200 times per minute. Destroy key enemy units to gain access to your most powerful abilities and destroy enemy units in general to shatter their morale. These features make you think like a predator instead of a turtle. Units all have a unique character: Axemen destroy enemy armor, swordsmen are hard to take down, cavalry charges and spearmen can hold the enemy back.One of the most fun things you can do in this game is charge and shatter enemy forces with your cavalry. Graphics are clear and informative. Often in strategy games you zoom out (like you should) and all the character models turn into a vague blob and even blend into the environment. What a waste of time making all those animations and models, the only thing you see when playing is unit icons anyway. Thankfully Winter Falling doesn't fall into this trap.One feature I'd like to be added is the option to restore a formation, because often you split the enemy forces up and you need to regroup after defeating every enemy formation separately. Currently this regrouping is messy, and in a messy formation the enemy can easily focus their damage on a unit that is not covered by his allies.

The devs have apparently never seen an American farm or talked to a real vet. The hillbilly music playing constantly in the background isn't bad, per se (it's pretty good, for what it is), but I don't particularly like that style of music. No vet would send an intern to scrounge around in the forest for "healing herbs" (which he can't even identify) or let him be sidetracked into becoming a delivery boy for the local farmers. He's ON THE CLOCK. Not to mention the fact that farmers don't generally leave clumps of goat cheese and bottles of milk just lying around the farm to collect later. Another action adventure RPG from the team at Dynamic Zero.Following on from 2020's futuristic "Surviving Titan" action adventure RPG, Arcane Vale takes us back to a more classic fantasy style setting, with swords and sorcery, dungeons and taverns (maybe some dragons). It's not long before you're fighting beasts with barely an axe to your name, but with a perfectly timed dodge roll and a few hacks n' slashes, you haven't been thrown into the deep end...yet.Just a few hours into this game and you can tell the world is going to be a big one, with lots of loot to be found in all sorts of scenery, levelling up to be done, skills to hone and what every adventurer needs between dark dungeons with danger around the corner, a bit of chilling out by the water for a spot of fishing.You can rebind your keys if you need to (make sure you test the binding, some symbol keys aren't working yet), or use a gamepad. Both work well, but I think the mouse will give you better accuracy with ranged weapons, especially firing on the diagonal.I'm looking forward to progressing through the story of this game, seeing what's in store as the map is revealed, and hopefully kitting my character out with good gear before venturing into that alluring dungeon entrance.

While the game is fun for a few hours, it really needs some quality of life updates before I can truly recommend it. As with most crafting games, the worst problems are with the inventory management; the game needs more inventory space, more tabs for sorting, and crucially, the ability to craft directly from your chests. (If I had my way about it, every single crafting game in existence would have this feature, but I swear it's overlooked every time.) It also doesn't have quest markers or a particularly useful map, despite having loads and loads of quests and NPCs. It's also a bit short for a game of this style, though that makes sense with a small development team so I can give that part a pass.

Are you here because you're digging farm sims with some extra stuff like dungeon crawling and secret finding? Or perhaps the dungeon part is what you like more than planting and/or fishing? In that case Arcane Vale might be the game for you. Otherwise you might be a bit disappointed that this isn't much of a farming game and the greenery part is a secondary aspect of Arcane Valley.Your character leaves their home island to embark on a journey to find a treasure. They have half of the map and are directed towards the guy who has the other. Will you manage to find the other part? Or perhaps settle down and become the local farmer? The slightly disappointing part is that there's not much farming potential and the home you can buy in the game serves more of an item storing purpose than anything else.The graphics are fantastic. The game has some amazing pixel art. The combat is very fluid and relies on player's reflexes.How long is the game? I've managed to finish it in 13.9 hours with all achievements unlocked. I feel like there's so much potential that could've been unleashed into quadrupling the content in the game. You have many different aspects that aren't really used fully, like fishing or farming being a source of income but there doesn't seem to be any actual use of the coins other than buying some basic weapons and armor since the best ones are either dropped or crafted anyway.Overall I recommend Arcane Vale. The game is very pleasant and fun to play.

Astonia: The Return of Yendor is a remaking of the 2002 Intent game Astonia 3. It is a free-to-play, isometric, tile-based, point-and-click MMORPG for old school RPG lovers that takes place in a world still recovering from the invasion of demonic forces. There are no quest markers or handholding here, so you'll have to rely on NPCs and your brains to complete quests and survive. Over the last 10+ years, I've seen a lot of changes to this game, and am always excited to see what's coming next! New players have the choice of three classes. Want to be a stoic warrior that cuts down his foes? We got you. How about a powerful mage that harnesses the powers of lightning, fire, or holy light to clear his path? We got you. Or even try out the new cutthroat rogue that uses a bow to take down his foes from a distance, or a sword for more up close and personal fighting. Experienced players will be able to fight their way through the labyrinth and defeat the gatekeeper to unlock new potential for their classes by Arching, or be reborn as a seyan'du, a fierce fighter that has proven his worth and has been blessed with the powers of might and magic. In terms of quests, it's your standard high fantasy RPG affair with a few extras thrown in. Help NPCs by clearing out the evil in the world by killing skeletons for magical skulls, uncovering plots gone awry, clearing out nests of vampires, and even aid the ailing military. You also have the option of delving deep into the Random Dungeons of Yendor, clearing out skeletons to find shrines that give an array of boosts (sometimes, at the cost of your own life). There are also repeatable challenge tunnels

Alien Shooter - Last Hope is a new game in the series. Fans of the series will be familiar with the format. Blow up thousands of aliens, rinse and repeat. I mostly enjoyed the game even though it is a bit short. The new turrets are handy and actually make for a new type of strategic game play.What I disliked: Level design is boring. It's also annoying when the aliens break out of walls behind where you've been, so you're forced to fight in front and back. I guess that's what the turrets are for, but it's still annoying having to dodge the constant rockets flying around everywhere.Weapons and items have been nerfed. The magma minigun is clearly doing NOWHERE near the amount of damage that it did in the original game. I'm sure the devs thought it was needed in order to balance out the extra damage output from the turrets, but still, it didn't feel right. Hell, even the flamethrower seemed to produce higher DPS than the magma minigun. Invulnerability shields also seemed to have been nerfed, as they don't last as long as before. I played on Standard difficulty and the blue aliens with the rocket launchers are way too tough. Other Alien Shooter games found the correct balance which allowed you to kill stuff easily while still always feeling challenged. This game felt bad, aliens weren't dying fast enough. I'd still recommend the game to fans of the series, though.

Finally, I started making a bit more money. But still, I was confused. Is there a time or fuel limit on my digging? Why would I want to "stop" the oil? Noelle in Butterfly Soup correlates this, but as an uptight Asian high schooler with infallible grades and whose mother lives vicariously through her. Inwards they both refuse to buckle down completely to their family's impulse to grovel the american dream. Both characters navigate this via choices in-game, and players watch them choose themselves in response. review: Bought this game awhile ago and am looking forward to really sitting down and progressing through the story lines. They are SO well written so far. The artwork is absolutely gorgeous as well. I think a true testament to how well this game develops it's characters is how devastated I felt after I, a person with no prior experience playing VNs, fumbled Ashlie's route and hadn't been saving regularly. The blow up between the two felt so grounded and Inaya's hurt was palpable. Inaya is such a likable player character to me, and I really wanted to get all of the good endings. Speaking of endings, I truly love how this game gives players the option to skip to good or bad endings if they would like. The romance is so compelling that I do get the urge to do that, and it's also a valid way to consume this story. But ultimately, I would like to give myself the chance to appreciate the lovely writing along the way, and am excited to encounter all of the other characters Validate has to offer. Link to review: Tl;dr You get a throwback to a genre that died for a reason- sure visual novels were birthed from the ashes of them, but they’ve at least added an extra dimension that freshens things up for a sect of the gaming populace. Pure text-based adventures feel cheap and outdated, and OSS goes out of its way to make those facets worse than they already are through limited artwork, a sparse score, and inconsistent SFX. The writing, which should have been the saving grace, throws half its lot on identity riddles that rapidly lose their emotional momentum via being poorly strewn in the hub, while the other half is focused on an odyssey hampered by some of the worst filler I have had the misfortune to experience.As the title implies, you get a number of puns in the script that relate to the literary and compsci fields, making it fun to read (if you’re familiar with those topics), and the personalities you encounter on your voyage can be even more fun to get into dialogues with. But they are spaced out between objectives that are a chore to complete courtesy of their compartmentalized sub-goals that depend upon menial labors and external memorization/penning.If you find text-based adventures appealing and were one of those guys who drew their own map of the original Legend of Zelda from the 80s, then perhaps you’ll like what Open Sorcery: Sea++ has to offer. For the rest of you, steer clear.

I'm not sure what I expected - this is very much a text only game, with clicking on text and navigation "go north" style being pretty much the only gameplay. That's not a problem, though: visual novels have less gameplay and can be engaging. I guess my issue is the writing. The setting is some strange Jungian collective consciousness style ocean that's operated by... code? The idea is very appealing, but the way it's presented is... not. It's a mixture of self-reflective poetry and programming. I should love this: I dabble in poetry and code for a living. Maybe it's because the writing feels very alien and self-focused. Arrogant, perhaps. The protagonist's train of thought doesn't fare too well on the tracks of my mind. Shame. I'm not recommending this, but this is a very subjective opinion - based on the fact that me and the text of the game didn't really click. Maybe take a look? Who knows, maybe it'll click for you.

Du Xun, a local citizen of Bu Liang Well is struggling to make a living in this dangerous den everyday with his childhood friends Xiao Ling and An Qi, until the governor general of the town is suspected being murdered. Though he isn’t aware of being dragged into a much larger conspiracy larking behind the incident...+ Afford price with around 8 hours gameplay on average, the puzzle solving is unique with its signature ancient Chinese culture elements + Excellent performances by the casts, the real film experience + Mysterious, yet hilarious story + No bugs being found in the entire walkthrough -Visuals can be improved on 4K cinematic displays I honestly recommend this game to all FMV fans, since it is really different from any other ones on Steam. Ampersat is an unusual Nintendo Switch game (somehow here on Steam, I guess so PC gamers can pretend they accidentally bought a Switch). The game is a hybrid dungeon crawler, RPG and top down shooter/brawler. The premise is that your little village has been surrounded by evil towers because the letter "Z" stole all the other letters from the village... yeah, everyone is an ASCII character... kind of like Rogue/Hack with graphics that arguably aren't all that much better than text. Quirky premise aside, such a game could work really well if it wasn't designed for handhelds and had very high implementation quality. Ampersat was designed for handhelds and does not have very high implementation quality. One important note is that even though this is an amateur project, it does seem to be sincerely and genuinely made. I couldn't find any flipped assets, plagiarism or any other kind of insincere actions from the developer, but unfortunately genuine intentions alone are not enough to produce a brilliant PC gaming experience.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets with crap 2D retro pixel "art" textures on them, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s. This very poor quality visual style is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with. It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game. It looks bad as a result of their decisions,

Apersat is a game about learning the alphabet, and how important every letter is to being able to understand anything. That's right, you actually can't tell what the hell you're looking at in a lot of the menus until you're far enough into the game. At its core, it's pretty simple once you know what you're doing, especially since the game makes a conscious effort to be as clear as possible since not being able to read is already a mechanic, but the higher levels will require you to remember which enemies have which abilities, and since there's 52 different kinds of enemies (although many are bosses), that's still a lot. It actually drags the lategame down, since the main challenge that later levels provide is having more enemies, including the ones which turn off controls. Your character actually only has two abilities when you're in combat - move and attack, and both have multiple status effects that simply disable them. It's a bit strange that the game never stops incentivizing melee combat, even though in some late levels actually trying it will result in you being hit by an enemy with "stone", and then another with "fear", and now you can't play the game anymore until you respawn. Until that point, though, the game has a nice rhythm and trying to work out incomprehensible lines of dashes before you have all the letters is a nice side activity.Overall, it's a fun enough top-down arpg that gets enough mileage out of its gimmicks to be worth playing.

I'm playing without DLC and have 425 hours in game.Idle Cave Heroes is an rpg idle game with incremental elements and pixel art style characters. There are 3 characters you'll have in the party. They are Connor, Robin, and Julia. Connor is your tank meant to keep Robin, the archer or damage dealer, and Julia, the cleric or support and recovery specialist, alive. Your characters will live die and repeat till they chip away at enemies hp. On boss floors, the enemy must die before you do or they full heal and you will fight the same enemy and gain zero progress in perpetuity. It is a very slow idle game that requires you to be rather active for an idle game to make progress at a reasonable speed. You will upgrade the village, your characters gear, abilities dark equipment, artifacts, relics, and idle abilities as you progress. You'll hit points where you have to grind dark mana till you can prestige via the dark ritual in town which unlocks at floor 15 to repeat the grind from floor 1.Now for my opinion...I'll be blunt... It's not idle at all early game so unless you plan to grind for a long time actively, don't pick it up. If you don't mind spending a couple days to a week grinding the game, you'll probably start to feel the idle mechanics of the game. There are 2 types of idling in this game which I'll call active and passive. Active is when the game is on and progressing. Passive is when the game is off and progresses instantly when you come back. This technically has both even though offline is severely handicapped by pet
Definitely worth checking out if you're looking for an easy way to spend your free time.

I really enjoyed the story, even when I was rolling my eyes or cringing at some of the dialogue (it basically is just your typical shonen anime).But be warned: don't start with this game. Even if you started with Trails of Cold Steel I, that would be like watching only the Captain America movies before Infinity War, not having seen Thor, Black Panther, and so on. You would be missing out on countless details, inside jokes, etc if you haven't started with Trails in the Sky. At $15, this game is an excellent alpha title. I'd say it's better than many beta titles in development. The game is charming, the soundtrack is decent, and I laughed at the light humor sprinkled throughout the game.This game is similar to many top-down Zelda titles but with a fleshed-out, challenging combat system. The stealth mechanic is handled wonderfully, the equipment system is fun and allows an enormous amount of customization, and there is a shocking level of detail to the game. Grappling enemies adds much needed depth to the combat system and is quite satisfying. See that pot? Pick it up, fill it with water, and huck it at the nearest enemy for a decent chunk of damage. Or skip the pot and grab the enemy, drag them to the water, and casually drown them for extra crafting materials. Not enough? Push them into a bottomless void or throw them into other enemies. The random generation makes levels replayable and interesting. There's also a multiplayer mode which involves serious cooperation, though it has some bugs for now. I had so much fun with my friend coordinating stealth attacks and accidentally suplexing each other into oblivion.I eagerly await the next update for Good Night, Knight! Best of luck to the dev!

I like Good Night Knight.I Recorded My Progress with Relevant CommentaryPlease watch if you prefer a more Audio / Visual experience, I do try to make it fun and enjoyable: Good Night Knight is an Indie, Twin Stick Action RogueLike / Roguelite RPG Dungeon Crawler with Pixel Graphics and Procedural Generation. It is good.Think of the dungeons of Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, with Procedural Generation of the dungeons, an interesting and bold use of lighting and fog of war, and a stealth system that encourages backstabbing, if that is your style. I personally prefer to run in and cut em down, but to each their own.Unlike Legend of Zelda: A Link to the Past, I have yet to see hearts drop from containers and defeated monsters, making the dungeons far more dangerous here than in that legendary influence.Good Night Knight is tough!The use of Lighting is interesting, as Good Night Knight remembers that you don’t have eyes in the back of your head, and your character cannot see anywhere they are not looking, and certainly not directly behind them!Your character sees in a 180 degree arc in front of them, and sight is blocked by obstacles like dungeon walls, pillars, and corners, encouraging the player to play attention to where the monsters last were, and where they could possibly be, as they make their way towards you. Pay special attention to the objects they disturb on their path towards you, as they can be a vital clue to avoid getting got!Beyond the excellent and innovative use of Fog of War and visibility, Good Night Knight has a stamina system, that feeds the attacks, sprints, and dashes of your knight, and intelligent use of your stamina is vital to avoid taking damage, which is difficult to heal

I found this game absolutely delightful and very more-ish.The irreverent dialogue fit the setting very well and there are tons of nice little wacky things - i.e. amidst your quest to overthrow a tyrant, there is a cadre of cats scattered around looking for the Great Yarnball, that you can do, or not do, as you see fit. Once through the intro, the game basically lets you do what you want and go where you want, and its possible to stumble into places you have no business being and sometimes even survive. Fast travel mechanics are introduced but world resources respawn so I found myself usually preferring to walk. There are also quite a few long term quests that span the map that you can do bits and pieces as you go. There's "skulls" on the map with difficult boss encounters that you can keep trying until you eventually can beat them and they give very nice loot.The skill system has a lot of originality in how it is setup. Many skills have negatives but you can pick and choose to find effective builds. Also the skill tree has non combat bonuses, i.e. the tinker line can reduce upgrade costs and some of the INT-based skill lines (casters) can do things like increase the amount of things you forage etc. These little touches really helped build a diverse and effective party.Pros:Original setting & storylineLots of hidden stuff to find/achieve/unlock/doUnique skill systemFreedom to design character and build NPC companions how you wantLightweight crafting/upgrade system No timewasting mechanics such as corpserunning etcCons:A lot of explicit

Here's the breakdown:Story/Writing-It's a goofy meme-laden narrative of 'how COVID-19 may or may not have happened' that makes fun of a lot of the conspiracy theories surrounding it. It's reasonably funny, though the grammar is bad at times. I also appreciate that they took the time to include some actual safety info. Very responsible of them. The goofy narrative is the main entertaining thing about the game. I enjoyed some of the humor, but some of it was a little dumb. Gameplay- The gameplay is basically dialogue and cutscenes interspersed with a few small minigames. The minigames are simple, easy, and at times a little clunky, but it's clear there was actually some good effort put into them, and they are enjoyable. The game takes around twenty minutes to complete. Graphics-For the most part, it's just standard RPG Maker graphics. Nothing special. Music- The game primarily uses royalty-free music, and while for the most part it is decent, it has an issue that sometimes happens where a track starts playing before the last track finishes, resulting in something that is very unpleasant to listen to. This happens around two or three times over the course of the game. Overall-This is a silly little game that's a good way to burn 20 minutes. It's not really anything worth writing home about, and I'm not sure I'd actually pay anything for it, but for a free to play game, it's worth a look if you have a little time you need to take up with something.

Cards/DecksI am big fan of the cards/deck! It adds such an important layer of strategy that keeps you on your toes the entire match. Though that may not be friendly for casual players, more serious players will be rewarded for theory crafting decks. It's great as well that even if you end up playing against the same team composition, different deck compositions generally lead to different play styles from each player. If the player base grows big enough (hopefully), I think it would also be great to add a ranked system. I don't think it would be a fun experience for casual players to match against people who spend a lot of time theory crafting and just have better decks and better team compositions. Moreover, rank will be sort of a reward/incentive for players to theory craft and innovate new strategies. Otherwise, people who dedicate time learning the game will just beat up on players who are casually clicking characters, and that might get boring quickly.Overall, it's a fun game that's easy to learn, but also rewarding for more serious players.

Fishing Paradiso is the sequel to Bear’s Restaurant by Odencat. You start as a young androgynous person who has lost their memory (seems to be a running theme!). You’re greeted by a giant cosmic entity and told that you’ve gone to heaven, but that this might not quite be heaven for you just yet, and then wake up again, this time on a tiny island with a small blue bird. If you played Bear’s Restaurant, this little guy might be a bit familiar.While it is a fishing game, or a Tropical Fishing RPG as the devs call it, at its core, this is a game about connections. Fishing is the main game mechanic, and you need to catch specific fish to meet the needs of those you meet in heaven. As you fish and progress, you learn more about the people around you.While you technically don’t need to have played Bear’s Restaurant to enjoy this, I do highly recommend it. Not just because it’s a lovely game in its own right, but because it very much adds to the experience in Fishing Paradiso.The controls are pretty simple and leveling up your skills is as easy as just catching more fish to get gold. If you’re having issues finding a certain fish in one area, your little bird friend can use some birdy ninjutsu to change all of the current fish at your location. There’s even rare or special fish that will show up as different colored shadows compared to the regular fish, as well as some fish having unique shadow shapes, making it a little easier to hone in on specific fish requested by your fellow heaven-dwellers.The art style is adorable, made in the same style as Bear’s Restaurant, after all it is a sequel. game_name: Love n War: Hero by Chance II
review: I played both Hero by Chance and Warlord by Chance back in the day, so there was no way I was going to miss this one. To no one's surprise, I loved this game. It has what made the previous games so fun, plus some gameplay improvements to make it even better. This time, you can send entire formations—even your generals—to kick your opponent's ass. The art is as lovely as usual, except for the AI-generated backgrounds; they don't fit the game's art style at all. So yeah, check this one out if you liked the previous games; it won't disappoint you. However, you should first play the prequel if you haven't played the previous games because the story starts right where it ended.

I can see why people might be turned off of this game, but I honestly think it's really nifty. There's a functional open world, lots of AI populating the towns(even if they can act weird sometimes, I find that amusing more than problematic) and the translation doesn't seem to be too bad. There's obviously a lot that can be done to improve the title, but it's early access after all. My main issue so far has been the erratic physics system, which wouldn't be so bad if the whole game wasn't built around grabbing, stowing, and carrying small objects in a physics system. It's very easy, for example, to crouch down, try to close the lid on a storage chest, and accidentally brush the side of it, flinging the chest and all your hard earned belongings into the air. I lost several expensive gems this way - would be nice if there was some kind of physics dampener, or a way to track items you've lost.It's a unique title. Honestly the fact that the NPCs consist entirely of anime girls whose skirts spend half the time spazzing out doesn't even bug me, it's cool to just have a sorta functional open world game made for VR for once.

I first played Long Gone Days when there was only a chapter to its name, but I remember being very impressed. Now, with more content in my hands, I can offer a more informed review. Wonderful! There are themes of personal freedom, oppression and morality. All done with such a delicate touch that it doesn’t come off as patronising. Burke and Adair stole my heart, but they’re all endearing in their own way. The sprites and backgrounds are done in a beautiful pixel style. The character portraits, the CGs and the visuals during the shooting part of the game are anime style (sort of, it feels a bit more mature than that). Some things may change in the final version of the game, but I have complete trust in the developers’ sense of style. I’d say it’s a mix of turn-based shooter, exploration and visual novel (different actions/answers lead to different outcomes). There is quite a bit of text to read, but it’s very engaging, so it never feels like a core.The game isn’t complete, so you may wonder if it’s worth it to buy it.Well, that’s highly subjective, but in my opinion the current chapters are worth the price already.I bought this game at full prize, and if they ever publish it on mobile, I’m going to buy it there too :)

There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. The game is highly unpolished, everything looks fuzzy due to clumsy application of Unreal's post processing and filters... something that will never be fixed.The poor quality of this game is reflected in the general public reception. At the time of this review, SteamDB shows the all-time peak player number was only 3 players. That's right, only 3. review: Oh boy, where to start with this game? For starters, since it is this studio's first attempt at typical JRPG, I won't judge it too harshly on that front. However, I will criticize the story because it is the main selling point for this game. The story and characters were fairly good. There were comedic bits that honestly did bring a chuckle to me. Character interaction and their growth was done well I'd say, especially for Mikazuchi. Every character had something unique to bring to the table. Although the weakest link in the group would definitely be Oshtor. He does carry around the occasional snark but other than that, he seems like a typical upright MC that you could find in a multitude of other JRPGs. You could say that I expected a bit more from his character. The combat system was fairly simple to understand once you got the hang of it, but honestly I missed the old action rings. Learning the timings of the moves and pressing just at the right moment to make critical hits is something I wish this game could implement. Gameplay-wise, Shunya is both the weakest and the strongest. Her field attack being a projectile makes her supremely good for catching monsters off guard, but during combat most of her stronger skills are locked behind a wall which other characters don't have to go over. It's an interesting mechanic, but it needs to be thought over a little more. Game dungeons are linear and require little to no puzzle solving but I wish we were able to fast travel between checkpoints within the dungeons themselves. review: I'd read that AQUAPLUS had made Monochrome Mobius as a gateway game for the series... in that regard I'd say they've failed without question. If you're a returning fan, though, I'd definitely recommend this. While, in itself, there is a lot left to be desired, I greatly enjoyed this game. As Utawarerumono was traditionally a visual novel format, it's slow in the first couple chapters (maybe three/four hours?). Still, after that, there was always something to pay attention to. Many times, having played the other games, I went "Hey, I know that reference!" or "I remember you!" (it's a prequel after all). Point is, while there are gaps in the story itself, there is plenty of new explanations on many things that were treated as mundane in the main games.Overall... relative 8/10. I had a lot of time to play, and thus put up with the games' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, so I still had a lot of fun. If you go in with lower expectations (imagine you're playing one of the first games from a new studio), you'll have lots of fun.

Shine Within is a short RPGish game that was clearly heavily influenced by Undertale. You play a nameless human, instructed by a disembodied voice to carry out various tasks to justify your ultimate purpose. Gameplay takes place in an underground environment populated by benign monsters, whom you help out in exchange for the statue pieces you need to advance. As you approach the conclusion, things get a little more sinister and you are given cause to doubt that the Voice really has your or anyone's best interests in mind, and you get presented with the choice to go along, or not. It's not a bad game by any imagining, but if I had a complaint it would be that it leaves a little too much buried in subtext. We don't need walls of textual exposition, but revealing a bit more, more explicitly would have certainly helped. As of this writing I've only completed one playthrough so I don't yet know if the provocative "The End???" concluding screen indicates a second run would be different and thus add replay value, but even if not Shine Within is enjoyable enough (and free), so it's worth checking out.

I was hyped as hell for this after loving the first installment - it comes as a shock that I'd feel the need to give a thumbs down for this after 9 hours of playing.More isn't necessarily better, something that too many studios fail to appropriately grasp: - The overworld is tedious, as it's essentially here to inflate gameplay time through not-so-good real time combat. The whole point of the game is the turn-based tactics, adding anything else that isn't 10/10 in between makes the whole experience more annoying. It makes going back to earlier levels a chore, too. - I don't remember the first installment having so much constant reinforcement right from the get go. Suddenly, it's not about strategizing against a specific enemy setup, but rather managing to survive long enough against an unending onslaught of enemies. What that does, is make you feel that the issue isn't so much the strategy you used, but rather the fact you haven't farmed enough to get better gear for your characters and level them up. It leads to a vicious circle as the difficulty makes you flee the level before you can grab all the loot (and sometimes even the epic one), which means less stuff to improve your characters, which means the next level is gonna feel even tougher, and so on and so forth. Of course, the solution for me would be to lower the difficulty. But once you do that, you absolutely stomp the enemies and there's no challenge/thinking needed anymore. Some of the enemies' powers (damage, stuff they spawn) are literally halved between the third highest difficulty and the second highest.This leads an absolutely gorgeous game full of personality and promise to be a tiring experience that felt like a chore right as I was entering

Everything is lovingly rendered from top to bottom, from the character portraits bursting with color, texture and emotion, to the lovingly hand-painted backgrounds on every new screen. The remaster does an excellent job bringing these elements back to life- I've caught myself staring at little details and brushstrokes in the scenery that I never noticed before- and the character models look a lot better now too. I've been thoroughly enjoying a long overdue replay of these games. Thank you to all the developers, artists, voice actors, musicians and other creatives that put their heart and soul into these games- your efforts have not gone unnoticed. <3

Munch is a dark, heavy metal-infused roguelite that's as brutal as it is beautiful. You start as a lowly creature, but with each devoured soul, you evolve into a grotesque, powerful being. The game's core loop of eat, evolve, and obliterate is simple yet endlessly satisfying.Each of the 12 monstrous forms you can transform into offers a unique playstyle and a killer soundtrack. From the hulking behemoth to the nimble energy-bender, there's a form for every taste. The combat is fast-paced and visceral, with satisfyingly chunky hit effects and brutal finishers. The game's dark, gothic setting, coupled with the heavy metal soundtrack, creates an immersive and intense atmosphere. The pixel art style is a perfect fit for the game's tone, and the boss fights are epic and challenging. The game's level design, while sometimes a bit repetitive, is atmospheric and well-suited to the game's style.However, Munch isn't without its flaws. The game can feel a bit grindy at times, especially on higher difficulties. The level design can also be a bit samey, and the game's difficulty curve can be steep. Despite its flaws, Munch is a highly enjoyable and visually stunning roguelite that's sure to please fans of metal music and monster-themed games. If you're looking for a challenging and stylish game to sink your teeth into, Munch is definitely worth checking out.

When I saw the trailer for Gripper, I found myself drawn to it. It looked like it had some concepts that I loved; Fast paced gameplay, sci-fi apocalyptic aesthetic, battles with titanic bosses... So I tried the game. And let me just say, while the game does have good ideas... They fall flat. First, the story. I'll be brief because there's not much to talk about. The story is bare bones, the characters are one-dimensional, and honestly it felt like it was added as an afterthought. While I was whatever about the characters, it's a bloody shame that there was no real world building, because the setting was interesting. They just didn't do anything with it. The dialogue is also... not good. The writing is weirdly paced and often feels inorganic. Plus, there are several instances where the subtitles don't match the spoken dialogue! It really felt like not much effort was put into the narrative. But hey, you don't need a super compelling story if the game is fun to play, which begs the question: is it fun? The answer is... complicated. On paper, the gameplay has everything it needs to be good; high speed action sequences where you blast through tunnels, the ability to Akira-Bike-Slide on command, and top-down battles against massive bosses. However, in practice... it doesn't do either of these things particularly well. Let's start with the tunnel sequences, because these are the most egregious. You may be noticing a theme here, but on paper, they're good because you blast through 360 degree tunnels at high speeds, being able to pivot in the full 360 degree range to avoid obstacles in your path. However... MANY of the obstacles aren't visible until you get close to them. The problem is the distance at which they become visible

Gripper is one of those games that feel like it's on a very shaky foundation. Don't get me wrong, when the tunnel like sections and open arena combat are working the way you want them to, it can be fun and a challenge. But the shaky foundation doesn't like a lot of variation in gameplay: and almost expect you to go one way and one way only. The thing is, if you do go outside the bounds of what the game wants you to do, even for a moment: then all hell breaks loose. Like, I'm not talking about not listening to the game's very oddly written story or the instructions given to you. I'm talking about going left versus right against a hazard in the tunnel sections: and running into a hazard that has appeared so quickly in front of you, you have no chance to dodge it. Or a boss fight where the bosses leading shots are so accurate that you are wondering if the game is literally predicting every movement with the limited turning radius at times. These things start to add up quickly: as it starts to feed into a frustration that you will not only be able to shake, but will continue until you just say “nope, no more for tonight”. How do I feel about the story? It's bland, like the majority of H games out there. It's not the first time this sort of premise has been used, and there's quite a few strategy games that employ this sort of plot device that you can pick up on DLsite if you scrounge around a little and look for SLGs.Pretty simple, you can move your units as many tiles as you want if they're your tiles(indicated in blue). Touching an empty red tile or trying to attack an enemy will end the turn of the unit that was moved, and if the enemy on a tile is defeated, you will capture the tile as well. Aside from that, I mostly found myself using the archer to chip away at enemies on first hit, deal damage with the soldier, and then finish off with mage. I almost never utilized the Knight or Armor Knight, and somewhat utilized the Guardian Dragon-- they do virtually no damage and cost too much to heal to be worth using.Don't engage an enemy if it puts you in a point where 2 or more enemies can attack you at once, try to bottleneck them if you're having issues.

Rating: ★★★★☆Shogun Showdown, currently in Early Access, seamlessly merges the strategic depth of "Into the Breach" with the addictive deck-building mechanics found in "Slay The Spire." Despite being in its developmental phase, the game manages to provide a compelling and engaging experience that held my attention for a substantial 35+ hours.The strategic depth of positioning and timing in battles, reminiscent of "Into the Breach," is combined with the accessible yet nuanced deck-building elements. This makes the game suitable for both newcomers and seasoned players, offering a satisfying blend of simplicity and depth.While the game is on the right track, the roadmap highlights areas for improvement. One notable suggestion is the introduction of more varied music to prevent potential monotony during extended play sessions. Additionally, expanding the variety of in-game shops and introducing a system to manipulate the shop type could enhance the strategic depth, adding to the game's replayability.In conclusion, Shogun Showdown successfully combines the strengths of "Into the Breach" and "Slay The Spire," offering a satisfying and addictive gameplay experience. With a few adjustments and additions, the game has the potential to stand out in the turn-based strategy and deck-building genres. If you're a fan of either of the aforementioned games, exploring this Early Access title is a solid investment

It takes a while to get used to. It feels like it was done to make it feel like a 1980’s horror VHS film. The game also has no voice acting which seems strange in a non indie game. Still in the end I feel these artistic choices all worked for the game that was being created here. I definitely think it’s a lot more niche. I can’t foresee recommending this game to any of my friends…but if you love murder mysteries and visual novels this is a pretty strong one.A weird game can certainly be a fun game and I enjoyed my time with this game. I think the biggest issues with this game aren’t the art style or lack of voice acting, but instead just how short the overall story is. 15hrs is like the max you are going to spend on this game and it’s probably more like 10-12. That’s pretty short for a game in my opinion. In a visual novel I really want far more ability to interact with the story and make choices. This game does give you more of an ability to look around the scenes and sometimes to journey to locations which adds some nice immersion to the game. However, the overall choices in this game are just very limited. In my mind this game should have multiple paths to journey down that can lead to potentially different clues and outcomes. game_name: PARANORMASIGHT: The Seven Mysteries of Honjo
review: Paranormasight is a thrilling adventure game that is sure to captivate gamers who love anime, film noir, and mystery. The game has a gripping story that kept me hooked from start to finish. The game follows the journey of several diverse characters who are trying to solve a series of murders linked to the paranormal.The timeline gameplay mechanics in Paranormasight are well done and fascinating. The game allows players to travel through different timelines and interact with characters from the past and present to solve the mystery. The gameplay is challenging but not overly difficult, making it enjoyable for gamers of all skill levels.The graphics in Paranormasight are well-drawn, and while there isn't much animation, it doesn't hinder the game experience at all. The game's art style is reminiscent of classic anime, which adds to the game's overall charm.The music in Paranormasight is fantastic, and it really sets the mood for the game. The music is haunting and adds to the game's eerie atmosphere, which is perfect for a mystery game. But also, the excellent jazz tracks serve to lighten the mood every so often as well. It's an excellent pairing....just like a porterhouse with a nice merlot. ;)I also really enjoyed Paranormasight's inclusion of fourth wall solutions, which were really fun to use, yet not overdone. The game breaks the fourth wall in a creative way that adds to the game's overall charm and makes it stand out from other adventure games.In conclusion, I absolutely recommend Paranormasight to adventure gamers and to people who love anime, film noir, and mystery. The game's gripping story, well-done gameplay mechanics, fantastic music, and creative use of fourth wall solutions make it a must-play for anyone looking for a thrilling adventure game.

game_name: PARANORMASIGHT: The Seven Mysteries of Honjo
review: One of the more remarkable visual novels I've had the pleasure of experiencing, 'The Seven Mysteries of Honjo' is a wholehearted recommendation for enthusiasts of mysteries rooted in Japanese history and the occult. Masterfully-expressive illustration and framing. Multifaceted and highly-memorable cast of characters. Strong writing that circumvents tired tropes. Shallow illusion of choice. Infrequent translation issues. No voice acting.

game_name: PARANORMASIGHT: The Seven Mysteries of Honjo
review: is a horror visual novel. You will play as several characters in the course of the story. A dark ritual has unleashed curses all around the Sumida ward of Tokyo, Japan. You must keep your wits about you and think outside the box if you want to prevent disaster.While this is functionally a visual novel (you will spend most of your time here reading), it does feature somewhat original gameplay elements: .It's also worth noting that this is very lean as VNs go: dialogs mostly go straight to the point, there are no interminable monologues, most of the descriptions are optionally readable in Files... I don't think it would overwhelm players who aren't huge fans of reading.Funny tidbit: the game starts with the usual disclaimer about it being a work of fiction and having no relation to real events, characters, or ... but the credits mention the cooperation of the Sumida tourist office XDI had a great time unraveling the many mysteries of Honjo. I recommend this game to any fan of Japanese horror stories. Even if you aren't normally into VNs, this one might not overstay its welcome.I suggest avoiding spoilers as much as possible, as figuring the plot out is the most satisfying part of the game, in my opinion.

tl;dr: I personally wouldn't recommend this to someone who wants a fulfilling metroidvania experience.I understand where all the praise for this game is coming from. It is gorgeous, and it really nails the dieselpunk aesthetic. From a visual standpoint, an overall experience, this game is a 10/10.Unfortunately, once you start paying attention to the gameplay, it becomes clear that there's a disconnect. This game has everything a metroidvania should have, on paper at least. It's got the distinct areas, the unique movement mechanics, the unlockable abilities, the boss fights, the traversal puzzle rooms, the secrets and backtracking, etc. However, in practice, these elements don't really mesh together well.For one example: You get three very unique weapons by the end of the game, but their full use is locked behind memorizing combos. Most combos aren't even useful in most encounters, so you end up with this unfulfilled potential of weapons that you use to do the same attacks over and over. Another example is the boss fights. You can tell that someone(s) put a lot of work into the boss animations and movesets. However, they must not have worked very closely with the people working on the main character's movement abilities. The first 3 attempts at most bosses have you end up getting stunlocked to death just because you didn't anticipate one of three different juggling attacks that the bosses trap you in. A final example is the map layout. There are a lot of unique areas, but in most cases, you're only going to go through each once. The story will throw you into an area, you'll go through it in a relatively linear fashion, beating enemies and solving puzzles as you go, and then you'll leave 90 minutes later with a new ability and a couple of collectibles. This game is not a traditional FPS, at least in the 2 hours I’ve played. I’ve spent much more time figuring out how to buff my character, heal myself, and use my weapons effectively than pulling the trigger. Yes, there is significant gunplay and melee action, but this game is much more for people who want to take their time and notice details and figure out mild, but important puzzles to progress. This only really becomes apparent after you finish the first and only earth stage, which is both graphically underwhelming and kind of dull game-play wise. I almost quit before getting to the alien world, but I’m glad I stuck out that first 20 minutes because that’s when the game begins to shine.A lot of the story is told through dialog with other characters, and is pretty well written in a sarcastic, dark humor kind of way. Don’t skip it, as otherwise you’ll be pretty lost as to what to do next or at all. There is a radar/mini map with areas of interest highlighted, but you’ll miss out on upgrades that make the game winnable. In your default state you’ll be too weak and underpowered to make much progress.Although the game is definitely worth playing if you like this more cerebral, slow paced type of FPS gameplay, it’s definitely got its weaknesses. There are bugs that are annoying but not game breaking, and I did get one crash. You walk very slow given the scale of the alien world, and while you can run at a much faster pace that drains stamina quickly. It’s also far too easy to die at first on the alien world (but at least there are lots of save locations). Gamepads work fine for movement and shooting, but not at all for interacting

One of the worst offenders of "more = better," and by more I mean more enemies and grinding. Get used to confusing mazes packed with fast-moving monsters that are impossible to avoid. You can expect up to 100 fights or more in some of the later dungeons, only moving several steps before being detected forcing you to fight. EXP and money are way too low per fight. The game expects you to put hours upon hours to beat the game. To add on to this, there's a fast mode which helps with combat. However it makes you prone to crashing. Essentially you want this on 24/7 to speed up the tedious grinding, but then you're at risk of having all progress up to your past save erased on crash. Here's an example of the gameplay loop currently (normal). Find a statue, fight enemies around the statue, save after every 2-3 fights to avoid losing progress on crash, level up 4-5 times (approx 30 - 40 fights), build up TP, restore HP and save again, rush to boss room escaping all encounters to avoid using up all HP/MP/TP before fight actually begins. In addition in the 1 hour I played I kept seeing the same room descriptions come up again and again. I would have expected a text based game to have many versions of 'monsters in a room' but they all said the same 'A wave of hostility hits you as xxxx'.Combat is reasonable for turn-based. Some strategic options about silencing spell casters, focusing attacks on your tanks (since no rows, everyone stands at the front including archers), healing your characters etc.Skill trees seem quite limited. 4 main abilities in a class that can be unlocked and then upgraded a couple more times, and then points put into passive abilities. The game is going more for many classes than particular customisation of one class.Loot is reasonable, but simple. Very often you will find weapons that do double the damage of your previous weapon (although perhaps that changes once you progress more floors down).I realise this is early access - but comments by dev in September say it is close to full release.As a suggestion, I would say the Dev needs to spend $50 of hiring a freelance writer from a freelancer platform to write tons of nicely written variations of room text to give a sense of atmosphere and reduce the sense of repetition.

There's a good card game in here, but it's held back by a few issues for me.Something about the "physicality" of the cards doesn't feel right. Most cards require two clicks to play. Once to select and once to target. You can occasionally just drag a card from hand to target, but not always. It never seems intuitive to me when I am allowed or not to do this. This sounds trivial, but it is a constant annoyance. When I play a well made card game, I almost forget about the interface, and am thinking and acting on my ideas almost directly. But here, I am constantly distracted by having to fight just a little with the UI.There are on-hover visual effects on a lot of cards, but it often lags just a little bit. Not much, but just enough to make everything look sluggish and unresponsive. This is especially noticeable when an animation effect is in progress elsewhere on the screen.Probably related to the above: the game is extremely resource intensive. While some of the 3D scenes used are nice, it doesn't seem to warrant just how much this game gets the fans on my CPU spinning like no other game. I seriously cannot understand how this game chokes up so much resource. At the end of the day, it's just a card game, it shouldn't be resource intensive at all. I should add, this was even though I was running the game on "low" settings, and even though my PC has great specs.It's a card game with a lot of unlockables, but there is no where I can look up all cards. Vampires' Melody is not a game, it's a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure e-book that's been dumped on Steam masquerading as a game. As a visual/interactive novel, this doesn't feature any notable gameplay, it's just a lot of clicking through badly written dialogue that would never have been accepted or published in print, which poses the question, "How did something this badly written end up on Steam?".To answer that question: When someone hoping to become an author is unable to get published in print, they spend $100 and dump their high school fan-fiction onto Steam, under the guise of a game.This E-book features Choose-Your-Own-Adventure elements where you make some decisions that don't do anything to change the fact this is just an E-Book. Nobody finished reading a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book and said "Boy, what a great game I just played!". Because E-books aren't games. And neither is this.There's a somewhat garbage high school anime club dropout fanfiction as the "author" writes all about his waifu who is a suspiciously young looking "Vampire" anime girl. Really makes you wonder what goes through people's minds when they write this kind of stuff. But that just furthers the pointlessness of this non-game. Visual novels/e-books are tedious at best... imagine the best novel you ever read, be that Hitchhikers Guide to the Galaxy or 2001: A Space Odyssey or Twilight (if you have terrible taste in literature), but then translate that to a format where the words dribble out and you have to click your mouse every time you wanted to read the next sentence, instead of just turning the pages. You'd think it was garbage.Now imagine that experience, but with much worse writing (because if these guys could write professionally, they'd be published authors and this would be on shelves in bookstores, and they wouldn't have to pay

No reason not to give this prologue a go... but current game design feels very strange... err... bad.I can't imagine gameplay loop wasn't inspired by Gloomhaven. That's a good plan - Gloomhaven is a really good game. But there's things in Gloomhaven's design you can't just jettison without making the game weird. Gloomhaven has a tight economy around movement. Maybe you find that frustrating, but you can't just lose that without breaking stuff. Here your character gets 6 hexes of movement free (while your enemies seem to have very little) and you can mix and match movement with actions. Fun and flexible right? Well... except it means nothing matters, because you can trivially kite everything. I feel like at one point movement was card based, and they ditched that to make the game more accessible without really considering it much. That's not a good pattern. Did they playtest this prologue, and were they happy with the tactical gameplay that's here? The hand economy feels weird/confused. You redraw to 5 each turn, keeping what you have. Is "discarding a card" supposed to be a cost? Because it's absolutely a payoff that helps you push through bad cards. This means that most turns you'll be using both your "discard for melee" and "discard for movement" options. If possible, you'll also want to use the "discard a card when you disengage from an enemy" thing (which seems like it should be a cost not a benefit) each turn too. If you're going to have "madness" cards that trigger on discard (as they do), giving everyone 2 (or 3) free discard effects a turn is going to make them very difficult to balance (or make their "hard cast cost" irrelevant).Is getting a new card when you kill an enemy supposed to be a punishment?

The story and characters are very basic and best described as "fine," the art and presentation are a little cheap, and the game technically runs very well. However, it's the mechanics that are a mess, and the bulk of the game's content, and I want to explain how annoying this game is to actually play. Combat itself is a pretty basic round-based combat system. Nothing really to remark on fundamentally. But let's discuss what you can actually do besides use equipped items to buff/heal, and that's arts. Arts are every spell and attack, from free ones to the most expensive. There is no "attack" or "defend" option, just arts. Using them is just clicking on them, but how they work is a mess. Someone on Steam edited their characters' stats to test out what they actually do, and it turns out, every art works off different stats, with absolutely no in-game mention of this. The result is some very frustrating outcomes, like the guy who starts with a bow and has high agility but is terrible with bows, for example, that would lead the average person to just keep using bows with him, having no luck, and assuming he just sucks or bows suck.
