This is a decent first attempt at a horror game and it's not awful. It's priced appropriately too. However, I still cannot recommend it. To begin with, the entire game can be completed in less than an hour. There are only three levels and two of them take place in the same small house, one during the day and the other at night. The third level is not really scary and involves backtracking through a dark forest and getting lost while moving at a snail's pace. There is also an issue with lighting where candles and other lights cast a bloom that washes everything out in white and creates some strange shadows. I also experienced some random frame rate drops in 4k resolution with an RTX3080 and i9 processor no matter what graphic settings I selected. You also cannot manually save the game, so if you quit playing you must restart the level from the beginning. You also cannot remap the controls and there is nothing showing you that the lighter is number 4 on the keyboard and using the flashlight is F. You just have to figure that out on your own by pressing every key on the keyboard until you find what works. There are also some of those cheap quick jumpscares, so be prepared for that. Like I said, it's certainly not the worst horror game and this developer definitely has some talent. I am still interested though in future games from this developer.

Also in Skyrim the merchants don't regenerate gold quickly, so it can be a few days before the merchants gold coffers fill back up. Pop back in an hour and they may have 25 gold, a day later it maybe upto 200 gold and it slowly tops up in a more realistic fashion. Tainted Grail suffers from the 'billionaire' merchants fault. You can turn up at a merchant and dump thousands and thousands of golds worth of garbage on them and they buy it all at the going rate. Even merchants who categorically state they don't buy iron or weapons will happily buy iron and weapons off you. Obviously it makes no sense as any merchant with tens of thousands of gold on them would not be standing on a beach buying rotting shirts off an adventurer. game_name: Atelier Sophie: The Alchemist of the Mysterious Book DX
review: After about 20 hrs, I feel rather indifferent to this game. It's definitely more beginner friendly than Rorona (the only other Atelier game I've played), but the side characters aren't as interested. That's to say, they all start off interesting but their stories never go anywhere that made me feel invested like in Rorona. Graphically, I actually prefer Rorona's style. It may not be as technically impressive, but it had a strong water color aesthetic that was more pleasing to look at. I also prefer the hand drawn style of the character portraits versus the moving models of Sophie. Sure, it could be infuriating, but I also felt like I was working towards a goal. While in Sophie I can work at my own pace, I now feel like I'm just spinning my wheels trying to make progress, but seeing little results. On the flip side, I'm far more comfortable with experimenting with alchemy than previously. I have a feeling this will help me if I go back to the older titles of the franchise.In terms of combat, it's more of the same except I don't really see the results of the passive skills my party unlocks though I don't feel like it's hurt my enjoyment of battles.Overall, I feel less inclined to play the modern Atelier game (let alone finish Sophie), and more interested in playing the PS3 era titles.

Profit margins are razor thin and a single minor misstep or bout of bad luck has the chance to turn the game unrecoverably lost.The game requires a huge amount of preexsisting knowledge to make decisions, which you can only gain by trying, failing and reloading. On top of that even if you have that knowledge the game has a bunch of very random instant game overs on top.This is not just a question of hard difficulty and an unforgiving world as the developers try to put it. I encountered several unwinnable situations with no ability to know that they were unwinnable beforehand.I was really looking forward to this but very sadly I absolutely cannot recommend this game in its current stage, especially at its notably high price.The core systems are awesome and hit my game tastes very well but the resulting whole is exceedingly frustrating. In my opinion the game requires effort from the developers approaching a complete rework in several areas.I am honestly crestfallen. I love some of the systems and am devastated that what I see as incredibly poor assembly completely ruins the game for me.

review: I really REALLY wanted to like this game, but it's just far too random at its core. Seems like enemy squads have laser focus and always all aim for the same unit on my side while my own units ALWAYS spread their damage out way too much. Ends up being a frustrating slog of my squads never taking out any enemy squad members when they need to and then losing 1-2 in the process. Visually, the game is stunning, the story and characters are pretty good so far, and the music is good. But 6 hours in and the randomness is already getting to be a little too much to enjoy. Permadeath being locked to the hardest difficulty is also a severe misfire. Modern Fire Emblem figured it out with Awakening. Difficulty options and permadeath options need to be separate. If they can tighten up the combat, ESPECIALLY against bosses, then they will have something special here, but as it is, I'd recommend waiting until they get it in a more enjoyable state.EDITTried it again, and while the permadeath issue has been fixed, the randomness is still too much for me to enjoy. Enemy squads still focus their damage way too much. You do get an "aggressive" atack mode eventually that supposedly makes it so that your units target lower HP enemies, it barely does that and you get hit with a 25% increased damage debuff through the enemies next turn, so it's not even worth it. I'll stick with fire emblem for my tactical fix

I really like autobattlers and this game has a lot of fresh ideas. The map, quests, equipment, characters being good/bad/neutral, and certain gear or quests requiring a specific disposition or race are all refreshing for the genre. I am not one to nitpick usually, especially on a decent game with so few reviews, but this one has a glaring flaw... your friggin' gear does not stay stashed and will disappear. Your party has extremely limited inventory space and there are a couple of ways to stash items, store them in a keep or dropping a loot crate. This in itself seems like a silly way to handle storage as your crates look exactly like other regular loot crates you'll find all throughout the game and you'll have to travel back and forth to each crate for specific items since the contents aren't shared across all of your crates globally. But overlooking the implementation approach, the system is bugged and your crates won't be there next time you load in, or items disappear in the keep! This severely impacted my enjoyment of the game as I lost quest items, keys, and components for legendary gear I planned to build. By the end, whether or not to keep any item I found was a judgment call on what other valuable item to toss to make room. Seems really easy to solve, such as simply adding more inventory space, since storing it doesn't impact much except adding tedium. Also, I am pretty sure if you save, achievements are disabled? I was still able to beat it in spite of this but cannot recommend it with such a game breaking bug. Will update to positive if fixed.

Once I graduated from university I hoped things would become more interesting but even once I had more time and money available to me, there wasn't anything I really wanted to do with it. The social system is non-existent; you can't spend time with your friends, you just slowly gain friendship points with them over time. Engaging in your hobbies gives you happiness points but after a few years I already had more of those than I knew what to do with. I could buy a bigger house or a fancy car but I didn't really see the point. In real life people feel massively compelled to aim for these materialistic goals but I don't think the game did a good job of incentivising you to care. I liked the idea of having kids (who I would need to provide for) but the social system was so grindy and bland that I lost interest. The first is an enhancement to your basic attack, basically adding an element and some debuff that corresponds with that element. The second is an actual ability, but all the ones I've tried just feel like either a ranged or melee attack with the similar element and debuff associated with the element. The third is some barrier ability that buffs your element attacks. In fact, the whole element system seems restrictive because, from what I've seen so far, elements build off of each other. For example, you regain more mana dealing damage to a burning enemy with certain upgrade nodes. It doesn't feel like there is a reason to mix and match.You'll be seeing the beginning sequence a lot because the first boss is a huge difficulty spike. It feels annoying because the dodge roll's invincibility feels ambiguous and is clunky with the cooldown.Where Dead Cells offers fluid and fast movement options, this offers nothing but a dodge roll on a slight cooldown. The game feels prematurely launched, though playable and enjoyable. Steam only allows for recommended or not, and in good conscience, I cannot recommend it to most buyers in the current state. A few more months of development and patches will definitely make a far more enjoyable experience. Here are my thoughts after some about sixty hours of playtime.Games like Hammerting and Oxygen Not Included sort of function through entropy. You must complete the game before resources run out. Advancing allows you to stave off entropy to a point where it may no longer even really be a factor, lending the end game to being more of a sandbox. Hammerting doesn't feature much - if any - of an entropy system. By mid to late game, the systems allow unlimited water, unlimited ore (i.e., ore crushers), and even the dwarves themselves don't seemingly die. This isn't necessarily bad, as the game could be oriented toward a more relaxed approach. ONI requires you to fundamentally grasp heat capacity, physical states of materials, and more. It isn't a game for everyone. Hammerting could appeal to a more casual crowd, however you cannot entirely let your foot off the "challenge" gas without having sufficient alternative systems to keep players engaged. I feel like those systems are lacking.Exploration is not particularly exciting. The lack of entropy in resources means that the value of discovering a huge vein of copper is exceedingly tempered. An ore crusher on even a small vein of ore means you now have - what appears to be at least - an unending supply of minerals. A new statue? That'd be neat if I could move it to my base as a decorative item, but the passive bonus to more headcount is nice if you are really in need of more dwarves.

I've spent a significant amount of time babysitting the terrible AI that either fall into caves and can't get out, or just idle around for no discernible reason. The rest of my time has involved very tediously assigning attribute points on every single dwarf every few minutes, and going in and out of the world map just to accept the same quests over and over again. Aside from those fairly major sticking points, Hammerting is pretty good. Maybe wait until release though.

It's much better now without the microtransactions (for those unaware, it used to be a mobile game with pretty intrusive in-app purchases), but the fact of the matter is that your decisions just don't matter in the long run because any individual fight could end the entire run through no fault of your own simply because all of the high-value cards shuffled to the top of your deck. On top of this, once you start losing, the mechanics of energy mean that you're more likely to continue to lose, since you need energy to manipulate the card draws, and you only get energy by winning the game of blackjack. There are many small balance changes that could ease this out -- I personally think it would be interesting if you could see how many of each number are left in the deck, so you can weigh your decisions a bit more accurately, though I've also thought that improving the player's core stats so one run of bad luck doesn't instantly end you could work -- but as it stands, it just doesn't feel fair, and what could be a very engaging game about playing the odds and rigging probabilities turns into a frustrating slog against unfair RNG. Anuchard is a console ported 2D retro pixel top down brawler with lightweight RPG elements. It's badly made with a plethora of problems from the lacklustre and uninspiring story, highly mediocre and unpleasant gameplay, and outright terrible technical implementation.There's some wacky story about you being a warrior who gets knocked out (yawn) and you're the mystical bellwielder so you must grab your bell and go fight waves of crap pixel enemies, badly. From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics. It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.While there are options to change the resolution for the game, all this does is scale up the simplistic 2D art assets used to make the game, which makes little or no difference to the graphics quality. Without any other substantial graphics tweaks, it's not possible for gamers to improve the lacklustre 2D visuals.The controls and game handling are notably very clunky and unsmooth here. It's janky and unsatisfying to play... and any experienced gamer will tell you, the handling, responsiveness and general gameplay feel of the control scheme must be well polished for this kind of game to succeed. Unfortunately, this is something the developer seems to have phoned in, with little to no apparent gameplay testing. Movement is sluggish and it feels like there's half a second between animation frames when you attack enemies... did they not test this game at all before inflicting it on gamers? They dropped the ball on this one.To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold

The game is pleasant to look at! It was odd to see some non pixel art things (eg the food) against a full pixel art world but, eh, who cares, it's coolMusic: Average- Music in video games is a really important facet for me. I'm the kind of person to have hundreds of hours of soundtracks downloaded from everything I've played. This music? I wouldn't bother listening to it outside of the game. I'd love to see something similar in the future, just with better mechanical execution.

Bite the Bullet is a somewhat broken console ported 2D retro pixel side scrolling shooter. There's a few gimmicks like a mechanic that allows you to "eat" your enemies to recover health, but this doesn't make the game remotely better or more interesting than any other shovelware 2D retro pixel game. The game is broken for many users under recent builds of Windows 10 and 11, launching past the first splashscreen into an endless black screen... you can terminate this by switching desktops (win + -> keys) and then launching task manager to kill the stalled process. Surely the pinnacle of game development... not testing their game or making sure it runs on Windows. If you can get it to work, from a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.A choice was made to use obsolete, decades old retro pixel "art" as a substitute for contemporary PC graphics. It's unclear if this is due to lack of budget or talent, regardless, the overall visual quality of the game is extremely low as a result.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.The game features no proper level design or game/story flow/plot, as they opted to try to use samey repetitive procgen algorithms as a substitute for adding such content to the game, to avoid doing the important job of level/map design. As a result, the game doesn't actually have any content worth mentioning, just endless, boring, repetitive, soulless algorithmically generated sameyness. Developers must learn that procedural generation is not an acceptable substitute for content.Because this is a console game, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies. Everything from the excessive "click & hold" actions to dismiss/continue, to the excessive menus and steps to perform actions, shows a complete lack of understanding of UI Design and User Experience. Item storage is the same. Weapon customization had great potential, but is also a complete UI/UX failure. The bright point of the game is that it runs smooth and looks good. IF... game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: The game crashes randomly while playing. When combined with manual saving and long dungeons, this means its extremely easy to lose very long periods of playtime. I was hoping NIS would do a better job with their ports.

game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: A very barebones port that changes next to nothing from the PSP original, which might've been fine if it weren't for the fact that NIS took a sledgehammer to the game's postgame content. A total of 16~ optional dungeons alongside various rewards tied to those dungeons were removed from the game completely due to licensing issues. The main game is seemingly untouched, so this might not be a deal breaker if you aren't looking to do any of the optional content, but you're likely still better off looking elsewhere instead of supporting yet another lazy cashgrab from NISA.

game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: Unfortunately I have to recommend the PSP version over this release. That is until someone mods in the Dengeki dungeons, which is probably possible given there are mods for the original Disgaea PC that add the DS content in. But it doesn't exist yet.If you have the talent to do so, please, I would love to see a mod that redoes some of the less upscaled visuals and adds the missing content into the game. The Dengeki dungeons were a very large and sizable chunk of content and it's missing from the Switch and PC versions of this game.This is the only PS2/PSP NIS rerelease on PC to not include all gameplay content from previous versions of the game, so I have to mention it. (Technically Rhapsody is missing the DS content but all of that is just pieces of Cornet's story from Rhapsody 3, which is on PC, it's not worth hunting a Japanese DS copy for).Keep in mind that I wasn't one who cared about the online mode of Disgaea 5 being cut, and Disgaea 4 PC's online, I'd usually turn off because the netcode in that port is ass-backwards and adds entire seconds to half of the actions in the game.I doubt anyone who complains about the cut online in Disgaea 5 realizes how small of a part of the game it actually is, given how the only time it matters is netherworld invasions where occasionally some kind-hearted stranger puts a team optimized for your levelling as their invader team, and also how there's like 50 pre-made NPC teams that can show in offline mode instead.Luckily, Disgaea 7 doesn't have that issue Disgaea 4 has, online pings don't freeze the entire game for seconds in that one. I cannot stress how ass it is to actually play

game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: Flat out the worst "classic" game in the NIS library. the humor barely makes up for the over the top generic idea of the story, the rate at which the main character grows stronger is so bad it makes Disgaea 6 look like an absolute master piece (which Disgaea 6 is the absolute worst game in their modern library to date) and simply put, i genuinely wish they would have let this completely outdated and worthless game stay in their past. and this is coming from not just a long time fan of NIS, but someone who has put over 10k hours across all the games i could find before nis ever posted the first disgaea remake on steam. to anyone who is reading this and thinks this looks like a good intro to nis games, you might as well just go back to playing the latest flavor of the week triple A game you usually play. you'll have way more fun and not waste 20 bucks on something that shouldn't have been put on this platform.

game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: They cut 16 dungeons worth of content from this release without any warning on the store page. This scummy kind of practice does not deserve any support whatsoever.

game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: Been looking forward to playing some of the older NIS games, this one included. I wish I could say I was as stoked on it as everyone else but the game loop wasn't doing it for me. Managing hunger and weapon condition during dungeon runs seemed designed to artificially cause the player to run out of steam and fail. Failing feeds into the weird leveling mechanic where you get better base stats on every death. Many times I found myself unable to find food in the dungeon and failing even though I was doing well. Leveling your base stats does mean you do more damage, which allows you to use weapons less often or just use your fists but I didn't find this strategically rewarding.Another thing is cash. You're just not going to have much of it between runs and you'll lose it when you fail. I'm sure someone is thinking "well you're not playing the game right" and maybe so but this isn't my first rodeo, I shouldn't need a manual on how to afford a healing potion. Grinding for cash on easy levels seems monotonous even for a casual Disgaea player like myself. On top of that, it seemed like there were too many game mechanics of little value for the added complexity being introduced. The facilities, combat mechanics, enemy hearing, the body enhancements, the power gauge and monster staffing of facilities.Story was okayish for what I played but couldn't finish as I wasn't finding joy in completing dungeons.

game_name: ZHP: Unlosing Ranger vs. Darkdeath Evilman
review: ZHP is a very good game. The problem is that the steam version is a hamstrung version of the original game. 16 different Dungeons were removed from the game and while none of them were necessary for the game's completion they did help to speed up the grind and be entertaining side stories. Now maybe this is due to being unable to get permissions to use the extra content from when the game was originally released and if so that can't be helped as licensing problems are like that sometimes. What CAN be prevented is the lack of transparency to the customer by not mentioning the fact that they have taken a lions share of the content OUT of the game and that this game is basically a discount port of the original game. Do yourself a big favor and buy the original release on the PSP instead.

Absolutely not. Not, "it was good but." Not, "I wish there were a middle option." No. Just, no.If you want your choices undermined so that the plot of the series can move at a snail's pace, or if you like to watch any character development reset at the whims of the author, give it a try. I wanted to write a long essay about why this is just...not it, but the long and short of it is it doesn't matter. None of it matters.

I'm beginning to wonder what the editors and "beta readers" for this series actually do - because it's not evaluate the relationship beats, plot points and structure in anywhere near as much critical detail as they need. The whole plot feels baggy and unfocused, and while there are some good "moments" between the detective and their Love Interest, the connective tissue between these moments is often incoherent.This book also seems to fundamentally misunderstand the point of a slow burn romance, both for A and for M - the slow burn routes are, I suspect for coding reasons, forced to follow a similar structure to the routes with more emotionally available LIs, which leads me to question what the purpose of a slow burn route in these stories would be. It certainly does not create any additional tension. Often when tension is created between two characters (be that between the detective and the LI or with ) it is resolved disappointingly quickly.The detective's responses seem to be forced - their reaction to Rebecca, their manipulative, absentee mother, has no effect on how the narrative presents her or on how UB reacts to her and the relationship more generally; the climactic moments of both routes fail to allow for adequate choice of responses where in previous books it has been much more possible to replay the books with a wide range of LI relationship dynamics; and the lack of ability in this book to question seems like a glaring missed opportunity.In a genre that is quite literally supposed to be about , the progression of this game is beginning to feel stilted, which is very disappointing. While I would wholeheartedly recommend Books 1 and 2 to a reader, I would not recommend Book 3 as it fails to deliver on the promise

Reading this book felt like breaking up with a darling. I never review games on my profile, but I had to try for this one. Funny enough, I cannot do it. I cannot bring myself to write negative things about this. Doing so gives me a painful pang in my heart, and I think that's a huge testament to the brilliance of the first two installations of the series. The Demo portion of Wayhaven, which consists the beginning six chapters of this book, put a smile on my face and a little flutter in my heart for more than a year. It was everything that I could hope for. It is still the one brilliant thing about this book, from the pacing, promised plotlines, team-bonding, angst, everything. That's the part I'll take away with me.For myself, as a longtime fan, I wish I could stay there, in that sweet little literary promise. After being through with this book twice, I don't have the rose-tinted glasses that I loved so much to see Wayhaven through anymore. That's why it feels like a breakup. I know how great potential this has, and how great it could be, but it doesn't work out. And while it was a little crushing for me in the first days, that is okay now.I still love Mishka, and her consistent wholesomeness, cheer and optimism. I have such respect for how she single-handedly tackles what must be a gargantuan project, and the joy it seems to bring her. I still care for Wayhaven, from the dog in the fire department to Verda's adorable little family. But it brings me sadness to think that now might have fallen out of love with Wayhaven and my LI.

This book is for the fans, but the story loses sight of what made Book 1 and 2 so great. Writing this much takes a lot of time and effort and I know that Mischa put a lot of love and care into the interactions with the Vampire heroes. But that's all we get. The overall plot, the world-building, the antagonist, the lack of anxiety, of tension as you play, it all adds up to a lackluster result. I don't feel like the Detective really is a detective anymore. She has settled into her role as the chosen one and doesn't really have to work for it. Any training she does is superseded by a romantic moment, which is great if you love the romance, but how are we supposed to believe that she could survive if the world is as dangerous as we are constantly told this Supernatural World is? The MC just easily overcomes every obstacle with no lasting consequences. There don't seem to be any credible threats, any hard choices in this book. One of the few "bad" things that can happen to her is that one of the other teams decides they don't like her. They say that she didn't work for her position on the team, and honestly, I feel like this is a valid point to take. Nonetheless, we don't have any choice to acknowledge that maybe we did get ahead through Rebecca's connections rather than our own hard work and grift. We just get reassurance from our Love Interest that they are just haters and everyone should like us, because we are so great. I know this is fantasy, but come on, is this one of the things that bothers us? In a world where we are fighting to survive, we are worried

I love Wayhaven Chronicles. I have for years now. This one isn't hitting the same. I have high hopes for the next one, though. :)

For those who like it short and sweet: If you haven’t played the first two games, I advise you to stay away from this series. Far away. Unless you’re into emotional edging and love roleplaying an UwU tween angst machine, anyway. The most glaring problem is the pacing. Put bluntly, it sucks. This game is pitched as a romance, but three full installments in and two of the LIs are still stuck in first gear. There are “moments”, but no relationship available and no steps towards one. It’s hot and cold, back and forth, one step forward and two steps back. Any progress is immediately retconned or completely ignored. Why? Because the author promised to have just as many “moments” for the slow burns as the other two LIs, but she never promised they would actually mean anything, because you aren’t allowed to have a relationship until book 5 or 6, no matter how stupid and contrived it becomes!A good example of this is M. In this particular installment, M’s path is phenomenal. By the end of the game, M is clearly in love with the MC and all but says so, both to the MC (“You think I could do without you now?”) and to a best-friended A, (“Let's just hope she's as relieved to have me too.”). At the end of the game, M looks at the MC and takes a shot of hard liquor to “Never have I ever fallen for a coworker.” M hates food and even the mildest thing aggravates their senses, but they downed liquor described as window cleaner. Looks like love, right? Not so fast, buddy, there are seven books in this series!The author has said M is still clueless about their feelings. All that in the previous paragraph? That means nothing. M

This series is too long for its own good. Three books is okay. But SEVEN?! (source - )This should have been the last book in the series. No one would have batted an eye if it graciously wrapped up the story and relationships and went out with a bang and fanfare. Worst of all, the first 2 books were the perfect set up for a final installment. But Book 3 is not the last book. It's a filler entry and it shows. By extension, Book 3 ends up dragging the whole series up to this point down into the pits of mediocrity. The poor pacing and drop in story quality is frankly jarring. The author may have written themselves into a knot - and it's only the third book out of seven.While the previous 2 books were good on their own merit without the romances, this one isn't worth reading UNLESS you wanna see more interactions with your favourite LIs. I would say those are good, but there are 2 issues that sour the experience. If you're and A or M fan, you're screwed, moreso in case of A. The edging is funny to joke about, but frankly, it's not actually even funny anymore. And secondly - you can't separate the romance from the story, so you will have to suspend your disbelief for the bits that don't make any sense.In the end, it's a filler book with too many words and not enough substance, and it both overstays its welcome and stuns you with its abrupt ending. There are probably many things I could point out (main/support characters characterisation, world building, etc etc) but I don't care enough to do that. This book is boring. And that's probably worse than just being bad.Do read the first 2 books though.

The English isn't resized meaning that it overflows in many different spots, artefact beads in particular being unreadable.The game is far too easy off the bat, being beatable on the first try without needing to do too well at all, the final boss being the easiest out of the four main bosses I ran into. The lack of originality and innovation doesn't end there ... for some reason almost every game from China HAS to feature Sun WuKong (the monkey king) .... no idea why, its the equivalent of every western game starring Robin Hood!?There's a wealth of material to draw from (Japanese devs did with Dynasty warriors etc.) but no.... I beat the game on my first run....... not because I'm really good, but because I just mashed every skill that wasn't on a cooldown......but I apparently have to beat it multiple times to get the ending to a story I don't really care that much about. This is a button mashing game. You have an unlimited dodge that functions as an i-frame, but there is so much stuff going on at the same time that you are better off just holding down the basic attack button and mashing the 1, 2, 3 and 4 key for skills, along with right click.There are a lot of currencies in the game to upgrade this or evolve that, but I don't really care about any of it since +(random percentage) to max HP, attack etc is the only thing that really matters. You could do a lot worse for 8 bucks, the game functions fine, but it's just too button mashy and too easy with no actual evolution of enemies or yourself. I'd say builds can have variety, I guess, but when you are just spamming every skill not on cool down it doesn't really matter. If you don't want to button mash try Nightmare: The Lunatic. It got a 1.0 release and I left a great review for it. If you want something more mash centric, play Hades or any of its many clones. Just uh... skip this one.

I am in a very much on the fence with this title. I love the deck building progression system, the core mechanic of drawing a hand of passive bonuses each turn and then deciding how best to utilize them or whether to suffer some extra damage so you can hit harder that turn, its fun, the puzzle-esque combat is great.All of my gripes come down to how unintuitive and jumbled everything comes across. For some strange reason your enemies' areas of effect are disabled by default and turn off after each dungeon. This is necessary information in order to play the game and should ALWAYS be on. Further, certain enemy attacks or abilities are not explained, multiple times I've been standing near a mushroom and it will explode and deal significant damage, sometimes they explode after one turn, sometimes two, I still cannot figure out what triggers them to detonate.Many of the cards and abilities are unclear, one card says that my umbrella will emit "Nasty Spores", and I'm unsure what those do, I tried it hoping to figure it out for future characters and the ability killed me.Campaign Vs Roguelike Mode: I played primarily the campaign mode because it seemed to have faster progression, it looked like you needed to grind A LOT of runs to unlock new classes in Roguelike mode, but the overworld map in Campaign mode is also rather difficult to parse out and I really wish there were quickmenu options since the game teleports you to the center of the map each time you finish a dungeon.There is an absolute gem of a game here, it just needs some polish. I will be watching for updates and will adjust my review accordingly.Warm Regards,Will

I really wanted to like this game. The art style is cute and I can see the passion that the developers have for it and the engagement with the community. There is even 5 or so seconds lag every time you enter a stage before your cards show up to offer bonuses.The core gameplay has potential but the way the game starts is pretty damn overwhelming when within 20 minutes there's so much open on the map. I really wish I had a better sense of direction because a few of the dungeons just feel impossible to complete at my level. Not to mention worthwhile loot feels few and far inbetween. i'm just clicking and attacking maybe using a spin every few turns.I won't be refunding this game because I have faith that the devs will iron things out in the long run but for now maybe wait until then before you purchase.

My problem with the game is that its a really fun game that seems largely untested. I actually like the game, and am going to continue to play it, but there are a bunch of glaring problems that make me think the game left early access due to time pressure, and not because it was actually a finished product. I will keep playing, and if the devs fix all this ♥♥♥♥ I complain about in this review (balance problems, and performance issues), I'd be happy to change my review, but I don't think I can recommend the game for anyone looking for a finished product.It was pretty smooth sailing with some minor frame drops until I got to the 2nd boss fight, and that's when everything fell apart.First off, the design of the second boss is genuinely hateful. He summons bone piles which can block movement, as well enemies, including necromancers which can animate those bone piles into skeletons. This by itself was not a big deal. It becomes a big deal when you consider:-The map you fight him on (or at least the map I fought him on) was basically a big square circle that you can't move through the center of.-He had like 700 hp. At this point I was riding a pretty busted buff combo, and had +30 damage to all of my attacks *almost trippling my base damage*. Even with my souped up damage, it took me between 15-20 attacks to kill him.-The turn after you melee him he jumps across the map. Thats right, you can get 1, maybe 2 attacks in before he leaps away.All three of these things together means that while normal fights were taking me a few minutes, the boss fight took me nearly forty minutes. I was never in danger.

I cannot believe I am, for the first time in my life, lamenting procedural generation in a video game. But this game has far too much of it. Almost every banner, title, or description in this game has some form of randomly-selected with seemingly no character limit. And normally that wouldn't be terrible. After all, other games come up with NPCs on the fly and provide unique weapons with mishmash stats. However, this game takes the idea and runs. Sometimes, less is more and a few times now the random title or character name legitimately pushes other text out of the speach bubble. Greedy Dungeon is a deck-builder in which you enter dungeons of increasing size with the goal of basically just exploring rooms (battling AI-brain-dead enemies along the way). After your run, you spend your gained resources on purchasing and upgrading cards. You may build your 30-card deck as you see fit. The core gameplay/update cycle is passable for awhile. Unfortunately, the extremely limited mechanics, enemy diversity, and lack of interesting negative statuses, lead the battles to become extremely, extremely, repetitive. Even this is OK for awhile, until you reach the later rank dungeons, where in lieu of an actual challenge, you are treated to increasingly larger damage sponges. I had planned on finishing the game, but decided that life is far too short for such tedium. There are some other pointless aspects as well, including a fatigue system (which punishes exploring but then gives you twice as many fatigue potions than you will ever need), and the fact that loot clogs your hand but may be easily purged and stored by the automatically-granted allocation of "banking" opportunities.The only positive to be taken away is that this game can be had for ~$2. If you have oodles of time and don't have oodles of money, then you may give it a try. Otherwise, you should pass.Overall: 3/10

A fresh look at the genre. A great genre that was a little bit spoiled by crooked copies of Slay The Spire. Combat is based on positioning (movement), turn order and most importantly a ton of all sorts of cool tricks and ways to interact with enemies, allies, environment and even interface.Everything that is in this game can be combined with each other, to get some interesting solutions. Everything in the game can be manipulated, one way or another.You don't notice it much at first (maybe if I was smarter, I would have noticed it all at once), but with every hour of play you start to open your sharingan, or 3rd eye if you follow the theme of the game.By the way, the game is tagged as a card game. But the cards here are not exactly cards. Basically, you don't have a deck, but you collect skills, which with few exceptions are always with you. You see what enemies are going to do. And in that sense, there's almost no randomization in the game (in this part of it). That said, every fight is not a problem with only one solution. Usually if you can't defeat your enemies with method 1, 2, 3. After thinking about it, you find a way 4, 5, 6, which work and at the same time these methods can play completely different from each other.And the cards are just, well, creatures on the battlefield.So in a way it's not a card game, but ideologically it's still a card game.I don't want to get your expectations too high, it's a game after all, not IV painkillers. But it's not a lame parody of StS, and it's not a game where they just threw everything in a pile and didn't do any work on it.

The game is an excellent, faster paced version of the Civilisation-type strategy genre (4x?), with a greater emphasis on combat. Most of the typical elements have been stripped back to their core; and the complexity of the game in maintained in how the developers have rearranged elements such as politics, economy, and general resource management. DO NOT PLAY THIS EXPECTING CIVILIZATION At it's core, Ara is a production chain management game that uses a civThere are some really innovative ideas here, and most of them are executed well. First off, the region-based map system is a huge breath of fresh air. It makes city expansion feel much more deliberate and is a better fit for the spread-out 'district' system that Civ 6 popularized than a generic hex grid. Additionally, substitutions in the production management as you unlock new resources keeps even some of your earliest setups relevant and able to be repurposed. The game does have some notable flaws. While micromanagement itself is no issue, the UI is not well designed to reduce tedium. At minimum, there needs to be some sort of 'change all' button for improvements to reduce the clicking required when you get the next generation of tools available. Additionally, the pacing can feel a bit odd, especially in era 1 on large maps when nearly all space is filled rather quickly. Civilizations disappearing between era transitions helps, but then you have large areas deserted for a long time due to the inherent benefits of rushing your city cap as early as possible. Ultimately it feels like a respectable 7/10, that can become an 8/10 with some early patches. $60 is a bit much for the current state of the game, but I would recommend the game on sale to any production chain fans.

I spent quite some time with this one before it came to Steam. And it seems the game has received a boatload of improvements since then, the pathfinding is better and so it the enemy AI, and there's some quality of life enhancements.Now, the game. It's an RTS, and one of early 3D ones. You're in command of military group trying to eliminate all hostile threats to rebuild the new world order. There's plenty of RTS staples here, like base building, scattered on the map point capture, loads of units and research... except there's a lot way more research and units than average. As a matter of fact, it would take you hours upon hours to explore the whole tech tree, so you really have to pick out what you really want to focus on and ignore researches you don't plan on using - and that's factoring in that often the battles here last longer than in more established competitive RTSes - this one is quite a turtler's delight with long range artillery and dedicated counterbattery fire mechanics, incredibly generous selection of defensive structures, and slow pace. Also, another important feature - all the vehicles require a custom design, which includes selecting their propulsion (tracks, wheels, VTOL drive, etc), their hull, and their weapons. Also a name, if you feel like adding some flair - which means there's a lot of unit options ingame, and you can adapt your forces to current demands with ease.The campaign plot is about a military group trying to recover lost technology to assist in their rebuilding efforts. Early on in the campaign they jsut have to deal with bandits and marauders running at them with guns or with cobbled together vehicles, but as plot advances they encounter an entire hierarchy of technological advanced groups,

Tails of Trainspot, a Hashi/Bridges logic puzzle game, falls short of expectations due to a myriad of issues that hinder the overall experience. Priced steeply for its brief content, the game suffers from noticeable grammatical errors resulting from its Japanese translation, adding further frustration for players.The lack of adjustable graphics and sound settings leaves much to be desired, and the finicky mouse controls, a result of the game's origins as a Nintendo Switch port, only add to the disappointment. Players are forced to endure lengthy, nonsensical dialogue upon replaying levels, adding unnecessary tedium to the gameplay.The much-touted "endless" online mode is anything but, as players are given a mere 60 seconds to complete all levels. This jarring time constraint not only disrupts the immersive nature of logic puzzles but serves as an ill-conceived substitute for genuine difficulty, undermining the game's core appeal.In conclusion, Tails of Trainspot fails to deliver a satisfying and engaging experience for fans of logic puzzles. With its multitude of problems and lackluster execution, potential players are better off exploring other titles in the genre.

This is a fun and cute little puzzler. Each level provides a layout of "stations," which are each marked with a number indicating the number of tracks that must connect to them. Stations can only connect to other stations directly north, south, east or west of them, and stations can be connected by one or two tracks. Based on the station layout, it's up to you to figure out the track layout that satisfies the required number of connections for each station.The puzzles start very simple, but the game begins introducing other mechanics that complicate things. Some stations have a hidden number, which can only be determined by satisfying the stations surrounding them. In other cases, there are two "abandoned" stations, only one of which can be restored, so you have to determine which station will fit into your layout and which will break it.For almost all of the game, the only constraint is funding. Each time you draw a track, you spend funds, and each time you remove a track to correct a mistake, you are only partially refunded. So the game rewards you for logically working out the required connections, while a brute force or random approach may result in running out of funds. Towards the very end, the game includes several timed puzzles, where solving a level quickly adds additional time to your bank to use on the next puzzle. Puzzle solutions are awarded up to three stars, based on how many funds or how much time you have left, at the end of the level. There are even a few minigames interspersed between the levels.Overall, this is a fun little puzzle game that's worth its price. The only criticism I would probably offer is that the puzzle difficulty ramps up a bit too slowly. The final

Submarine Titans is an ancient game from 2000. It's a whopping 23 years old at the time of this review. The game lacks proper widescreen aspect ratio support (it's locked at 4:3) or support for any modern gaming display resolutions, hasn't been modernised or updated to run smoothly on modern gaming PCs. Despite this lack of modernisation, it carries a pretty high price tag for such an ancient game. This seems to have been put on Steam as a nostalgia gouge.It's a run-of-the-mill base builder/resource harvester/army builder RTS (a great format for games and it's a shame they've mostly stopped being made). The only big differentiator here is the underwater theme, you build an underwater base and your units are attack submarines. The gimmick never really caught on.From a technical perspective, the game doesn't meet basic minimum requirements that most PC gamers expect as standard.There's no options to change the resolution for the game or customise the graphics settings. There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the very badly dated graphics. Another problem here is that you can't alt+tab out of the game properly, another shortcoming that should have been picked up with even a basic amount of software testing. The graphics will be distorted if you try go back into the game after switching out. This is extremely frustrating in the modern era of gaming and it's a shortcoming that gamers are unlikely to accept.These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.Submarine Titans is relatively expensive for an abandonware nostalgia gouge, at $5 USD, and it's

The puzzles presented are well-crafted and require a dose of reflection and strategy to solve. Some situations can be truly challenging, but the feeling of conquering each obstacle is extremely rewarding.One of the most pleasant surprises in Diefrosty is its soundtrack. The game's OST. The music blends perfectly, complementing the gameplay experience exceptionally well.Despite being a relatively short game, with an average playtime of 3 hours, Diefrosty delivers a unique and memorable experience. The peculiar theme and creative approach make the time spent worth every minute. It is a perfect game to pass the time in a relaxed manner, offering stimulating challenges without becoming frustrating.Considering all these aspects, Diefrosty is a true a good Indie. If you are looking for a different chill puzzle game and provides a captivating experience, do not hesitate to acquire this title. Its original concept, simple gameplay, challenging puzzles, and incredible soundtrack make it a solid choice for indie game enthusiasts. Get ready to immerse yourself in a chilling and self-destructive journey filled with fun and satisfaction.

Ostriv is the next Banished. That's all that there is to it. Banished was abandoned, but Ostriv will not be. The reason that I know it will not be is that its developer just posted a development update with at least 10 new buildings, some improvements to houses, and additional work on new features. That's unremarkable aside from the fact that the country the developer lives in is currently under attack by the second-largest military in the world.Ostriv already currently beats the functionality of Banished out of the box. It also doesn't have a number of the gameplay problems that Banished has; things scale much more reasonably. There are some features that are clearly still in development, including an economy, health/education/governance systems, and closing the loop on some of the production cycles. My only concern, since raising concerns in the past has gotten results from the developer, is that the game doesn't have a great endgame. That's true of all of this genre though, and I don't expect Ostriv to solve it yet, particularly not while the core game loops are still being constructed/expanded.

I think my only major criticism would be that the internal economics, wealth distribution, and taxation systems could have been much more sophisticated, realistic, and challenging, especially given how the game's already existing and well-thought-out mechanics are perfect for a system that dynamically changes individuals' demands, spending, and satisfaction based on their wealth and income. You would also expect people, even in mostly closed and isolated feudal economies, to care about the actual value of their money compared to neighboring regions. In the current settings of the game, a player can easily tank all prices and wages in their town, allow an extremely small amount of money to circulate within households, and make absurd profits from immigrants who bring a good amount of money with them via wealth tax. I would also like to see an automated market system where townspeople can sell their own harvests, similar to what exists in Manor Lords.Nevertheless, the game is amazing overall, and I would recommend it to anyone even slightly interested in city-building or management genres.

A great turn-based tactical game, with plenty of class combinations to consider. All characters are story-based, and each have inherent strengths in the form of stat distribution and attack patterns, but this can be extensively augmented through equipping upgradeable class books with give further stat bonuses and extra skills.Level ups happen during the battles, resulting in immediately stat increases and the unit getting its health and spirit replenished (Battle of Wesnoth style), and that's always satisfying. All my units stayed within 2 levels of each other throughout the game, so XP seems to scale based on some calculation of action taken and current level. I found my healer was consistently the lowest level, while the units that regularly damaged or dispatched enemies were the front-runners. A lot of the learning curve has to do with mastering positioning and knowing how far each of your characters can attack. Once you figure this out, and assuming you have equipped classes that provide HP and Skill Point (SP) replenishment, the game becomes straightforward. is a free-to-play and easy-to-learn turn-based puzzle game with nice logic and quite a bit of variety to keep the mind entertained. The puzzles are split into different Chapters, each having a number of puzzles in the campaign. You can move from one level to the next after you have solved the last one.Pretty soon after starting, you will be gradually introduced to the different modifiers that are present in this game, and you will have to recognize what they do and learn in order to progress, especially in later-on-levels. Your goal is to get to the exit (green cube) before the enemies blocks catch up to you. They can catch you on the exit block after you final move, so you do not get a free turn, even at the end.The modifiers include stun trap (loss of turns), switches or plates on the floors that alter another part of the level (color designated), teleporters (to a specific tile), mines, bombs, etc. There are also character power ups that give you extra moves, cow your enemies, or provide a shield. The enemy types are ones that follow you, to ones that mirror you or do just the opposite, there are ones that pace back and forth and also ones that move twice as fast as you do.If you win, you can move on. If you lose, you can easily reset the level and try again. In the early stages, it was very easy, a few seconds per level and pretty soon you feel like there's no challenge at all. Touhou Mystery Reel has a lot of potential, and I can see the final product being absolutely fantastic. As of writing, the first two chapters have come out, and I have finished both. First off, the gameplay system. Rather than having traditional health, Touhou Mystery Reel (TMR from now on), has a "posture" system, where hits decrease your posture bar while it slowly refills. Once the posture bar is emptied, Cirno will be knocked back, and a red circle will appear in the center of her sprite. Until the posture bar refills completely, any hit will kill Cirno. However, being a fairy, Cirno cannot die, meaning that "dying" just lets you respawn immediately. At first, this may make the game seem incredibly easy. After all, how can a game be hard if you can't lose? TMR sidesteps this issue by having the bosses be brutal, at least the two that are currently out. The two bosses can be devastating, with the lack of a game over state allowing the game to pull some wacky shenanigans, like the second boss having a one shot move if you are late or early on an air intercept. This is quite the unique dynamic for a game, and I'm eager to see the devs take it further. Cirno also has skills, ranging from a simple charge attack to projectiles. Cirno can only have one skill at a time, with any skill you get just replacing the other. Some skills, like Fairy Punch, have a single use and are practically jokes. Others, like Quick Draw, allow you to fight the boss in a way the basic skill does not. Again, having only two stages so far, this mechanic has not reached its full use yet, though I expect more interesting skills in the future.The story

This feature makes Timemelters a refreshing and engaging title, reminiscent of classic RTS games with a twist.The game's design encourages experimentation with multiple solutions to each level, enhancing replayability. Despite its linear map structure, the diverse objectives and mechanics keep the gameplay fresh and challenging. The co-op mode adds another layer of enjoyment, allowing friends to tackle the campaign together, even if only one person owns the game.While the graphics and character models may not be top-notch, the art style in the cutscenes is charming, and the soundtrack complements the game's atmosphere well. The story, involving witches and time travel, is captivating, though some players might find it less compelling than the gameplay itself.Timemelters does have a learning curve and minor kinks, but the developers appear to be responsive and committed to improvements. Overall, it's a standout indie title that combines creativity and strategic depth, making it a must-play for fans of puzzle and strategy games.

This is honestly unbelievably good, the level of innovation and creative gameplay design reminds me of some of the best experimental outcomes from the PS2/Gamecube era of gaming. It's deeply fun and satisfying, and the way the game acclimatizes you to the 4D strategy is so seamless that you barely notice it happening until you're late in the game and suddenly you're coordinating a multilayered defensive strategy using 4 different timelines, not even knowing how you got to the point of being able to keep track of it all. This isn't the strongest story, nor the best voice acting, but it's 100% worth a try regardless because I haven't had this much fun with getting used to a mechanic since the first Portal.The one caveat to all of this is that at the end of the day this game feels like a proof of concept. The core mechanic is rock solid and perfectly implemented, but the limited number of spells don't allow for as varied a set of approaches. The maps are designed almost like puzzles with a specific correct solution, instead of as sandboxes that let you take any approach you want to a seemingly insurmountable challenge. I'd love to see something more along the lines of a system where you build a set of spells you have access to over the course of a campaign, letting you engage with the environment in a unique way based on your playstyle. Something like a 1 v 1 vs mode might be interesting to see as well. This is all the kind of thing I would hope to see as an evolution of the concept in a sequel, but for a first game breaking in a new idea, this is amazing.

I’d like to preface this review by saying it was written while the game was in Early Access and that fact was taken into consideration while writing this. AMazing TD is an interesting take on the Tower Defense genre. It reminds me of the Tower Defense (TD) games I used to play as custom games in Warcraft 3 and Starcraft 2. It probably reminds me of that because it is a standalone spiritual successor of a Starcraft 2 map I had played previously called Entropy TD.It’s a deceptively simple appearing Tower Defense game. You build living statues as your towers and they deal with the various waves of enemies. The longer you can keep enemies from exiting the map, the more likely you are to eliminate them. Building a maze and well placed, properly upgraded towers is the key to victory in these sorts of games. AMazing TD goes beyond the basics by also having power fields on the play field that modify the game in some way. Fields that slow, speed up and teleport the enemies, increase the range or damage of your towers or even offering you extra gold are some of the field effects to watch out for when planning your maze. It’s not exactly that forgiving of a TD game either. If you don’t build in a logical way, such as going quantity over quality, you likely won’t survive. Some towers I found to be far more useful than others but they each do have their uses. Experimenting to find the most versatile towers is part of the challenge and fun of TD games. There are various enemy types to contend with too. You might build yourself an incredibly long well thought out winding maze with teleporters pushing enemies back to earlier points in your maze

This is an amazing free addition to the board game that turns a negotiation-based competitive game into a marvellous cooperative experience reminiscent of the noteworthy indie video game, FTL. As of reviewing this in late 2022, I've played through once in a three-player game in August and scored a very difficult, skin-of-our-teeth victory. A large positive part of our experience lies in the freedom players have when kitting out their ships; since everyone is trying to optimise their ship for a different purpose, you are more likely to get ship parts and crew that scale well with one another, unlocking interesting combos. A prominent negative I can mention is that the frequent typos break immersion in the scenarios presented.An additional benefit is that this theoretically makes the two-player experience good. Competitively, the base board game depends so much on negotiation that the solo mode is an interesting negotiation-free puzzle and three players allow the game to shine, but the two-player experience is caught in an unsatisfactory limbo between the two. Cooperatively, this limbo space no longer exists and the players can work together on the puzzle presented.Finally, I want to mention the pleasing aesthetic of the game; I don't particularly remember the audio, which I'm sure was fine, but the artistic style shared with the base board game feels simultaneously retro, arcade-gamey, and futuristic with its pixelated appearance.EDIT: I have more recently played the game with four players and it stretched out too long. The duration of the game scales out of control based on the number of players. This should strictly be played with three or fewer players.

If you play for long enough to get to the hard dungeons, it's pretty important to have a clear overview of your options, and most of your decisions are made based on this information.And lastly, as others have pointed out, the unique art is no longer present, instead replaced with what I consider fairly lazy art. for example, if you were to pick a race (Kin in DD:Rewind), all the classes they could be would have unique art, whereas for this game I only saw a mannequin face for the different kin, and nothing else. That is what I mean when I say it feels like lazy art.

I suspect that new players will therefore tend to prefer Rewind -- much like more seasoned players will tend to prefer the original. It was a good decision to release Rewind as a separate game for this reason; imagine the outcry if the original was re-mastered in-place!You simply will not find a better dungeon puzzler with Roguelite elements than Desktop Dungeons. I think that both versions have something to offer, and I recommend trying one, the other, or both.

This is truly an SGS game "on steroids," and please pardon for using that cliché, but there is no other way to describe this release. In this reviewer's experience with several SGS games, The Korean War was a "big" game release - and the campaign is still being played to this day - but this one is simply spectacular.The previous SGS "Wars Across the World" series remain enjoyable mini-games usually at attractive pricing, but this one is a totally different animal. It should list-price for far more than the company is charging. With the introductory discount, it went for less than $30 US. It is worth almost the Matrix "War in the East 2" price of $80 retail.And an "animal" this game is. If one is concerned about the AI, just play NATO in one of the advanced scenarios, and you will be faced with a relentless attack by the Warsaw Pact. Good luck, Commander - you certainly won't be bored.The almost infinite variety of land, air and sea units and their descriptions and capabilities - often with headers in the native languages of the many owning country represented in the game - are thoughtfully presented in living color. (The NATO icon option is functional, but don't miss the vanilla displays.)The game is turn-based but almost feels like an RTS, depending on the "delay" level the player chooses during different phases and battle displays. The developers have piled on the complexity of the various combat elements in a modern battle setting (compared with the previous (and excellent) SGS offerings), while not burdening the player who wishes to "click-through" the combat phases.It's true that the Advanced scenarios feature a large number of air and land units to handle, but even for an oldster like this reviewer, the load is quite manageable

But if you add specialist units as appropriate for the terrain and units you are about to attack, or defend against, will be key to victory. Well can't say we can give SGS NATO'S Nightmare a thumbs up at this point. Been playing computer wargames since the 80s and this one is failing to deliver on a variety of fronts. As a veteran gamer I expect 1) game documentation which explains the basic gaming systems for starters and none exists, which makes it very difficult to get going and enjoy. I have had multiple play throughs where I literally only live for the first 3-5 jumps because I didn't receive the basic life sustaining resources and my crew died.This game is similar to a city builder but instead of being able to build the "city" you have to take what you find and hope that it is what you need. This adds a unique feel to the game but makes it brutally difficult even on the easiest settings. You actually cant build anything in the game, you can only relocate certain buildings and combine parts of existing buildings to repair them into working order. At it's core this game is a resource management game. You have to be mindful of how many crew members you bring on board as they will eat through your resource supply and cause you to lose the game if you don't keep an eye on it. Tohoku Kiritan is a VOICEROID character popular in Japan. VOICEROID is a type of text to speech software widely used in the Japanese Let’s Play scene. The Japanese way of doing things dictates that if you can substitute something with a cute anime girl you definitely should and it makes anything automatically better. Instead of using a webcam to record their faces most Japanese let’s players prefer to use anime characters as avatars and if they don’t possess cute girl voices, then the VOICEROID package provides an easy solution for both needs. The characters can serve as narrators or commentators to the provided gameplay thus putting more focus on the let’s player’s script writing ability rather than personal charisma, while also boosting creativity and providing greater freedom. As an added bonus most VOICEROID characters double as singing software on the VOCALOID or UTAU platform and therefore come with an already established fan base in the music scene. Of course this approach to let’s plays and streaming is largely unknown outside of Japan because of the language barrier. It’s also the reason why you may have stumbled on this game’s page without knowing what it’s about.What you should take from all of this is that Kiritan is a cute little girl who likes to sing and play games and now she gets to star in her own video game. There are many popular VOICEROID characters: Tsurumaki Maki, Yuzuki Yukari, Kotonoha Akane and Kotonoha Aoi etc but in the game you will meet Kiritan and her two older sisters Tohoku Zunko and Tohoku Itako. Once upon a time, there was a thing called Shareware. They were essentially game demos on floppy disks, and you could buy them off of spinning racks everywhere from drugstores to retail. It was the dark ages of gaming, and the shareware games were not, typically, very high quality. To wit: Hugo's House of Horrors. Man, that game was terrible.THIS game made me nostalgic for those games. There is no reason why the amount of effort put into this should have such awful results, but here we are. Typos are one thing, but the camera randomly changing to a different orientation while you're not moving? The mining tool not mining resource nodes you're lasering because the node doesn't feel like it? [Review posted during Preview window, where game was free to playtest]Moonbreaker is a tabletop wargame wrought digital - skirmish-level warfare true to the miniatures and hobby culture it is inspired by. If you have experience in the tabletop wargaming space you will find many elements of Moonbreaker very intuitive and recognisable.In particular I see what may be influences from Warmachine/Hordes - specifically the assassination mechanic wherein you lose the match if you lose your Captain model; the small model count, quick game time (between 5-30mins at the extremes, most ending within 10-12mins) and high level of variability present a space where creativity, synergy and tactics play a part in building an easy to pick up, hard to put down, well presented miniatures experience.All of this is to say nothing of the remarkable painting system, where you can customise your models using a very intuitive interface including airbrushing, washing, drybrushing, etc - alongside opacity and brush-size sliders to fine-tune your application of colour and allow you an incredible degree of control over your crew's aesthetic.This is still the beginning, but it's worth keeping an eye on.

Outcasts of Orion is an autobattler roguelike combining a solid game loop and varied strategic potential to offer an engaging experience with much replayability. You draft from a variety of randomly presented abilities and units to craft your squad and discover unexpected synergies. The game does struggle a bit early on in conveying the appeal of its mechanic, but given some time, it reveals an underlying layer of depth that keeps you coming back. If you are a fan of either autobattlers or strategy roguelikes, this game is worth giving a shot.------------------------------------------------------At its core, Outcasts of Orion plays as an autobattler with positioning as the central focus. Each unit has a defined pattern of attack and behavior that can be predicted and taken advantage of. Similar to chess, it is key to know your own unit's compatibility with others and to think a few turns ahead to emerge victorious. Early parts of the game start with a basic rock, paper, scissors type of dynamic, with additional unit classesmaking an appearance to add more variables for consideration.However, the game shines brightest in its factions. Factions are a set of units that share unique traits and abilities where each faction offers a different take on existing unit classes. For example, an assassin can stealthily execute an enemy, blind and stun an enemy, or turn an enemy into an ally to swarm the field.All are examples of how different faction can fulfill the same assassin role in differing ways. Beyond just careful positioning, there was much fun to be had in experimenting with different factions to discover unexpected synergies and exploits.Though the game leads strong with a tight core game loop, the game does come with some areas that could be improved. Mobile accounts can not be linked to Steam, so all my play time has been on mobile.Onmyoji: The Card Game has quite a few unusual mechanics that make it quite distinct from other CCGs. When building a deck, players choose just 4 Shikigami (units). Each Shikigami has a unique set of cards and players must pick 8 to put into their deck. If you want to use a card, you have to take its corresponding Shikigami and stuff a bunch of its other cards into your deck and then you can only pick 3 other Shikigami to pair it with. This makes the game relatively easy to balance without the need for a rotation system and there's a lot of thought involved with finding the right combination of frontline firepower and backline support. Having 2 action points standard every turn rather than a growing supply of mana also helps with balance and there's a lot of decision-making involved with getting the most out of these limited actions.The game has 2 solo campaigns. The first consists of a bunch of interconnected character-driven stories. These aren't super long, but there's enough of them to last a while and the characters are charming enough. The second has a more intricate and dramatic plot, though it still isn't especially long. Neither of these are worth playing the game just to experience them, but it's nice to have them. Solo players may also enjoy Kaidan, which is a sort of rogue-like mode, but it's a bit on the easy side.Matchmaking for ranked play tends to be pretty quick. Unranked times out and pairs the player against an easy bot after 1min30sec and this happens to me roughly 1/3 of the times I queue. There is also a rather fun autochess mode that isn't especially popular

What a deceptively adorable cozy building game. From the first moment, it presents eye-catching and visually pleasing images: the wilderness, the constructable buildings, the mice. Oh, she's just an anarchist, ready to incite an uprising against your royal authority. Er...At first glance, Ratopia's obvious progenitor is Klei's Oxygen Not Included. Both games have side-on base-building, colony logistics chains, assignable jobs, and cuteness galore. One important difference, though, is in character control: where ONI's characters may be tasked only indirectly, by ordering to go clean the toilets or carry a brick, Ratopia allows both indirect and direct task completion. Along with the colony's ever-increasing commoner rat population--the pawns to be set to work generally--the player directly controls a Rat Queen, whose regal appearance may be customized. This character, the most powerful and stylish of all ratkind, can mine, fight, and survey her domain via player input. In my view, this is a delightful and previously unseen mixing of active and passive control systems.A quick word about the Queen: the game models a simple sort of politics, perhaps inspired by Dwarf Fortress. Many rats have beliefs about royalty and law. Some are delighted to see Her Highness, while others are disgusted. There's crime and punishment, economic classes, and differing expectations based on rank. Taxes may be collected and welfare may be distributed. If the Queen dies, though, it's no victory for democracy but instead a game over screen.In comparing games like ONI and DF to Ratopia, there are obvious questions to ask: how do the heat and gas mechanics work? Will the rats eat all the plantable seeds? ONI and DF

Ratizens are paid individually for every single task they do, and they have to buy services and necessities from their own wallet. Luckily this is possible to achieve (but plenty challenging to keep stable) because Ratopia has the most robust and built out taxation system I’ve seen in any game. You truly have all the tools to try out any way of building your tax scheme to ensure upward mobility while keeping a healthy state treasury (I’ve found taxing bathroom use to be very effective!). You additionally can use trade to try and make up for budget shortfalls. There’s even a foreign currency you’ll have to exchange for and can even manipulate the rates on if you want to go bitcoin mode with it! UPDATE: issues with physics have been fixed in the latest patch!If you're willing to ignore frustrations related to touchy physics and gamepad layout, specifically aiming, you'll find a puzzle game with nice visuals.The whole thing begins with a malfunction in a seed-planting dome. Kyle Seed, the scientist in charge, receives an automatic message from the facility and races there on his bike after grabbing his backpack. While he is fixing the issue and it appears like the day will be saved, a storm materializes above the dome, and the machine is struck by lightning just as Kyle is standing underneath it. The machine shrinks Kyle to the size of a mushroom and drops him to the bottom of the dome along with the seed containers and energy cells required for the seeding process.The first thing you notice is that despite the game's visuals that might lead you to believe this is an action adventure or a metroidvania, Big Earth is actually a platformer with physics-based puzzles. The main hub, which changes slightly after each stage is finished, is where you’ll find everything. You can choose which stage to concentrate on first, but you still need to complete them all.Platforming and logic puzzles are found in the linear sections that make up the stages. Because you pass an antenna that saves the game and raises a barricade that prevents you from going back, you can always tell when you enter a new section. However, the game doesn't let you replay previous stages because there are no collectibles and your main objective is always on the main path.A nimble protagonist makes for really enjoyable platforming. Kyle can double jump and dash through the air; I'm not sure if the machine granted him additional abilities or if he already had them in normal

It's pretty much Fights in Tight Races--take FITSpaces and make the agents combat cars instead. The tactical grid and the card capabilities are very similar--cards might move you UDLR some pattern of squares, then let you either hit or move into something next to you in some sort of target pattern. The challenge is lining enemies up while staying inaccessible. Totally the same thing here.But here, car parts are your equipped gear and fundamentally change your deck when installed--each has a set of cards that swaps out with them. You can do this before any round, so you essentially get a meta-deck full of sidebars. Equipment is stored, and you can build up a versatile arsenal and strategize.And the fights themselves are dynamic too, with lane modifiers timing in at any moment. You also can't always use all of your cards because gear changes are essentially modal stances, and not all cards work in all gears.Staying in the right powerband is part of the game too. FITS is my favorite deckbuilder out right now, and this is pushing that same button, plus adding just a bit more chaos. And the Car Wars ambiance is spot on. I love it!

The art style and music are great, I absolutely love the over-the-top goofy atmosphere.
