The team mechanic is executed perfectly, which is impressive since I've never seen the concept done with a deckbuilder. Each character has their own unique cards and additions to the card pool, allowing you to mix and match their abilities, buffs and debuffs are applied specifically to each character, and you have to choose who to give each item to (there are some very strong relics that lead to some wild builds when used correctly). Sometimes it's even worth it to let a character die, which removes all their cards from your deck and adds a curse, a really interesting concept that adds a lot of risk and reward.Overall there is a lot of depth and customizability in runs, and the final act is amazing. My only complaint is that the enemy design is a bit repetitive.

Save yourself the frustration and disappointment and steer clear of this title. There are far better gaming experiences out there waiting to be discovered.

Your board game person is now a wagon that can hold stacks of things and it's being transferred from another island through a boat that grabs from one crate and puts it on another on the main land. Either you can go in blind and do a survival mode run, a randomly generated map you must evolve to the highest peaks for victory often taking several hours or even days to accomplish, or going through 8 campaigns. Each campaign gets harder than the last and is basically your way to learn the basics of everything, or you could just play the campaign to beat it which is always an option.There are no enemies like the usual. The only enemy is a stupid building placement you did 3 hours ago that gets crammed between everything. Spacing is your worst enemy and it's your job to make sure you have enough of it for it not to trigger your OCD.A solid 10/10 in the genre, underrated as hell and wouldn't recommend it enough.

The environment is rich and every piece of the scenery brings a memory to Adam. The devs putted everything together really well.Cons: The achievement system isn't working correctly. In my first playthrough I only got 2 achievements. Two pages was missing so I decided to replay it today because I was curious to know more about Adams life and to my surprise the achievements that should have appeared in my first gameplay showed up in my second lol. The flashlight's light is irritating when you reload the weapon it shines too much. Sometimes the sound of picking up ammo is sooooo low that we can't hear it. The game's music could have been a bit more crafted to create a scarier atmosphere with more jump scares. These are minor details that don't ruin the experience, but since I see the devs update the game regularly, here's my tips for future updates.I recommend this game to everyone who likes history and escape rooms. If you enjoy exploring the scenery to find an exit, this game is for you.

The game's narrative is thoughtful and thought-provoking, exploring themes that are relevant to our world today. It's a refreshing change from the usual horror tropes and clichés, and it keeps me engaged and eager to find out what happens next.If you're a fan of horror games, do not hesitate to pick this one up. is an old-school tactical turn-based strategy game where you lead a group of soldiers from one level to the next facing various enemies on the planet Anthracite. The singleplayer campaign has a story, and is of reasonable length (approximately 15-20 hours) and there is also online multiplayer available as well.The game starts off with a good tutorial where you will learn everything you need to know to get playing. With 3 difficulty levels, the game is accessible and you can also keep replaying levels if you need to do so. Often you might find that redoing levels is ideal for getting the items from those levels. You can then take them to subsequent levels once you find them. The game is very strategic, and the tactical component features free movements around a gridless map. Often you might find that waiting in areas of good coverage might be better than jumping out at first opportunity. Seeing what your enemies will do can help shape your plan for the rest of that level.The battles are turn-based with limited number of action points. These can be used however you wish, move, attack, or attack multiple times, etc. The objectives are always clear, so you will not be wondering what to do from level to level. Plus the levels are not too long, so replaying can be fun as well to try other strategies.It has a top-down old-school look. It looks fine for trying to maintain that old-school look and feel though it's not particularly noteworthy.The music fits the game, but after a while it might be too much of the same.This game can be fully played with a mouse (and a keyboard).In my opinion is €12.49 a fair price. The game offers enough gameplay to justify its priceIt is a very good game

The game really doesn't give you the time to amass a lot of resources, and requires relatively precise play to have any chance at all. Ironically your first playthrough is the weakest as in all subsequent playthroughs you get starting bonuses to choose from (though the options are randomised from a selection). The game throws a few disasters/events at you (roughly every 20 days); Eclipse, Flood, Locusts, and plague (before a big-finisher after that).The Eclipse feels thematically appropriate. It seems like the big-bad of what you were expecting after the intro. Then it just never reappears again, back to just generic darkness in the night. It's the big run-killer for newcomers but really comes down to just getting 150-200 wood stockpiled to outlast it.The Flood is bad RNG. You get these flood wall platforms you can build to stem the flood increase, but you have no idea where the game will spawn the flooding patches and it usually wrecks a lot of farms and places you've already built-up so that there's no good way to block it. Turns out, it doesn't matter, you can just tell everyone to avoid the deep water and almost no one ever dies here. It doesn't feel like enough of a departure to me.Miscellaneous nitpicks include the tedious analysis in some puzzles of which cards need to change before they're brought to their target spaces, and the fact that card suits don't matter, only colors. It's also notable that you don't have to alternate colors when stacking cards, though perhaps this would clash with the stacking spaces that only accept a particular color.If I evaluate SokoSolitaire purely as a Sokoban-style game with no expectation of twists, the puzzles are solid- and so you could consider this review neutral more so than negative- but in my view classic Sokoban puzzles tend to suffer from travel tedium, and this game is no exception. Many puzzles, especially later on, will require you to slightly adjust one card, take the long way around to slightly adjust it in a different way, move this card across the level to make room for another card, and so on. Wild Bastards is different from that, and I love it. And what's more, I love the characters. I wasn't too crazy about playing as multiple characters. Just let me collect different guns. Right And Down is a deceptively simple turn-based roguelite dungeon-crawling card game where you navigate a grid of tiles trying to get from the top left corner to the exit in the bottom right. On each turn you have only two choices: move right, or move down. To win a run you need to reach the end of level 50; you lose if your health is reduced to zero.Every character starts with one item, which grants some kind of passive bonus, and one ability, which can be triggered by moving in a particular pattern. For example, the Brute's Brutal Hack ability inflicts 4 damage to all enemies after you move down followed by right three times.Moving onto a tile does something depending on its type:1. Armor. Increases your armor by the amount shown on the tile.2. Monsters. Immediately kills the monster, but you lose health equal to the strength of the monster shown on the tile. If you have armor, your armor is reduced first. Killing monsters also gives you experience, used to buy additional abilities at campfires (see below).3. Coins. Increases the number of coins you have by the amount shown on the tile.4. Potions. Heals you for the value shown on the tile.5. Items. You can have up to 16 different items (including your starting item), but you can have more than one of the same item and their benefits stack. Items cost an amount of gold equal to the value shown on the tile and are automatically acquired if you have sufficient gold.6. Traps. Inflict some kind of negative status effect, for a number of turns equal to the value shown on the tile. For example, poison damages you every turn; blindness prevents you from seeing further than a one-tile radius; burn prevents you from healing; freeze

SGS AK brings me back to the days of the classic board games but with a flair. Really fun to watch Rommel with his Panzers break through the British lines! Or the SAS roaming deep behind the German lines cutting off supply lines.In some ways this reminds me of the classic "beer & pretzels" type of board game that can be played in a few hours. But then you have some larger grand scenario spanning the entire campaign. Is the game perfect? No. But it offers a lot of "Bang" for the Buck/Euro. And knowing how the developers are from some of their previous games I know they will work hard to improve the AI and add even more complexity to the game. I'm sure they may add even new cards

Unlike most build/craft games that provide pre-made walls, furniture, or even whole buildings, this game provides a very unique and highly capable build system based on primatives. Through the use of these primatives, you can craft significantly more complex objects than can be found in most, if not all, other survival games currently on the market. The only similar crafting system I have seen is found within Second Life. Unlike Second life, however, there is no limit or cost to the number of prims that are used, so you can build really complex objects. That being said, this game does lack a few of the nicer design elements found in second life: you cannot upload your own textures, prims cannot be spliced into sub-shapes (i.e., a quarter sphere, holf a torus, etc.) and you cannot place different textures on different sides of an object.You ability that this game has, though, is that the different material textures are linked to resources. So, if you choose to make your object out of wood, you will need to chop trees. Stone, you will need to mine (the voxel based world is also a great feature). Total eye candy of a solitaire game, with pretty great music and FMV cutscenes to entertain you now and then. Probably one of the most unique and entertaining ways I've ever played solitaire. Note that this game does not use the more popular versions of solitaire like golf or klondike, so this may be a new way of playing to you. Just like many other virtual solitaire games, this one also features triggered special abilities that can heavily change the outcome of your plays. In this game you need to play very strategically with your special abilities, so be prepared to think carefully about your moves and not just fly through cards.There is a short storyline campaign in which you act in the interests of a spy organization set in a cyberpunk world. You are given the chance to pick your 'quests' from a selection of offerings with slightly different challenge levels and rewards. The story campaign actually acts as a slow tutorial, teaching you all the various tactics the game employs so that you have a solid start in the open modes such as Skirmish and timed challenges, which are pure solitaire games. There are leaderboards and achievements tied to your skill in the other game modes.Definitely worth a try if you've already played other solitaire games before and would appreciate a completely fresh take on it.

It's practically a cliche at this point, but this is another one of those games that really needs a sideways thumb option.Let me start by saying the UI is slick (if sometimes hard to read), the presentation is fun and there is very obviously some real love put in this game (especially in the cutscenes). I did not encounter any bugs.Unfortunately, the actual solitaire sucks. I'm not sure what variant this is, but it's miles from classic Klondike. All cards are placed face-up at the start into 8 stacks. There only as many sets of cards as the number of "teams" (basically suits) the mission has, so the vast majority of missions are 3 or less. You can only move one card at a time (never a stack, whether ordered or not) and face cards get "charged" with their abilities as you place cards. "Charged" face cards can be played on top of anything. What results is a version of solitaire so comically exploitable I'm not sure it's even POSSIBLE to have a hand you can't win.The abilities each "team" has can be somewhat interesting, but I found all but the last 3 or so counterproductive (though a couple of them are actually negative by design). You cannot choose when to use an ability and when not to. Once a face card is "charged" placing it anywhere but an empty stack activates the ability. Basically, the closest thing to challenge this game musters is occasionally forcing you to shoot yourself in the foot.It's pretty short, too. I completed the campaign and a couple skirmishes just for the achievements in under 3.5 hours. They just introduced a new game plus mode, but I really don't see the point. At $12 the price isn't completely out of line for what you're getting,

This game has some fantastic features that make it instantly worth playing in my opinion. The game consists of two modes, a strategic map with elements that remind me a lot of Mount and Blade, along with the tactical battle mode which is very similar to the Fire Emblem games, but with massive quality of life improvements.For me, the biggest draw to this game is that it rewards you for playing it, regardless of what exactly you choose to do. It doesn't waste your time, and it has some UI and time-saving gameplay features which really should be default in the strategy genre. My favorite such feature is probably the ability to auto-resolve battles in mid-combat, but in a close second comes the idea of "auto-resolve safe" battles. Basically, every battle in the game is rated from 1-10 stars in difficulty and if a fight is at 1 star, you can auto-resolve it with a guarantee it won't kill any of your party members. But since you can auto-resolve in mid-battle, if you start a fight that has, say, 4 stars, if you kill enough people, the game will track the difficulty of the remaining fight, and if you can reduce it to the safe threshold (1, at the start of the game, but it goes up to 3 by late game), you can then auto-resolve it safely from that point. I used this feature almost every time I had the option, but you are rewarded for taking the time to kill enemies manually (you get more XP for manual kills).Honestly, there are a lot of things like that in this game, both in terms of specific mechanics and in terms of the design philosophy. There are some brilliant choices that have been made in the creation of this game,

Once you get in, it really opens up, but I feel like I was well-equipped within the first hour to figure out the rest.The pace ramps up as new cities appear on the map needing power. Your substations can only handle so much power draw before they become overloaded, after which they can and will explode. I feel like it gives you enough time and space to figure things out and try other things without punishing you too hard for failure.It will be really cool to see what else gets added as things develop! There seems to exist a lot of misunderstanding around what Against the Storm is about, so I'll approach it from a fairly high-level angle.Against the Storm is a superb adaptation-focused roguelite logistics simulator wrapped in a pleasant city-builder skin. It is notably faster-paced than a typical city builder, and revolves around optimally using a small, mostly-random subset of a very large toolkit to solve local optimization problems in a time-bound setting. The toolkit is so broad, it's difficult / impossible to hold it all in your head - well, my head anyway - which means a modicum of intuition and experience is needed to solve the problems the game revolves around, resulting in a delightful situation where every playthrough is different enough that common patterns are fairly scarce and have limited usefulness.The game's aesthetic is notably peaceful, rather calm and largely non-violent, with excellent sound design and decent graphics direction. The time pressure imposed upon by the game rules is the main source of pressure, with few other sources, and combined with an extremely wide selection of difficulty levels, it might lend itself well to those of us who struggle with anxiety. If you value adaptation and exploration in games, enjoy frequent - perhaps scarily so - updates, and like a challenge that, as developers intend, is always solvable, while helping your subjects survive in a harsh environment, this might just be a game you could enjoy.

It's free, and for that, why not check it out? That said, it definitely has some serious balancing, progression, and pacing issues that are ignored in other "reviews". If I paid a couple dollars I wouldn't be frustrated for obvious reasons, but this game is definitely not worth the indie standard, which is why it is free. Healing and sustain functions are so sparse and/or ineffectual that they are rendered pointless. Damage is the only thing that matters because it is tied to the inappropriately labeled "parry" ability (which is really just a block function), a decision that while being novel, makes little sense. There is also the issue of methods the player character employs that NPCs do not employ, and vice-versa. The idea that not having a bullet in the chamber at the end of a turn delivers damage to the player also makes little sense. Sure, it's interesting, but that is a band-aid for an otherwise dull experience. All of these things contribute to the greatest issue, which is that the "meta deck" for the cards the player has unlocked is glaring easy to identify as you progress through the game. The odds that you survive is more so based on luck, rather than strategy or experience with card play-order variations from the five round chamber, with the chamber being the most unique set piece of the game. It has potential, no thanks to balancing, with hats off to the creativity.

I’ve been looking for a game like this for a while now. Burger Bistro Story sees you managing your own fast food diner. This game is an actual business management game in the sense that you are actually managing a business, as opposed to the countless work simulator meme games you see nowadays.The game starts with you selecting the uniform colour for your staff and naming your diner - I called mine ‘Born to Grill’, my second idea was ‘James Bond Burger’. You start off with a very basic menu and only one staff member besides the manager but these will quickly expand as you progress through the game. To help you get a start in the game there is a fairly lengthy tutorial when starting out but since the text boxes that explain key features are quick and snappy it ends up being nowhere as intrusive as it could be. Eventually you’ll reach a point where the tutorial messages stop and then you are free to do whatever you want.One refreshing aspect of the game is that your staff do not need to be completely micromanaged. Staff members move much slower when they are tired so it’s recommended to hire more people than you need as when they get tired while working they will automatically take themselves to the break room and swap themselves out with someone else. Creating new food items is also fun. When creating burgers you have free rein to add any ingredients you want to make your own bizarre concoctions. As your restaurant ranks up you can add more ingredients to your burgers. When you start out simply having a beef patty and cheese between two buns will be a grand accomplishment, but once you rank up enough times you’ll be making impossible tower burgers

I wrote this ones an ardent Aussie Rules fan, I had high hopes for the 'Australian Football Coach' game. I was excited to delve into the strategic intricacies of my favourite sport,. However, in reality, the experience has been rather disheartening.The major gripe I have with the game is the balance of the simulation engine. In reality, yes, underdogs occasionally beat the top teams - that's one of the things that makes sport exciting. But in 'Australian Football Coach', this happens far too often. The randomness factor appears to have been dialed up too high, to the point where good teams are frequently beaten by average ones.One glaring instance of this imbalance was with West Coast. After they made the finals, I decided to conduct an experiment and edited their roster, intentionally reducing most players' ratings so most were in the 70s Despite their significantly lowered stats, they not only continued to win games but also consistently made the finals. Meanwhile, strong teams, that boast numerous players with high 80s and 90s ratings, consistently languished near the bottom of the ladder. In conclusion, the unpredictability factor in 'Australian Football Coach' needs significant toning down. Sports games are meant to replicate the unpredictability of real-life sports, but when it overshadows the skill and strategy involved, it's no longer fun. Unfortunately, this title doesn't seem to strike that balance, and it's a big letdown for fans of the sport.I hope the developers take this feedback on board and refine their sim engine. Until then, I'd recommend AFL enthusiasts tread with caution when considering this title.

BarricadeZ takes place in a post-apocalyptic wasteland, where the only things left are monsters, and you, a robot. Yet, there's a tiny spark of hope falling from the sky; a baby. Now you have to get to work, because of course the monsters are after the little bundle of joy. You have to build your own defenses, and that's the meat of the game. The gathering and crafting system reminds me a bit of Terraria (to name one), and is nicely done, imo. During the night the monsters will test your design for you, and failure is definitely not an option. Remember the defenseless baby? The monsters themselves are zombies, though not your standard garden variety. These are darker, both literally and figuratively. This whole game is quite dark and bleak. The graphics, the art, with smart use of color (or lack thereof), and the fitting music all add to the sinister mood. So far, there's only a little bit of story with more to be added, but what is there makes me want to know more about the robot, the baby and this game world in general (probably so will you, once you figure out where these zombies actually come from). For an EA game, it is very playable. The most glaring bugs are, imo, the many errors in the english text, which can be annoying when you try to figure out what this or that actually does. I really hope the devs will take the time and effort to address this issue. For those who like gathering and crafting with a side of towerdefense in an apocalyptic world setting, I definitely recommend this game!

Stealthing around and offing an overwhelming enemy never gets old. Whether it’s Hitman, Metal Gear, or Desperados, each quietly eliminated foe brings you closer to God (or at least the completion of your current objectives). Success is measured in baby steps and each one is a thrilling accomplishment.War Mongrels manages to tap into this energy to create an experience that’s both challenging and exciting. With a varied squad of heroes, a unique cinematic art style, and a worthy historical fiction story, it’s likely to impress those looking to fill another space on their digital shelf.War Mongrels begins with a pair of German soldiers who have decided that serving the Nazi regime isn’t all it was cracked up to be. One of these gentlemen volunteered due to his idealistic take on the current breed of nationalism while the other was an unwilling conscript who was pulled into the war machine against his will. Now that they’re both on the same page, your first task is directing them through their daring escape. The adventure that follows will have you collecting additional personalities for your squad and applying their many talents to take the fight directly to the boys in gray.The story offered by War Mongrels isn’t a new one, but it’s well done all the same. The comic-like cinematics between scenarios add an enjoyable, dark, and dramatic view of the era with an art style that’s incredibly unique. Nazi leadership, for example, is often represented with wolf-like features such as sharp teeth and predatory eyes while our heroes look decidedly more human. This works well for both those looking for something more outside-the-box as well as those looking for realism in the atmosphere as the scenarios themselves take on a much more realistic approach. This game was aggressively marketed as a mobile game with all the fun and none of the microtransactions. Admittedly, that interested me, as I've seen several otherwise good games that were held back by being mobile games riddled with transactions that flourished when they removed this monetization system, tweaked the gameplay, and just charged a flat rate for the game. You don't get to keep anything you "unlock", it more or less just shows you the character. Or if you want an example of a mobile game that was stripped of it's microtransactions and was more fun as a result, check out Dandy Dungeon.

Critique:-Runs feel too random, you do have not enough impact on what deck you're actually building, and in some runs you're literally unable to build any proper decks at all. Your only source of bullets (this games's cards) outside of events and drops are random pulls you can do at the shop. You can choose some aspects of the bullet you pull, but they're mostly unimportant traits, only sometimes do you get to choose what kind of bullet you actually want. The game would be hugely improved if it had bullet-type-specific banners, like actual gachas do, where you could choose which pool of cards to pull from. This fantasy-themed deck-building game defies expectations for a modern digital adaptation of a card game. The game is free to play, with some restrictions on progress, on Steam/iOS/Android but your account, games, and any purchases you have made apply to all three. The deck-building aspect of the game is what makes this game a cut above other card games because you only need to buy an expansion once and it is unlocked forever. There are no card use restricted lists so you are never forced to pay more money to keep playing. While the app does suggest you buy some in-game things, it is far from the normal digital card game world where the game is just trying to milk you in microtransactions. You and your opponent play at the same character level and have access to the same cards the entire game so there are no valid "Pay-to-win" complaints. The only part of the game (when I wrote this) that has any bearing on what you bought comes with the character classes/ancestries and you get most of those just by purchasing the $10 base game.One of the distinctive features of this game comes down to having both real-time and asynchronous play. If you have the time to play an entire game at once, you can do the real-time games (~15-20 minutes) or if you want to play in smaller sessions you can queue up for async games where both players alternate taking turns and you have up to a 48h window to take your turn. This format is best for playing lots of games at once so you can get in lots of variety this way.The game has lots of action and replayability, the community is thriving, and the developer team is constantly making changes to balance the game.

Cosmoteer is currently a good "first 20 hours" of a fully-realized space combat/exploration game, but it's been in development since at least 2011. There's no mid-game or late-game to speak of yet, and little to do beyond "curbstomp random enemy" missions. The ship design system is interesting while it lasts but is also obviously incomplete. There's a "small hyperdrive" but no medium or large, for example. Combat is extremely simple and ship AI is braindead. Co-op is fun for a while.The developer appears to have fallen into the Early Access Deathspiral: you release too early and need to maintain the appearance of progress, so rather than developing the core systems which take a ton of time and work, you constantly add minor features to satisfy players' feedback. Those players say, "Wow, what a responsive developer!" then stop playing (because there's still no actual game), and move on to the next Early Access Deathspiral game. Cosmoteer's settings menu is a testament to this feature creep: there's an option for almost anything you might want, aside from "be an actual game."If you want something more complete, play Starsector instead. 100 hours later, play it again with Nexelerin and a few other mods that sound interesting. Starsector hasn't had an update in over a year, but every update it does get is substantial and adds meaningful new content and gameplay. Unfortunately it's not on Steam (yet?) but it's also only $15 direct from the developer, and it might be the best $15 you've spent on a game.I did enjoy my short time with Cosmoteer and the developer is clearly talented. I hope it continues to progress and eventually matures into a full game, but as of today there's just not enough there for me to give it a positive recommendation.

Suika: but it's (tastefully) bouncy in ways! 🍈👙✨ is the SFW version of . If you're looking to play one-handed, that's the version you want, not this one. , so this version is a little obsolete other than the inclusion of different VTubers being optional skins for the "watermelon" (Sayu Sincronisity! 🔩).As a Suika-like, is fun and enjoyable to play with a variety of extra mechanics that freshen up the usual drop-and-combine gameplay. There are 3 items to use in gameplay: the "vibration" item that shakes/jostles the box around which can help make merges, the "grabber" which allows you to grab any orb and re-drop it where you'd like, and the "hammer" item which can remove any orb except the watermelon. With these it's possible to reach higher scores than other versions of Suika.There are also two other game modes: Speed Mode, which forces drops, and Waifu Challenge mode which has mystery drops and junk orbs to complicate things. I didn't play much of either of these, and they aren't necessary for 100% achievement completion.There is also a leaderboard, so you can see how you've fared against the other players! This is a lovely little indie colony builder. You have a total of 6 colony locations that you can develop each of which has different combinations of available resources and colonist needs creating a supply chain problem for you to ship the different goods around the system.To take just one example, the colony Outlands is on one of the outer system moons and as such needs to be supplied with Oxygen. There are four different ways that you can do this each of which has different pros and cons regarding how much manpower and shipping it takes. You can manufacture the oxygen in situ from ice but this is very manpower intensive. Alternatively you could ship in water from another colony which takes a lot less manpower but the water is very bulky to ship. Finally you could manufacture the oxygen in one of two other locations and ship it in which is less bulky than shipping the water but also requires more manpower or secondary shipping.Overall I really enjoyed this game. The only downside I have is that the price is a little bit high for the play time (it took me 6 hours to beat the game the first time and a total of 15 hours to do all achievements). Personally I think that it's worth it to support an indie developer but it is something to be aware of.

Let's start with the fact that I love Slay the Spire-like games, and I also enjoy a good Match 3 phone game. As you can tell from 5 seconds of video from the game, this is a very close clone of StS but with a Match 3 board reminiscent of the classic Puzzle Quest. Given that and the care with which the game was made, I enjoyed it enough to give it an up rating.On the negative side, I think it's so similar in many ways to Slay that despite the Match 3 boards, I quickly mined it out. There's not much new to discover, and the three classes all play somewhat similarly. That's not to say it's a bad game -- I had a good time, and I'm upvoting it because I love the genre and this is a decent example of it, but if you are only going to play a few games of this type, there are a lot better entries to pick up. On the plus side, the art is pretty and the game is pretty well-balanced, in my opinion. If you are a frequent StS-like player, you'll likely find it to be perfectly balanced; if you're new to the genre, you may find it quite difficult to win. The cards are well thought-out, and there are a variety of builds to try, but a lot of it feels awfully familiar. It's often more fun to have greater diversity of experiences on runs but have a less tight balance -- maybe an unpopular opinion, but that's how I feel about it.

A superb game that adds a new "gimmick" to the deck builder roguelite in the way of the match 3 board.Careful use of both your deck and the tile board are required in order to progress. The game takes a few runs to get into (I lost my first 3) but offers a good but beatable challenge rather than spamming a select few cards. The tile board also has enemy tiles that if left alone can damage you, curse you, heal the enemy or give them block... as well as a few other tricks on the bosses.Visibly it's pretty and each character feels different thanks to the unique bonuses each receive. Likewise, even the enemies feel somewhat unique with a number of them having special attributes or weaknesses. There's a lot of hidden control to these fights in using the weaknesses and traits against them. One elite does massive damage but is stunned by gaining enough of a specific symbol on the board, the barbed trait deals damage back to you when you attack them with cards but not with tile-chaining, and one enemy will change it's action based on your plays... and that's just a few, and doesn't even talk about bosses. While there are certainly a number of 'regular' mobs, there's still plenty of times you need to pay attention, adapt and actually think about your actions.It also has positive modifiers as well as negative, allowing you to fine-tune the difficulty to your liking.The biggest negative is that there's not a lot to unlock, and I felt I didn't get anything rewarded to me when beating the final boss and watching the credits roll. It would be great if each character had one unique unlock for that... but this is a SUPER minor negative.I'd love to see more

Raid and farming feel really weird. I went through with it because i like the Touhou ip. So when the drastic change happen i was very confused. I was sticking to this game because of the character more than the game in general. So for now i'm quitting but if there a major game mechanic change or if the character design become more solid i will be willing to try the game again.

*Edit, well it was.Game is currently being remade in terms of character assets to move away from Touhou Project.From what I understand, it stems from legal issues regarding the use of the IP to make money (Touhou is pretty strict about this outside of doujin works).A shame because the developer seemed to be a pretty big fan of Touhou and the art for the characters + cards are really cute and funny.From what I've seen, the game is still the same in terms of gameplay so the rest of this review should still apply.---In short, a Touhou themed Slay the Spire card battler gacha mobage.(Going to be referencing Slay the Spire (StS) a lot in the review, so if you're unfamiliar with it, check out a vid it or something)You basically pick a party of 5 characters that you have, each character having their own set of 12 cards as well as stats.It is interesting pairing certain characters who work well together based on what their cards do.Each character has their own play-style similar to how you'd imagine their lore abilities translate into a card battler, for example I mained Momiji who really plays around a [Shield Bash] card that deals damage and blocks at the same time, with a lot of cards cycling [Shield Bash] to/back to my hand.The cards you play don't deal a flat amount of damage like in StS, instead scaling off your attack/defense/BP stat that you get from your party characters and equipment relics that you bring into the dungeon.Outside of dungeons there are a whole bunch of ways to upgrade and augment your characters, if you've played a gacha game before then it should be familiar to you.The basic strike for example, does 30% of your attack and the basic defend card blocks 20%

On the other hand, once you complete several levels, there is a sense of progression lacking. Your characters don't get stronger, they just face increasingly more difficult enemies. I know that difficulty is relative (it's all the same if you make both your troops and the enemies twice stronger or not) but it's a psychological thing. As a player, I want to feel I've accomplished something. Especially if there is a "party" of characters like in an RPG game- similarly, there is no feeling of progression across the levels. It's not a bad thing (after all, there is still a level number, and you do read more dialogs) but it would be just better if there were some map for example where you clear regions from zombies, or at least a list of customers which get crossed out once you've delivered pizza to them.

From what I recall I finished that level, only to then run into one that was even harder. Since I hadn't unlocked anything more powerful, I knew that I was again expected to reconfigure my abilities - only now, there was less room for error. I wasn't interested in ramming my head against this puzzle, so I decided that perhaps my time with Pizza Apocalypse had come to an end.Perhaps I'm a simpleton, but I prefer to gain more abilities and become more powerful as I progress through a game, rather than reconfigure the same set of abilities to meet harder and harder challenges with less room for error.

I would describe Knotwords as some kind of mix between a crossword and scrabble, with maybe a little sudoku (and Picross if you're playing twisted mode). To further explain, imagine you're playing a crossword puzzle, but instead of each column or row having a clue like "a body of flowing water", instead the board is broken up into arbitrary clusters in which a list of letters can go into. A single word usually goes through multiple clusters, so when trying to unscramble a word, you will likely be drawing letters from a few different pools, but the rule of crosswords remains that every line and column on the board makes a word. Twisted mode is essentially the same, but each column and row of the grid has numbers telling you how many vowels are in that column or row.Sounds confusing? After you play the tutorial, you'll understand. Is it fun? I think so. You get new puzzles to play daily, and you also have 'puzzle books' containing many puzzles that you can play anytime you want. You can even go back and play archives of the daily puzzles that you missed. If Wordle is starting to feel too simple for you, or you just want another word puzzle in your life to blow some free time on, this is a great choice to look into. I think you can try it for free on the iphone/android app if you're not sure.

Upon finding out about Knotwords, I was super excited to try it. It's a clever new type of logic puzzle, and kudos to the developers for coming up with it! Unfortunately, this bungles basically every aspect of the implementation. Here's what I found in under two hours. WALL OF TEXT INCOMING* The puzzles are just chock full of crappy words (BOLE), archaic words (OPE), fragments and prefixes (ISO), variant spellings, sigh-eliciting inflections (UTERI, AMPLER, GOLDEST)... you will run into at least one of these in every puzzle. Even in *their own screenshots* we have ALB, OHO, and "HO," which... come on, guys. Some of this stuff wouldn't even cut it in a crossword, and Knotwords puzzles are just so, so much easier to construct.* The puzzles are randomly generated and it shows. A creative constructor could have a lot of fun with Knotwords, but in the 50 or so puzzles I played, I saw no hint of authorship anywhere. Other Steam puzzle games at this price point are packed with smart, charming puzzles made with love and care; Knotwords, as far as I can tell, shipped with 0 (zero)!* Seeing complaints on the mobile app stores I thought: how bad could the input system really be? It's bad. The cursor jumps around erratically, even doubling back to filled squares when unfilled ones remain in a group. There's room here for adding other AI camps which you could choose to attack or trade. An underground portion of the map would add a lot of variety and strategy as well. Give us more options to outfit them, bags/armor/ammo/weapons and make it easier to do so instead of having them "transfer" between storage places. maybe make a separate in game menu for it. There's a few path finding bugs that need working out and some quality of life changes need to be made to search multiple buildings at once whilst having a vehicle as a drop off point instead of auto running all the way back to base. It's a digital implementation of the card game. For those who've never played, the short version is that you have a market of cards, each of which correspond to a number(s) from 1 to 12. On your turn you roll a die and whatever result you get you activate those cards which usually give you money, or let you take it from other players, and then use it to acquire more cards. The object of the game is to build four of the landmark cards which are expensive, but provide a permanent bonus too. So it's a fairly simple game which would have been odd if they hadn't managed to implement correctly. The problem is the game lacks the expansions (DLC?) which go some way to mitigating the biggest problem the game has - there are numerous turns, particularly early game, where literally nothing happens because the number rolled doesn't match any cards. It's a minor annoyance when it happens at the table, however here it's exacerbated into a major irritation because, unlike the tabletop version the game feels the need to constantly interrupt the flow of the game to tell you spurious information - it breaks in at the end of a round every so often to display the current standings, despite the fact this information is also conveyed on the player display via little icons, or can be gleaned with a quick glance at the virtual tabletop (I mean it's not a particularly difficult thing to track). My review is actually mixed.In short, overall I don't have heart to give it a negative review because VR really needs games of this quality, where it feels like developers actually care and put some decent effort, and all of that at surprisingly low price. But at the same time controls are absolutely awful.Visual and sounds are pretty good, there's nice main lobby, different "arenas" etc., the art style doesn't aim for realism and thanks to that it's looks great. There's all the sounds needed and even some music. Many game modes, including multiplayer, singleplayer and training.But the controls... Basically you hold a button to jump into different (shooting?) perspective which feels awkward and confusing. To make things worse then you need to hold another button to lock the angle and only then you can do proper movement to hit the ball. Because of that at both stages your movement is one dimensional (height works a bit for some more specific movements but it pretty much doesn't matter) and has surprisingly little to do with your irl hand movement which is actually one of the most important things about the whole VR. It takes away all the joy because it's kind of system that feels like flat games, just in vr. I'd say wait for them to fix it but I don't think it's ever gonna happen as it seems to be core mechanic and is here to stay.So, I think I'll still play some more of it and I think it might be worth checking out, developers still deserve at least that but unfortunately I'm not too happy with this game.

If this was a controller based game, I think it would be enjoyable, but it's not.The lock-aim-fire mechanic is very much a 2d concept of the universe. In VR you have a much more refined control system. That coupled with really good physics and collision modeling should make for a relatively solid "pool hall" experience. However, this game seems more rooted in the, in my opinion, overly complex "controller" style mechanics.The simplicity of interact of pool, namely pick up a stick and hit balls into holes should be the core mechanic of a VR pool game. However with the stick "welded" to your hands and a "staged" shooting mechanic it loses the feel of a pool game.There are some that will prefer this and that's lovely. However, if you are expecting a "physically" interactive world like H3VR or Blade and Sorcery you'll have to look somewhere else.Note: There might be configuration later in the game that I am missing. I could not make it past the tutorial. This is partly because "locked" non-optional tutorials are highly annoying and usually a sign that a game lacks an intuitive design. Case in point there is a part of the tutorial that has to teach you how to step up and step away from the table.The other part of me not completing the tutorial is when I got to the actual "hitting balls" part of the tutorial I could only hit the first ball... On the second iteration of the "hitting the ball" part of the tutorial my triggers cease to function.All in all, if you like an "on rails" mechanic heavy pool experience, this is your game. If, like me, you are looking for a virtual pool table sim where you can grab a stick and start shooting, you'll have to look

You go there, read some text, level up skills, drop a few pieces of equipment into your character sheet and pick your next climb.The climbs are the majority of the game play. The mountains are not truly beautiful because to identify the terrain you can walk on, the textures look a bit like rabbit pellets turned on their ends. The areas you can't go look much more natural. But I understand why that was done in order to distinguish various approaches for the player. So while not a visual feast, the graphics are decent enough especially if you love mountains like I do. The sounds and music are nondescript but not annoying. No voice over work for the few lines of dialog which suits me just fine. You explore to find various paths and hit points of interest on the way. These can give buffs to your 5 main resources - energy, sanity, warmth, oxygen and health - or they might give you debuffs. "A Mountain of Potential, Buried by Poor Design."Insurmountable had the potential to be a truly unique and engaging climbing game, but unfortunately, it falls short in several critical areas. The most glaring issue is the camera, which is simply horrible—one of the worst I've encountered in any video game. It constantly gets stuck at awkward angles, making it nearly impossible to navigate the terrain effectively. This is especially frustrating in a game where precise movement and planning are crucial.Equally problematic is the pathfinding. Your character frequently takes inefficient or outright bizarre routes to reach a destination, often leading to unnecessary backtracking or dangerous detours. This not only breaks immersion but also adds an infuriating layer of difficulty that feels entirely artificial.Adding to the list of disappointments is the lack of atmosphere, which is crucial for this type of game. A climbing game should immerse you in the environment, making you feel the isolation, the tension, and the sheer awe of the mountains. However, Insurmountable fails to create any of this atmosphere. The visuals are bland, the sound design is lackluster, and there’s a general absence of the environmental storytelling that could have brought the game to life.These issues combine to create a highly unenjoyable experience. Instead of feeling the thrill of scaling daunting heights and overcoming nature's challenges, you're left wrestling with poor controls, erratic navigation, and a dull, uninspired world. The game’s concept is fantastic, but the execution is severely lacking.If you're looking for an adventure game that will test your strategic thinking and climbing skills, I'd recommend looking elsewhere. Insurmountable, in its current state, is more of a test of your patience than anything else. Save yourself the headache and skip this one.

So that's one thing you have to buy: Heroes.The second thing you have to buy are Professions. There are 5 of these. You get one for free when you start the game. These are basically a second set of cards you can choose from to customise the way your deck plays. Included with your base purchase are enough free credits that they throw at you to buy up to 3 more Heroes/Professions. I've been shuffling through WitchHunt for a solid 75 hours, and here's the scoop: it's a card-based strategy game that really tests your ability to manage resources, expand territories, and fend off enemies. The gameplay is smooth early on, with you hustling to combine resources and fend off enemy spawns triggered by your exploration. However, as you delve deeper and your tech (or spells) get fancier, things start to feel a bit clunky, especially around midgame.The story? It's delivered through letters from home—brief and character-specific. It's not the game's strong suit and doesn't do much for replayability, which, speaking of, feels a bit limited. Despite different characters and building options, the core gameplay doesn't change much, making each playthrough feel too similar.But not all is gloomy! The graphics are a delight for a card game, with each card flaunting unique, eye-catching designs, and the battle animations are silky smooth. The audio, though, is a mixed bag; while the background music is captivating, the constant swoosh of cards midgame might get on your nerves.Performance-wise, the game runs without a hitch in the early phases but starts to lag as you hit automation in midgame. A couple of bugs popped up too, like the infinite healing spell trick—neat but surely unintended!Despite its pitfalls, the game’s complexity and strategic depth provided me with dozens of hours of enjoyment, making the $12 price tag feel like a steal. Playing on the hardest difficulty at first seemed manageable, but lowering the difficulty paradoxically upped the challenge, making for some intriguing gameplay dynamics.So, would I recommend WitchHunt? Absolutely, if you're into card games with a strategic twist and enjoy managing and expanding in fantastical settings. It's not without its faults, but there's enough here to keep any card game aficionado engaged for hours on end.

It is less critical than previously, the game has definitely been improved; though my rating remains thumbs down.Original Review Starts Here:Were you expecting a city builder game where you can relax and plan your strategy, design your city layout and get your production chains going, expand your territory and grow your population?Forget it.This is no city builder. It is a city builder SKIN wrapped around a dice management puzzle game, which is both played against the clock (you can however pause and make decisions while time is frozen, a new and welcome addition by the devs reacting positively to customer complaints) and somewhat stressful. The theme could have been absolutely anything, but they chose a medieval village city builder, which is probably going to confuse a lot of players and make them regret their purchase as I do.Pushing the game even further from city builder territory is the incredibly frustrating Winter mechanic, where all your dice freeze (become unusable) if you send them to work in unheated areas. This forces you to build all your key buildings clustered tightly round a steam heater. This basically enforces your village layout into being clusters of buildings tightly packed round your heaters, and vast empty space everywhere else on the map. Not only ugly but very frustrating to interact with too (all these tightly packed buildings have work-spaces on them that you need to drop dice and resources onto).And now lets move on to the combat. Play far enough and you encounter an enemy faction on the map. And they will start to spawn raiders

This game has a fantastic vibe. It is beautiful to look at, the ambiance is chill, and the music is very peaceful. I also really enjoyed the "ring world" mechanic that simplifies controls greatly. It turns the game into an RNG machine rather than an actual strategy game. To make matters worse, dice become exhausted so you can easily find yourself in a situation where you lose a good number of dice AND a building because you have no defenders and you reroll a bunch of times, thus exhausting your dice. This is a game in which you are just not in control. Worst of all is that I don't think they can "fix it" because the dice and how they behave are a core aspect of the game.

I really want to like the game, but now that I'm several hours in I could never recommend it.Dice strategy is not the issue with the RNG. Dice collection is like deck builders with extra sides on each thing — it's entirely possible to plan enough to curtail the randomness of that stuff. It's poor planning as to how RNG will affect the layouts provided.The developer's seemed to be missing a key to the idea of roguelite-strategy RNG: limitations to RNG need to exist.It's entirely possible to start an unwinnable scenario from the get-go.Let's say you pick the character that starts with citizens. They don't start with stone. There is also no stone on the available map. The chances of you managing to expand into the next zone without that stone before your wood runs out is quite slim.Additionally, the unlocks do not make the game easier. They make it harder.This might change when you ascend die, but I haven't been able to figure out what that even refers to. The same character that starts with citizens does not start with any buildings the citizens are useful in. They are actually a liability, and make it harder to make those dice effective. On top of that, the vast majority of their buildings require stone — which doesn't spawn on the map with him (or hasn't in the runs I've done, which seems unlikely to be a coincidence). So now you're starting with *LESS* die that are actively useful.It's got enough unfortunate design decisions to prevent it from feeling enjoyable.

review: This is the type of phone game that's put together by a team of psychologists and cheap illustrators should be an offense to any self-respecting PC gamer.It's pretty devious. Here's an example:Your heroes usually trade blows with bad guys and slowly progress towards the right side of the screen. However, each time you click on the screen, you can do a tiny bit of extra damage to enemies. After opening a treasure chest, the game gifted me with an item, the Potion of Giant's Strength. This massively increases the amount of damage your clicking does, as it's based off the base power of your characters. Now you can kill very tough enemies with a single click!Suddenly your heroes advance very quickly through the dungeon all the way up to level 101 and you gets tons of money! But then you get as far as your clicking can take you, and you're forced to grind your party up the old fashioned way until you can beat level 102. This will take exactly as long as it would have taken had you not skipped ahead using the potion. Remember, you used the potion because you were having trouble fighting those monsters back on level 35. But now even your clicks aren't strong enough to beat the boss on level 102. You'll have to level up your heroes...and their skill level is way back at level 35. You got an incredible short term boost, but ultimately you're left with nothing have have in reality progressed very little. So you either get to keep buying stronger items with real money or you wait to grind, like a free player. It's manipulative in such a subtle, hidden way that I think it's morally wrong.

However, this week a Season Pass was introduced, and that was just too much. I get that Codename is running a business, but nobody playing the game wanted this. It is such an obvious cash grab and was so lazily implemented one of the new currencies for it is just called "Currency." The grinding that the daily quests that come with this Season Pass takes this game away from the charming idle game it was and just changes the game for the worse.There are bugs in this game that have not been addressed. Puzzle (Tetris)✅Unique room building puzzle➖RNG upon RNG upon RNG➖Not much to do beyond campaignIn Chambers of Devious Design you play as an evil villain that is continuously building lairs. There is a small and insignificant story involved here, but this seems like a severe afterthought just to ferry the play through multiple levels. The game world takes place on a 2D plane where you insert Tetris-like shapes together. The shapes can only be connected by the limited doorways that are randomly placed on each shape. This can lead to some interesting interactions based on the games win conditions. The narrative is small and insignificant, usually just a random conversation between your chosen character, of which there are around 8, and the mastermind. There are no lore or references to anything outside of the CoDD universe. CoDD gameplay consists of picking a piece, and rotating it until you find your desired fit. Before beginning a game, you first choose your villain. There are around 8 or 10, each with their own, somewhat forgettable abilities. This is one of the areas where CoDD really could have shined, is by making the playable characters truly unique. I played through 3 campaigns and found that all the abilities of the characters were boring at best and RNG at worst.After choosing a villain, you go into the game which tends to have a set win condition based on the level of the campaign you’re on. You start with a small square room with 2 doors on each side, leaving you 8 options for placements. Realistically, you’ll only use 4 because the doors are too close together. Then you pick a piece and smash em together to meet the win condition. Some of the win conditions consist of getting the highest score after x turns, reaching

Good concept, but not as challenging as I thought. Too much RnG for what is supposed to be a puzzle game.Random rooms, random abilities, random perks, random triggers, random shooting angles, random chain-lightning, random opponent targetting...Despite this, I finished the campaign at "Master" level in less than 4 hours with the starting character.Game needs longer campaign, tougher AI, less RnG, and certainly 1 or 2 more room types would help a lot. Player should have resources to spend on room rerolls, room modifications, and other abilities.I understand that it implies even more complex AI, and that's why I wish good luck to the dev :)I'll come back in a couple of months, if there is reasonable improvement I will be VERY happy to change this review to positive.

(Or could be just RNG)Second, RNG makes it a bit difficult to strategize. You could be going for a certain goal but the game may end before you can complete it because you don't have that room available, or because enemies can destroy you because their door location makes it convenient for that room that just showed up while your isn't.I think there are a few tweaks that can make it play more fluidly. For one, there could be a power that alters the location of the doors in a room. And probably a power that lets you select a room from a bigger pool for 1 turn. For pvp room destroying levels may be let the player build a few starter rooms without fighting. (But I know balancing a game like this can be hard)Overall, this is a game is not as light hearted as a puzzle game because of the competitive aspect, but it doesn't quite scratch the itch for a proper strategy game either. I unfortunately cannot recommend it.

I seriously want to love Cult of the Lamb; it oozes with charm and aesthetic, clearly a labour of love by the developers. However, what started off so fun fell rapidly into repetitive micromanagement and lacklustre dungeon-crawling. I saw a few negative Steam reviews posted and I must admit that all the criticisms they listed are exactly what I came to realise. I hate writing long-drawn out reviews so I'll leave a few jot-notes of things that annoyed me.- Unlocking tenets and the compound tech tree happens too quickly and you'll be left wondering why bother dungeon-crawling to collect cosmetic decorations- Farming is a micromanagement nightmare with your cultists refusing to harvest crops regardless if there is bountiful yield- The intended difficulty is too easy (in my opinion, having logged in hundreds of hours into BoI) with enemies having the same, telegraphed attacks- Dungeon crawling for potential cultists is invalidated as you can purchase them for 50 coins from a wandering spider, who also provides a discount those who are sick. If you chose the tenet that allows you to receive payment from your cultists, you can quickly amass well over 1000 coins and just purchase cultists when some die. Rinse and repeat.- The cowl that lets you start with an abundance of soul hearts is unbalanced. I fought one of the Bishops of the Old Faith with 13 soul hearts and proceeded to just bum rush him, not caring about how much damage I took and beat him probably within a minute.- The biomes are colour palette swaps and are largely uninterestingI will gladly change my review when an update arrives that addresses these issues and adds further content, but at this moment in time I cannot recommend a purchase.P.S. Cultists eating bowls of ♥♥♥♥ is always hilarious.

This game is basically a combination animal crossing + any rogue-lite. The problem is that it's too shallow on both of those comparisons so you'll never feel satisfied playing either part of the game. After about 2 hours of game play I felt that I already saw everything the game had to offer. To start with the rogue-lite element (crusade), its very quick and easy. Each crusade takes maybe 10-minutes and you can repeat the crusade if you've beaten the area boss +2 times so overall 30 minutes. Throughout the crusade you'll face against extremely simple enemies collecting the materials, blueprints for decorations, other random items that you need to develop your cult and face a "boss" at the end. The boss's mechanics are a larger + more hp version of an enemy you've already faced. After you're done with the crusade, you go back to manage your cult. Here is where the animal crossing-like part of the game starts and most of the tedium starts here. At the start, you have to interact with EVERYTHING and EVERYBODY. Through interacting you gain faith, loyalty, money, whatever to unlock more upgrades. At first, it was fun seeing the animations of the character interactions but then you'll start to realize that you have to watch the same animation that takes too many seconds, thousands of times. There are some upgrades to automate some parts of the game but to get any actual progress YOU have to interact with everything.Overall: Game play is too shallow.

I enjoyed the game initially but eventually (after I unlocked illustration) the gameplay grew a little stale. At this point, the majority of the gameplay is 1) choose your goals for the week on the map2) figure out what topics you need3) wait for the topics to roll in4) some minor decisions around how the stories should develop5) shape your paper depending on how the stories go6) publishThe crucial part is that step 5 is the most interesting part of the whole game loop, but the stories that you get, while they are RNG and can be interesting, never really change up the gameplay too much. You just wait for the stories to roll in and put the paper together every week, and it's mostly the same decisions and stories every week as you optimize for just getting the tags you need. You can tell there's a lot of love and care gone into this, it has a strong foundation to become a hot indy game. Let it cook a bit more tho.The game has premise! You spend each week trying to find out news stories around the US during the prohibition/stock market crash era. You then send reporters to investigate and write reports which you can then choose to edit and publish in your newspaper.Meanwhile you are trying to manage your business, financials, as space and interior are all important and affect how well your reporters and printers do. The game already has quite a bit of depth and really interesting mechanics.Some caveats:- It is still unfinished, you will see "Lorem ipsum" across newspapers, you'll see quests that don't quite trigger or make any sense depending on what stage you are with your newspaper. You may even still get reputation for failing a quest.- Animations are a bit wonky, perhaps part of the appeal. Tbh if the game mechanics and story are polished, I don't really care about the animations.- The game is quite hard to progress and reach the end game. Partially because some bits feel unfinished. There's not a lot of room for choice (even if it feels like it at first) if you want to progress, which is a bit counter-intuitive to the premise of the game.Things I'd like to see in the game:- More story elements. You start with the premise of helping your uncle and his debt. Nowhere is this mentioned throughout the story.- Historical events. The game already has a few headlines related to the time period and they add a great element of immersion. It would be nice to see how these affect the economy and the world around you instead of just headlines

PolyClassic: Wild is an asset flip, what Valve calls a "fake game". The "developer", Whale Rock Games, took the tutorial/demo/game asset pack from the real developers, Synty Studios, changed the name, dropped it onto a very basic Unreal FPS engine (and did very little else with it, it's barely functional) and dumped the result onto Steam. They're attempting to scam people into buying this, so they can get your money for someone else's work.The products that result from asset flips aren't "real" games. They lack depth and content, because they're just simplistic copies of demos or tutorials. In this case, "POLYGON - Western Pack" is just a low poly Western themed asset pack for use with Unity and Unreal 3D games, combined with a very lazy Unreal FPS game, and doesn't have any merit as a proper, fully fledged PC game, so this copy+paste of it can't be recommended.Asset flips don't involve any professional game development. Sure, sometimes they may change a few cosmetic things, swap out different assets etc, but at heart it's functionally identical to the asset they're ripping off.Asset flips like this are harmful to the gaming industry and to Steam because they reduce the visibility that sincerely made indie games should have, and make it harder for gamers to find real games from genuine developers.This game features a HUGE number of fake positive reviews from accounts known to be in the business of review manipulation/paid reviews. They're all written in either Russian or broken English, appear almost immediately after the game launched on Steam, all have a direct Steam purchase of the game, and the accounts are used consistently to write fake reviews for asset flips and other cash grabs/scams. The "Positive" review score on this game should be disregarded due to this review manipulation.Don't reward

I've come into the game late... It seems like the devs at one point acknowledged the UI was atrocious? But they have moved on from the game. There is a very smart foundation beneath this game, the mechanics all feel very very consistent, bots/path finding work great. The issues with this game are all pragmatic... The UI is not consistent, for example opening the Terminal tool shows the Terminal Overlay, but there are 2 ways to open it and only one of them allows you to interact with the overlay. Difficulty settings are far too simple... You can be broke with lots of natural disasters or rich with none.Map choice looks incredibly promising on first play through, choosing anywhere in the world to host your airport... In reality it is only done by country e.g. choosing Juno Alaska yields the same scenario as choosing NYC. This is just lazy, there is clearly a very simple dataset holding the map locations and attributes that could be naively expanded to differentiate barren wastelands from massive metropolis. Map is always the same, always too small and with a monolithic expansion process, this should have been done like Roller Coaster Tycoon allowing to purchase expansions by the tile. Further, the map should be able to extend longer and not so symmetrical. Subways exist... Meaning there is a "subway entrance" where people magically teleport in/out of your terminal, reaching the subway station completely eliminates the need for public roads of any kind (except to drop off contractors), so the entire early game is deleted as soon as you finish a bit of research. You will never be able to build any kind of shuttles or inter-terminal transport... The shuttles are only used for a brief moment as a crutch before jetways, and is utterly un-scalable,

这可能是我玩过最令人反胃的塔防游戏。它的经营部分弱的可怜，防御地形的随机性也极大地影响防御塔的强度。随机性方面：如果你运气好拥有一个S形的地形与合适的射程强化格子，那么你的渡鸦塔可以对精英敌人造成很可观的伤害。但如果你只有一条几乎笔直的线路，那你的渡鸦塔很可能沦为垃圾。更不要说在转角处的射程强化格的作用了。经营方面：经营要素非常之少，并且数值也卡得极为严苛。这是最令我反胃的部分。它是如此缺乏以至于存在一个显而易见的最优解，但前提是你需要反复、反复、反复地刷同样的关卡以获得足够多（我是指，几乎全部）的局外成长后，你的经营才可以顺滑地过度。如果没有？是的，你恰好缺乏一点资源，所以你需要晚一回合才能获得你的下一个工人，并且在下下个工人时你也恰好缺乏一点资源。于是一步慢步步慢，资源的差距便在一回合一回合的累计中拉到巨大。想要赢？好吧，你可以试着重复打十遍一样的关卡，然后获得超级imba的数值以取胜。塔防游戏是策略游戏的子类，但是在这里，你的策略并不是那么重要。去吧，去重复一样的关卡以获得超越策略的数值。Probably the most disgusting TD game I've ever played. The city management aspect is pathetically weak and the randomness of the terrain greatly affects the towers.Randomness/"Rogue" part:If you are lucky enough to get an S-shaped terrain with appropriate height tile, your Raven Tower can deal significant damage to the elite enemies and bosses. But if you unfortunately got an almost straight line terrain, your Raven Tower will likely become almost useless. Not to mention the impact of tile height at path corners.City build part:Very very very few options. This is the most disgusting part for me. The values are extremely harshly limited.It’s so lacking that there’s an obvious optimal solution, but only if you repeatedly played the same levels over and over and over and over again until you have farmed enough (enough=almost all) meta progression, at which point your city development can finally be done smoothly.If not? You just happen to be short on exactly 10 resources in meta progression, forcing you to wait another wave to get your next worker. And then for the next worker after that, you are also just short again. This leads to a massive resource gap accumulating over turns. Want to win?Well, you can try playing the same level ten times to get super overpowered (or by designed) stats and then auto win.Tower defense should be a sub-category of strategy games. But here, you strategy doesn't matter. Go, farm the same level repeatedly to get stats that beats strategy.

Every run is about the same as the enemy path doesn't branch out enough for this to make a serious difference.1) makes a difference as it makes you think whether to invest in resource gathering or in tower defense. You gotta estimate if your current defense is strong enough to fend off the next wave, so you can invest in your village to build more towers later and therefore more total towers than if you didn't invest. I like this difference, but I don't like the meta-progression it holds. To get through the waves you need a strong resource income, but you first need to unlock most village upgrades which require a resource gathered by killing enemies. So it breaks down to repeating runs to unlock the meta-progression for you to be finally able to make use of things. Something important to note is that this is not an idle game. You have to play actively.The game provides a vast variety of spells from different schools and systems for the player to focus on. While at times a bit overwhelming, the game does not really force them onto the player, and they can focus on one at a time.A brilliant feature I will mention separately is the augmentation system: spells can be modified in different ways, offering a tradeoff between the spell's stats. For example, by sacrificing some of the spell's power, the spell can have a lower cooldown.The amount of different spells and the augmentation system creates a playground for testing different combos and strategies.I am also a fan of the music and the visuals of the game - it sounds and looks great.All that being said, the reason I am not recommending the game is that the gameplay - essentially composed of casting spells, crafting stuff, and upgrading skills - is neither interesting nor engaging enough to justify the lack of automation features, especially auto-casting. With that addition alone the game would potentially be one of the best idle games, and I would love to play it more.

The game cycles too fast. Every free-to-play game has a certain "loop" to it, where you can play and have fun for a while and then the difficulty starts ramping up until you can't have fun anymore without either (a) grinding for an excessive period of time, or (b) paying some money. The cycle time on this game is only a few minutes. Now, typically, what defrays this problem is that if you close it for a few hours you can come back and have the PARTIAL benefits of grinding without having to sit there and stare at it. But this game is stingy af with the offline earnings, so you make squat from offline time anyway, and on top of that it caps offline earnings at four hours. So basically, you get to play this game for ten minutes, then quit playing BUT come back every four hours to collect your offline earnings - until you pay some money, and then you get the wonderful benefit of being able to just quit for several days so you can come back and play for ten minutes again. Bluntly speaking, the game is badly designed. The game should be fun for ten minutes, then NOT AS FUN for about twenty, and then effectively unplayable unless you pay OR leave it earning offline for about 12 hours. You could, of course, make it even more fun and give the player even more time... if you're not quite as greedy as the average F2P dev. But the player should be able to open this game and have fun at least once a day, not open it several times a day and find that it's still not fun, so they should close it and play a different game. I would give this a neutral if possible. But, I am leaning more towards negative.Nearly everything about this game is standard tower defense except the random card based aspect. There are no advanced features in this tower defense game. Maps are not dynamic in any way. Enemies won't loop through the maps. There's regular enemies, boss enemies, armored enemies, flying enemies, etc. Towers, as such, follow the same type of rules.So, let's talk about what is different in this game, and what makes it a nightmare to play. Each wave, you are given three random tower cards that you can purchase. Completely random and if you don't buy them, they go away and you get another 3 random cards you can purchase next wave. If you place a tower on the map and want to upgrade that tower, you are going to need two more of the same card to get that tower to 2 star. In order to get that tower to 3 star (which you are going to need to do for all towers you place in order to finish all waves on a map), you need to pull and purchase the same card an additional 6 times. Meaning you need to pull the same tower card 9 times. Now, you can also pay gold to re-roll three new cards if you don't get what you want. But, the randomness is such that it is entirely possible, and will happen, that you don't get to pull the cards that you need which means you will fail the level through no fault of your own. On top of this, you can run out of inventory space so you can also get a card you need but be in a position where you can't buy it.When things go your way

Think about it: You want a tier 3 tower? You have to get 3 level 1 of the tower and then 3 level 2 of the tower, and you CANNOT USE 2 of the 3 in each upgrade, the MUST be in the bottom bar UNUSED, a bar which has only 8 slots. You have 100 health, which is not a lot as enemies do a lot of damage (so expect to die in just a few hits). Each turn also drains 1 health, so you effectively only have 100 turns to beat the game. And sometimes it takes several turns to get to one enemy as two enemies are on opposite sides of the map and the enemies are both long range fighters who run away from you. So you end up taking 3-10+ damage just trying to reach the other enemy at times. You can use abilities to mitigate this, but they take several turns to recharge and it gets repetitive needing to depend on the same really strong abilities while being forced to ignore weaker, but fun to use ones.And some maps get you stuck in a lose-lose situation because of the health drain per turn mechanic. You could get a bad map where if you rush in to kill a enemy quickly, you take damage. But if you take the time needed to not take a hit, you end up taking 3-5+ damage anyways as it moves in a way that makes you have to wait several turns to attack it.You can heal by killing more then one enemy in the same turn, but because of the health drain per turn mechanic, you can spend several turns setting up a combo...which effectively makes the heal very small. it means you have to really min-max and do things as perfectly as possible.
