game_name: El Hijo - A Wild West Tale
review: El Hijo is a top-down stealth game that sees you playing as a young boy set upon reuniting with his mother. Taking place in the wild west, you must sneak your way past bandits and survive the harshness of your environment. That, and tackle with the game's many technical issues.The biggest problem with El Hijo is that it feels like a constant battle to play. Its controls are wonky and unresponsive, which is not exactly good when you need to react to situations quickly. Its stealth mechanics are poorly refined, coupled with AI that is just downright unfair. It gets to a point where playing it feels like a chore, and it doesn't take long for this to set in.The game does have merit, though. A good story married with stunning presentation and a charming visual style give it a definitive edge. The level design is expansive, with each one feeling alive. There's always lots of things going on, and some set pieces really do catch the eye.Unfortunately, I don't think all of that is enough for me to be able to recommend El Hijo, simply because it fails at what it sets out to be: a stealth game. If your a die hard fan of stealth games, or wild west settings, maybe get this on a heavy discount. There are four "math operations" that you can use to manipulate the special green blocks. The number and type of operations varies from level to level.+ Level design organically introduces these new operations, acting as a tutorial.+ All combines into a fun idea for a puzzle platformer! If not entirely original per se.It's free, so it's okay that it's fairly short, only 12 levels (plus a secret one).The puzzles are simple and there's not very much thinking to finish each level.Controls are simple keyboard WASD to move, mouse to use the operations.The store page mentions a level editor but I did not actually see it in-game. Unless you count the gimmicky secret level.- Jumping is clunky and at times unresponsive. This is very important to get right in platformers, and having made some platformers (albeit not published any), I know it's difficult too. This could use improvement.- Frame drops. For whatever reason, the game loses performance randomly. It's annoying and a bit unsettling, because of:- F-Secure malware warning for "Heuristic". Steam is pretty safe and I've never heard of an actual virus on it. For this reason and having played it, I obviously ignored the warning and seems I'm alright. Still, dev should get that sorted out with the scanners. (For the record, the file was .\Plugins\x86_64\lib_burst_generated.dll)My completion time was about 15-20 minutes, including the time looking for secrets/achievements. The last level in particular was a headscratcher, until my initial solution worked - the trouble was just the unresponsive jumping.Note that for 100% you need the DLC.For the developer, this is a moderate entry game into the business. While it's not great, it demonstrates some

Positives:+ It's free+ Good use of basic math operationsNegatives:- Errors, e.g. clicking on one block can lead to the adjacent being deleted. - The movement is clunky. Overall impression:It's a neat idea for a game but the movement and errors mean I wouldn't recommend.

Hidden Build Top-Down 3D is a Unity Asset flip, what Valve calls a "fake game". The "developer", Hede/Top-Down Games, took the Unity Store tutorial/demo/game asset pack from the real developers, Synty Studios, changed the name, slapped a lame hidden object template over it, and dumped the result onto Steam. They're attempting to scam people into buying this, so they can get your money for someone else's work.Hede/Top-Down Games has shown a repeat pattern of unethically dumping other people's work onto Steam as a cheap, nasty cash grab. Here's some examples so you can see for yourself:The products that result from asset flips aren't "real" games. They lack depth and content, because they're just simplistic copies of demos or tutorials. In this case, "Polygon Construction Low Poly 3D Art" is just a basic low poly asset pack from Synty featuring construction assets intended to be used as placeholders for fully developed games, and doesn't have any merit as a proper, fully fledged PC game, so a copy+paste of it can't be recommended.Asset flips don't involve any professional game development. Sure, sometimes they may change a few cosmetic things, swap out different assets etc, but at heart it's functionally identical to the asset they're ripping off.Asset flips like this are harmful to the gaming industry and to Steam because they reduce the visibility that sincerely made indie games should have, and make it harder for gamers to find real games from genuine developers.This game features a number of fake positive reviews from accounts known to be in the business of review manipulation/paid reviews. They're all written in either Russian or broken English, appear almost immediately after the game launched on Steam, all have a direct Steam purchase of the game, and the accounts are used consistently to write fake reviews for asset

This game is hands down the best game out there for making me click "Exit Game" and go back to playing Crusader Kings or Civilization 6.The number of random events in a turn is so high that it can be a stretch to actually classify this as a "strategy" game instead of as an RNG clicker game. Examples: an event that the game described as having a 5% chance to occur on any given turn happened multiple times per turn for almost 20 turns in a row; three turns in a row, I had my leader die due to a random event, wiping out literally an entire dynasty; the random map seed generator is cruel and unforgiving and it's not uncommon to load up a game and find out there are no elephants, horses, or camels (needed for cavalry units) within 6 city centers of your starting zone; the opinions of AI opponents have absolutely no staying power, and random events can swing their opinion of you from Peace (+350) to ready to declare war (-250) in one turn, with no actions actually taken by you.That said, if you want a historically less-than-accurate war sim that sometimes lets you city-build, this game certainly exists. I just think calling a game with such heavy-handed and overbearing RNG use a "strategy" game is inaccurate and dishonest.

In rougelites, especially turn-based ones like this without any execution challenge, the primary interest has to come from the gameplay possibilities of the random elements, particularly the upgrade system. Slay the Spire became a gold standard for a reason; it's endlessly complex despite just moving from room to room because of the endless levels of interplay and synergy between the cards and relics you can find. Infinite complexity deriving from finite mechanics.So the fact that gameplay in Ring of Pain boils down to clicking on the card you want to trade attack and defense numbers with, and occasionally do a single use ability, shouldn't preclude this game's combat being interesting. There are multiple enemy properties, attack types, and other things to interact with. But the problem becomes that none of these effects interact with eachother in interesting ways. The only real decision you can make at any time is to click on the least threatening card at the moment, and occasionally run away. The real problem is that actual game-changing properties are usually tied to limited-use items, and can't ever become part of your playstyle. It's a numbers game and not much else.

Terraformers isn't a bad "game", it's just very shallow, unless you're into "colonizing" Mars over and over again. I prefer games like Per Aspera, in which you're really working towards something. Terraformers on the other hand is your bite-sized variant, which also relies quite a bit on RNG.The game is mostly card-based. You pick from a selection of cards each round. These are your buildings you can place in your cities. Of course, you have to found cities first, and this is the most interesting part of the game. Where in Per Aspera balancing the various resources as well as the actual terraforming process, Terraformers doesn't really care about the latter. Your primary goal is finding resource spots and establishing colonies that produce metals, food, etc., and keeping your population happy enough. This morale mechanic is an ever-escalating number, which basically acts like a "soft enrage" timer. Your population will demand more and more from you, which, in theory, you shouldn't be able to fulfill forever, which is a weird design choice. Once your planet is fully explored and colonized there's little you can do to keep up with the insanely high demands. You'll get regular events that give you -150 morale per turn, for instance. Forever. But you can only gain morale via exploration, terraforming, certain buildings and space projects. Exploration simply ends at some point. Terroforming is done at some point, same as seeding life forms, and your colonies will eventually be out of building space, while space projects are comparatively rare and have a terrible yield (sth like 10 morale per turn). Now, by the time this becomes an issue in a normal game, you'll likely be done anyway. I still don't really like the never-ending escalation.The terraforming process is simply: increase 4 stats to level 3

I am a guitar player, and have been in many jam sessions where you would sit and play and everyone would take turns with rhythm and lead, and things would go fine until one guy, and you know it before he even touched the guitar, but he would pick it up and start to strike whatever notes he felt like. It would be in the wrong key. Notes would be off. The tempo would swing wildly in every direction. Every technique they attempted was like nails on a chalkboard. There was no rhyme or reason to the playing at all, and afterward, when everyone's ears and good musical sense had been thoroughly violated, then the guy would set the guitar back on the stand, and look around and smile as if he had just composed a a masterpiece. That guy is the one the developers have performing on this soundtrack.

It feels like a glorified auto battler and shouldn't be compared to Slay the Spire.Here's how the game breaks down (at least in the time of writing this)The story*Don't askVisually*Sprite for that retro style, similar to Shovel knight. (Modern game classic syle)Audio*Musics fine, SFX are fine. Nothing to complain about or swoon over.Characters*Each character has different stats and a different deck*While win goals are different, character's really don't feel unique hereProgression*Each Area has a set of floors and at the end of each floor is boss.*Each floor is Linear, no branching paths. (Note: In the description it boosts branching levels so its possible they didn't put in the effort to show that in the demo)*There are... Events, 1 per floor, always in the same place Combat*Before each fight choose 3 cards*Put cards over an opponent to attack it, if no cards are left, you can only attack front row.*Chance to get equipment which are bonuses that last as long as you have them.Your deck*It's not REALLY a deck. It's more of a pool with a % to draw certain cards so there's no guarantee to getting a card by deck cycling. *The three draws before each fight are the only draws you get.*No place to see what cards a character has, you just find out by putting time in.This game just dumps on all the upsides to card games, no deck building, no synergy or strategy involved here. Everything boils down to this....Step 1)Only play cards if not playing cards will kill youStep 2)Seriously, DON'T play your cards unless you absolutely have toStep 3)Get to boss and SPAM your cardsThat's the entire game for now.There is absolutely nothing here that makes me think of Slay the Spire.The closest it comes is the visual layout of the game, and if that's
Reddit humor level, yuck.As for the game itself... meh, quite unbalanced as of yet and the screen's way too cluttered.

I sincerely hope the bugs get patched and the game becomes more accessible to the average player, but until then, it's a large disappointment... I'll have to give it a pass.

Have you ever fancied taking eight goblins and some basic resources, selecting a patch of procedurally generated land on which to build, and starting your own goblin tribe?Goblins of Elderstone gives you this opportunity. Customise your tribe and their history, then set out with only an ever-burning campfire and a cartful of resources to make your mark on the world!Hmmm. Do goblins mark their territory? I'm not sure.Goblins of Elderstone looks pretty, with a colourful large-poly style. The game is played in full 3D with a reasonably well-behaving free-floating 3D camera. You can pan in three dimensions and rotate about two and it mostly works well, though the terrain and buildings do sometimes force the camera somewhere not quite where you want it. Models are mostly made up of smallish numbers of large polygons, with relatively clean and simple textures. They look cartoonish and really rather nice.The goblins themselves are cute little buggers -- even the skeletal ones! -- but there's very little variation between them. Each job role has a custom skin, some of which are wonderfully creative, but within each job there only seem to be a couple of variations. Though not essential, it would definitely add personality to the game if there were more changes in the basic appearance: different builds, faces, accessories, etc. As it is I didn't grow even remotely attached to any of the goblins, since they were so interchangeable.Buildings are more detailed than they appear at first glance: zooming in shows some interesting details. Many buildings differ from the others in size, shape, and details, with otherwise similar-looking buildings differentiated by the signs attached, such as the large hand tool on the top of the Crafting Hut. They all have a sort of tribal goblin feel to them, which is great.The game world
While the premise of this game has a lot of potential, there's a LOT of balancing issues that need to be addressed before it's really at a 1.0 stage.

I don't mind when a game is hard, but Goblins of Elderstone is hard for the wrong reasons. Good difficulty is when the player's skill can be used to overcome challenges. Bad difficulty is when the player is not given enough information to overcome obstacles, or even to know what's going wrong in the first place.Goblins will randomly stop working, regardless of traits or mood or any other discernible cause. The game will tell you a goblin is freezing or unhappy or whatever, but all you can do is make sure the needs are being met. You can't force a freezing goblin to go to the fire, or hand a worker one of the many tools sitting in the stockpile, or cram a handful of berries and frogs -- of which you have many -- down its stupid ungrateful self-destructive gullet.Defense Mode is not turned on, so I can't see any reason why they are not better at taking care of themselves or doing their jobs. If the game would tell me what's wrong, I'd fix it. Instead, I'm left to watch my goblins wander around like idiots, sometimes breeding, occasionally gathering something useful, but mostly just pouting because the scavenger can't find the frogs or loafing around because the guy in the lumber mill (who is not lazy) has plenty of logs and refuses to saw them.Maybe I'm missing something here, but I honestly don't see how that's my fault unless I'm just expected to intuit these things based on my vast knowledge of colony builders. I do not have vast knowledge of colony builders, and if that's considered a reasonable barrier of entry, I'm happy to take my refund and go.

Mosaic puzzle games are a dime a dozen on Steam, and their quality varies significantly. Some are good, some are bad, and then there are games like that are hard to decide whether to recommend or not.- Beautiful art- The background music is nice- Gameplay is barebones- There’s no options menu- It’s very shortLet’s start with the positive aspects of the game; the art is beautiful. On another note, the soundtrack may be composed of a single song, but it’s nice to listen to and fits the relaxed mood of the game.As for its negative aspects, the gameplay is barebones. There’s nothing that sets this game apart from the many mosaic puzzle games on Steam, even if the puzzles themselves are decent. It’s also very short, taking no more than half an hour to beat. Another problem the game has is the lack of basic features like an options menu or even a title screen. It loads the puzzles as soon as you click on “play” in the Steam launcher without giving the possibility to adjust the resolution, the volume, or choosing between playing on fullscreen or windowed mode. isn’t bad per se, especially considering this is the dev’s first game, but the gameplay is lacking, and some important features are missing. I would describe this game as a 'befriending sim' with a very shallow veneer of farming/resource gathering/'witchy' activities. The farming/mining/fishing is nowhere near as fun or sophisticated as other games e.g. Stardew Valley. And there are no customisation options - even very shallow ones - to make the game experience your own, e.g. the layout of your farm and buildings can't be changed or decorated, there's no home decoration, no character customisation or clothing options. So the game feels very linear and daily tasks are repetitive and grind-y. There's also a dearth of special/seasonal occasions which adds to the repetition.And even though this game majors on the social/befriending angle, which is largely ok, it still doesn't feel quite right. You can get to be 'good friends' with a character and they still repeat dialogue asking if you've met their family members (of course you have) and/or your character asks them really basic getting-to-know-you type questions that previous cutscenes have already answered. The voice acting is great though.I think this game would have been a lot better had it been done as an all-out graphic novel/choices matter game, and dropped the farming etc. As it is, it's a jack of all trades and master of none.

Hell Division is a thrilling third-person game that revolves around intense battles between combat drones. As a player, I was immediately captivated by the immersive graphics and seamless gameplay. The visuals are truly stunning, with detailed environments that make the experience feel incredibly realistic.One of the aspects I enjoyed the most about Hell Division is the wide variety of drones available for combat. Each drone has its own unique set of abilities and weapons, allowing players to customize their playstyle and strategize accordingly. Whether I wanted to engage in close-quarters combat or take a more stealthy approach, there was a drone that suited my preferences.The combat mechanics in Hell Division are top-notch. The controls are intuitive and responsive, making it easy to execute precise attacks and evade enemy fire. The battles are intense and adrenaline-pumping, requiring quick reflexes and tactical thinking. PCZ is your typical Picross game in terms of puzzles. If you played any Picross game (on the 3DS in my case), then you’ll feel right at home. The game’s charm and adventure part is what makes it stand out and worth playing for fans of the genre. The adventure part is lighthearted. Don’t expect deep and fleshed out mechanics. You have a small world divided in a few blocks. Each block has a few puzzles that bring objects, people or animals back to life (220+). Most of them won’t have much of a significance to the story but there will be puzzles that do and you will get some items that are either mandatory or to find some of the secrets in the game. For instance, you’ll need a lamp to go through a dark cave. Even if there is no significance, it’s satisfying seeing things come to life and the numbers of your checklist going up. The puzzles themselves are mostly simple-doable and they won’t reach the challenge you can expect from the Picross E games on the 3DS for instance. There are some NPC you can speak with, an inventory menu, world map and an in game trophy (achievement) tracker. Add the charming pixel graphics, catchy music & funny dialogue and you got yourself a good formula. The dialogues are often self aware and I enjoy them but humour is obviously very subjective. I also love the secrets the developer came up with and even how some of them are personal. In terms of cons, I can mainly think of 2 minor bugs and one design decision. Long(ish) objective review with a TLDR at the end.The concept of this game and art style is ok. I can see the goals the developers were trying to achieve. Pretty simple, straightforward. You + 3 other people are plague doctors, and are taken to a town filled with creatures. In order to cure the town, you must find ingredients scattered around the town and put them in a cauldron that is in a sort of 'safe house' you have. You must put the correct amount and correct ingredients in the right order into the cauldron to brew the formula. The game gives you hints through trial and error of brewing potions, but you must be careful, because ingredients are limited and do not re-spawn- so you have to be smart with how you test which ingredients are useful. You can also buy items from a 'shop' they have that can help you.Overall, the concept is enjoyable and would be a fun game to pass a couple hours every so often with friends, however there are currently many things that take away from this experience:- The towns and monsters are procedurally generated and chosen at random, which is a good choice and keeps things fresh. However, there is not much variability. This game would really benefit from more environment assets and a bigger list of creatures it pulls from. The addition of the immortal snail for example is a small but nice touch that I think this game could use more of.- Some of the items in the shop straight up do not work. My friend bought a fireball wand, it did no damage to anything. My other friend bought a dining hall pass, which also did not work. This becomes frustrating, due to the price of items vs the amount

A pretty fun and creative sandbox game which sets you up to create a sailing vehicle as well as managing it. This is to make to travel along some distance to reach the finish line in each level within the story where you are travelling home. It does have some poly bridge kind of feel as you get into the sandbox section that provides a limited amount of money and resource where you need to make a vehicle that can actually travel against the winds. Though it is not so much a typical vehicle as you basically just set up various kinds of rooms that each gives some speed. Some are simple rooms that doesn't require interactions, though the more you progress, the more complex rooms are available to be added onto the contraption that does require some involvement. There is some platforming involved as well as you would need to organise your rooms with walls of course since you can't move between floors in mid air. You would also need to set up the floors to be optimal so that the most amount of speed can be gained throughout the travel, but also be able to reach the different areas of the contraption so that you can actually gain said speed. It does have an interesting little story with some humour where you are a cute little ladybug trying to make it home for a little girls birthday. Results are based on how fast you are able to reach the finish line with the contraption you have built with the budget given where it is fun to try and create the optimal one. Overall it is an interesting little indie game for those who like to create things.

A very enthralling dark fantasy game. There's nothing else quite like it. Feels oddly like a cozy crafting/farming sim. You play as an old man that experiments on himself with potions. The results are usually punishing and disastrous. There is a logic here about why certain potion combinations lead to certain outcomes but it's also confusing in an intriguing and forgivable way. I found myself learning more about what the game wants me to do just from playing and being open to its mysteries.You're provided a stream of people to use potions on. It's satisfying to attend to their needs but not very rewarding. The potion-making controls seem finicky at first but I was hooked into the strangely hypnotic grind of it quickly. I was delighted by each new and noticeable change within the otherwise dour atmosphere. These occur due to successful experiments that change dominant elements. Light potions will result in the main character being able to see more easily and see streaks of light. Some dark potions will result in mildly horrific oddities scattered around the otherwise lonely house.While this game feels like it's small in explorable scope, the uniqueness makes up for that. I also just like it for being one of the only dark and twisted (accidentally?) cozy games I can even think of outside of Graveyard Keeper.

It retains the same player grading system, the same postgame unlockable modes, the same secret solutions to the games, and the same unclear control scheme as the previous titles. Generally speaking, how one feels about the prior entries will remains true for this one; returning fans of and should be satisfied with this entry. does make an effort to introduce some changes to the formula; unfortunately, most of these are for the worse. And... that's about it. There needs to be more types of races. The game already seems to be taking many inspirations from the PS2-era NFS games, they need to go further in that direction!- Other reviews have already mentioned the highway junctions that end into nothing except invisible walls; well, they should lead somewhere! Clown in a House is a metaphorical adventure through a house, with a clown. But it's not for everyone, this game is intensely personal to it's creator so if you can't jam with that then this might not be your thing. If you expect a regular point and click you are probably gonna be disappointed. This is more art than game.Spoilers Ahead.Clown in a House is not a traditional point and click game. You're used to being the protagonist in these, a 'good guy' the guy who saves everyone, but there is nobody to really save here. Clown in a House is instead more of a storytelling experience than a video game, but there's plenty of 'video game' feel to it throughout. The game is full of secrets, some endings may frustrate you to find (the closet door was intensely frustrating) but it's more of a self-introspective kind of piece for it's creator, Kirk. It's fitting since Kirk is coming away from Catghost that he'd create something in-between video game and art piece. It's clear that while the creator was going through some important things in life, that they've held onto it and stored it here, in his 'house' for you to check out. Notes are scattered, small monologues are present, and like any house there are parts of it he'd like you to see more than others. He's tossed a bit of comedy in for funsies, but it's important for people interested in coming in to realize this is more narrative experience. The creator wants to just share his 'house' with you, his innermost thoughts, even if it's not very 'video gamey'. Through this you'll see him struggle with some inner demons, and maybe actually come to terms with some things about himself through your actions as 'Geo' the

If you're am artist, writer, or creator in any way shape or form I highly recommend this game. Despite it's appearance, it has an incredibly realistic and raw discussion about what it means to create, your relationship with your creations, inspiration, motivation, and the people who consume your creations. As an artist, there were moments that really resonated with extremely deeply (especially the moments where you get to see Kirk's self doubt and self loathing).I think very early on it's very apparent that Geo is representative of Kirk's artistic motivation and once you view Geo as a part of Kirk it makes the game more enjoyable I think. Every time Geo would die and come back and Kirk would say something like "oh you're back so soon?" or "I didn't think you'd be back yet" just makes me think of how Geo's death could be representative of art block and his return is finding inspiration and motivation again.Overall it's a fun, silly game that can be very cynical and harsh but it's enjoyable! It really is a great look into the mind of an artist and what it's like pursuing a hobby or career in creating.

If you've ever liked "Skate" games this is fantastic VR version. Though very bare bones right now this game really stands apart from any other typical VR game as it uses motion controllers in an innovative way that should really be applauded. You essentially mimic the movements of street skating with your upper body only. It translates very well.The game itself is primarily a street skating course that is a downhill run that you score based on trick combos and jumping obstacles. The satisfaction of landing tricks is addictive, not too hard to complete, but hard enough to make good flawless runs rare. As it stands right now there are three modes not including training. Freeplay for practice, Ranked where you get a set number of "bails" before your turn expires and, Sudden Death, where you can not fall or your turn is over. The latter two having ranked leader-boards where your tricks/combos get calculated. The training course is a kind of warehouse skate park that is only seen in training and really should be utilized for a small indoor free-roam skate park. Instead it's a series of runs always going from point a. to b. It works well, but I find myself using the tutorial as a way just to practice jumps off of ramps I like. I don't have many complaints about this game other than it is missing a free roam style skate park. Also, sometimes getting the speed right can be janky. Getting max speed before a ramp can be troublesome as if you are not "pushing" right before the ramp you lose momentum. It can get physically tiring and frustrating. I'd like to see the momentum stay longer to have better control for timing big jumps/rail slides. All in all the games pros outweigh any

Well, I've been a fan of top-down, isometric racers a long time. I loved Super Sprint and even more so Ivan Ironman Stewart's Super Off Road. But the latter game is a different beast and one which also deserves a modern interpretation.This game is supposed to be a modern Sprint series inspired game, but where it fits in I am not entirely sure. People coming to this for the first time will find a fun and simple arcade racer, which a new generation may well enjoy without preconceptions. It represents a time a place where games where fun, simple, and brought people together around a screen.Where it falls a bit flat is that for the fans of the Super Sprint (and why would it try to emulate the 70's racer, which is basic in the extreme) this isn't quite what people would have expected. The tracks don't have some of the charm (where are the shortcut gates? Upgrades? Hazards are simply optional and not part of the challenge, either. So for me, it's not quite that game at all. But when playing it does have some of the charm in it's gameplay, and with friends it can be a lot of fun. The single player campaign is simple, and a bit too easy. The track designs are also not particularly exciting, nor is there a lot. You do get a Time Trail campaign and Obstacle one too. All the Campaigns will allow you to unlock car livery and colours, along with track builder parts, and it is the latter which is the games saving grace.The track builder is, while a bit clunky in it's user operation (why can we not highlight and move track parts that are placed? Copy? Mirror placed track parts? Flick between variants on placed parts etc?)

Very good little game without pretension, which inevitably reminds me of Super Sprint from the Atari ST era. There are still some small adjustments to be made, such as the car physics, which could be improved (jumps, crashes, etc.), but overall, we're talking about a game that provides immediate and straightforward enjoyment. I approve!

As a fan of isometric racing games I give NeoSprint a massive thumbs-up! It's very retro in how it feels and plays, with a good increase in AI difficulty as you progress... But not too difficult. NeoSprint revives the classic "Sprint" series with a fresh, modern twist. Atari really nailed it with this arcade racer. It’s easy to pick up but tough to master, offering something for both casual and competitive players, whether solo or in multiplayer.The graphics are bright and colorful, instantly capturing that old-school arcade feel. The isometric view works great for racing, and if you want variety, you can switch between the classic top-down or a closer view for a different experience.The controls are tight and responsive, just like an arcade racer should be. They’re simple to learn but take skill to perfect, especially when it comes to drifting and drafting. Every race is fast-paced and satisfying, with plenty of "just one more race" moments.The track-building feature is where NeoSprint really shines. You can design custom tracks with ramps, jumps, and scenic elements across four biomes: forest, desert, winter, and city. However, the editor can feel a bit finicky at times, especially when trying to place elements precisely. Still, when it clicks, it’s a lot of fun.There are nine different cars to choose from, each with its own unique handling, speed, and acceleration. You can customize them with various colors and Atari-themed decals, adding a nice personal touch.For solo players, Campaign Mode offers a solid challenge. You race against eight AI opponents through multiple Cups, and the difficulty ramps up over time. Unlockable car skins and decorations keep you motivated to push through. There are also alternate modes like Grand Prix, Obstacle Courses, and Time Trials, all of which add extra replay value.Multiplayer is where NeoSprint goes all out. Racing against up to seven other players on one screen is chaotic, fast, and a ton of fun. The ability to share and rate custom-built tracks with the community ensures that there’s always something

That being said, there's lots of added challenge in variety in the user-created courses and the obstacle course mode, that adds a lot of replay value, and it is helped by the fact the controls are tight and each car handles differently, so picking the right car for the course helps. The graphics are fantastic and the game runs brilliantly, and creating courses is a lot of fun. What would be nice, would be an online multiplayer in addition to local - playing online on user-generated courses would add a lot of replayability and challenge and would bring the game from good to great. review: is a free-to-play yaoi visual novel developed and published by ChaniMK. You take on the role of Kyle (whose name can be customized), looking for a job in marketing. He gets offered a job interview at a fashion company and immediately after the interview, he gets hired by Vincent Zircon, the boss himself. As Kyle gets accustomed to his job, he notices that Vincent's moods change. One minute, Vincent acts all teasing and mischievous, and the next minute, he's all kind and caring. However, it turns out that Vincent is the teasing, mischievous twin brother to Vernon, the kind, caring (slightly older) twin whom Kyle happened to bump into on his way to lunch. Kyle gets to know the twins, and it turns out that they're estranged (although they were once close) due to some family issues in which their dad wanted the twins to take over the family business. While Vernon was ok with that, Vincent wanted to pursue his dreams of starting a fashion business. Kyle tries to help the twins resolve their family issues, and perhaps, romance might blossom, but I'll end my story synopsis here to avoid spoilers and all that. ^^As for the gameplay, choices are presented as you progress through the story. Depending on which ones are made, you'll either obtain one of three endings: neutral, Vincent's, or Vernon's. There are some CGs shown as well as a few tracks although no voice acting. Also, Steam achievements are present although they won't count towards a user's global total until the game is out of "Steam is learning about this game".Now that I've gone over the story and gameplay, I'll move onto my thoughts. Hard Times is a hardcore homeless simulation/survival game where your goal is to stay alive for as long as you can. The game is set in a city where homelessness is not exactly a crime but everything else you do, including begging, scavenging, using the local fountain to bathe, or even plucking wild blueberries are, and so be careful of the cops or any nosy "upstanding" citizens who will call the cops on you! Scavenging is only part of the battle though! In this game, there's also a crafting system which I find a bit underwhelming since many of the "craftables" can be found in trash cans if you look hard enough. In fact, I'd say for some items at least, you'd have a higher chance of finding that craftable item outright rather having to find all the materials needed and then assembling them together.As a survival game, Hard Times will also force you to keep an eye on the many meters and indicators at the bottom of the screen like health, hunger, stamina, hygiene (the loo and the shower), and also body temperature. By making sure your indicators are all in the green, you should be able to have the time to explore every inch of the city, and even break into some previously-locked places. What's more, it also includes some light customization options that let you tweak the scenes to your liking, such as adding or removing clothes and accessories, activating a cross-section view, and increasing the speed of the MC's thrusts. game_name: A Last will and Testament: Adventure
review: I honestly thought this was a very well done game for one that is listed at just $1. While the momentum of the movement was a bit off putting, it didn't detract due to the nature of the game. The lighting scheme felt a bit smudgy to me at first, but after 15 minutes in I really lost focus of it and was just moving on the puzzles without thinking about it anymore. I had one issue where an item I picked up stayed in front of me despite being out of the examine screen and the item being on the table as well, a escape->save->load cleared the issue.The puzzles weren't extremely challenging but did take some thought. I didn't need to look up a guide or solution, but a few due to little instruction required some process of elimination for me to figure out what exactly needed to be done. But I got through it in a bit over 2 hours and felt proud of myself for figuring them out, and praised the game for being challenging but not hair-pulling difficult with it's puzzles.

game_name: A Last will and Testament: Adventure
review: I really wish Steam had a neutral option. The price is very low, and as I received the game for free I cannot complain there.However, there are multiple issues. The movement and controls are slow and sort of janky at times. The camera vibrated almost the entire time I played and the movement was sluggish when walking and slippery when running. The puzzles are okay, but nothing I haven't seen done better in other games, honestly.Perhaps my biggest gripe with the game is the achievements. 100 of them and the majority of them are just finding the same 4 or so objects over and over but in different colors. Other achievements are just handed to you for doing nothing. You get an achievement for clicking "New Game" even! It's just bloat to make the game feel like it has more to it. I started going back to just top off the few achievements I missed but grew bored and then annoyed at a particular achievement. Which has no indication of how to do it within the game and requires a guide made by the Dev.All that being said, for a dollar it's okay, but even then I'd say get it on a sale. The game has potential to be something more, but it feels like it may just been a quick and easy asset flip.Overall 2/5In other words, just below an average score for me. Not the worst, not the best. If the few issues it has are resolved it would be pretty decent.

Language Lab is a language learning video game using virtual reality technology. Developed by Language Lab VR and released in 2022, Language Lab strives to offer an engaging and interactive language learning experience. While it showcases commendable efforts, it also faces some challenges.One of the main strengths of Language Lab lies in its ability to create a simulated language environment, enabling students to practice their language skills in a controlled and interactive setting. Unlike English Teaching Assistant VR, Language Lab presents various language exercises, and vocabulary drills. This approach can be an effective way for learners to build confidence and improve fluency.Furthermore, Language Lab shows great potential in bridging the educational gap for students with limited access to traditional language learning resources or teachers. Its ability to reach remote and underprivileged communities can significantly contribute to expanding language education opportunities.However, similar to English Teaching Assistant VR, Language Lab faces some limitations. One crucial aspect where it might fall short is in providing personalized feedback and individual attention, which human teachers excel at. Language learning involves understanding cultural nuances and developing effective communication skills that might be challenging for a VR system to fully replicate.Moreover, technical barriers and the need for specific hardware and software could hinder the widespread adoption of Language VR. High costs and limited access to VR technology might restrict its usage, particularly in less affluent areas.Additionally, while Language VR aims to simulate real-life scenarios, it may not capture the complexities of human interaction entirely. Subtle non-verbal communication and the ability to adapt teaching methods to individual students' needs might prove challenging for a VR system to reproduce convincingly.Language Lab should have an extensive array of resources, including virtual textbooks, grammar lessons, and pronunciation guides. These resources are valuable assets for independent learning and can provide essential support

There is a lot of crafting of items (shelter, metalwork, food, pottery) to be done, and all of it takes quite a lot of effort, which will seem like a real grind to some, but to others (like me) it's highly addictive and realistic. There are animals to catch and fight off, and a large map to explore.The graphics are good, very similar to Medieval Dynasty in appearance, and the top-down perspective works very well for me. There's a third-person option but personally I don't want to look at the back of someone's head all the time, so I haven't tried it.It's EA but everything works very well - it's an extremely well-crafted game. The only real downside is that, for the moment, you're only getting half the game as the quest finishes halfway through, so you can't eradicate the horrible blight yet, and it keeps on spreading. The price is currently very cheap for what you get, so I'd definitely recommend giving the demo a try.

The game has a definite indie feel to it. If you've played any visual novels before this probably feels similar.There are a few unique additions this game brings to the genre though. I haven't seen that from this genre before, it's usually 2 completely independent animations playing, but this game does a great job combining them in a way I haven't seen before.The game also brings in a new element with the stealth feature, hiding and being unseen. Very interesting system and unique for the genre.For obvious flaws, the language is a bit broken English. Still understandable but needs refining. The lighting system for sunbeams is broken and overall the ceiling and other features are sort of hazy.If you can look past the rough around the edges portions, the mechanics of the game are quite advanced for the genre. Alright, folks, I need to spill the beans on this gem of a horror game called Happy’s Humble Burger Farm. We're in a golden era of horror games, and this one takes some interesting risks that pay off in surprising ways.First things first, the premise is killer—fast-food meets horror. I mean, how can you not be intrigued by that? You're stuck in some bizarre simulation, serving burgers and dealing with twisted creatures roaming around. The game satirizes corporate dominance and throws in some seriously messed-up elements that are both hilarious and creepy.But here's the kicker—the horror in Happy's Humble Burger Farm is more on the humorous side. The world it presents is preposterous, and you can see right through the simulation's facade. The Mickey Mouse-style cartoon characters, like Happy the Humble Heifer, are both mascots and a part of the nightmarish mystery. And let me tell you, the backstory found in the radio shows, TV shows, and flyers scattered around the city adds depth to the whole experience.Now, here's something I didn't expect—the horror aspect is mixed with the fast-food job mechanics. Yep, you heard it right. While serving customers, you have to cook patties, build sandwiches, all while the world tries to kill you. Cooking under duress is honestly a genius twist, and it works like a charm.Though the fast-food element could have been utilized more, Happy's Humble Burger Farm keeps surprising you with twists and turns. The game isn't too long, clocking in at around four to six hours, but it's a rollercoaster ride that never becomes dull.My only gripe is that the game lacks a bit of challenge. Making money and surviving quite easy but the low difficulty curve does allow for a smooth experience.In the end, Happy's Humble Burger Farm is a delightful, dreamlike horror experience.

Watch my play through here: Not to be confused with the Neil Marshall British horror about 6 woman spelunkers who find terrifying creatures down in the Appalachian mountains, The Descent is a first person psychological horror where you take on the role of a hardened journalist who wants to discover the truth behind disappearances at the Rockwell Coal Mine - encountering strange phenomenon along the way. Separated into 3 main chapters, players will initially traverse their way through the coal mine factory, starting to discover notes from some of the missing coal miners, then descend to the lower levels of the coal mine.First and foremost, this is a walking sim with 'collect object A to make object B work' mechanics - there are quite a few jump scares throughout the course of the game, a couple of which did have an impact, but others could be telegraphed if you've played these types of games before. The sound design needs to be noted and applauded - from the howling wind and creaking floorboards in the first chapter to the ominous 'clicking' of a Geiger counter letting you know that one of the ethereal ghost miners is nearby, the sound keeps you on edge from the beginning. Especially the section where you find yourself in a small maintenance hatch on the first floor of the mine!The lore surrounding the world of The Descent is decently handled - you'll find notes from some of the miners that previously worked at the coal mine, but the main focus is related to a father and daughter story. As you descend deeper you'll find out what happened to these two characters, but ultimately felt their fate remained a mystery. Pros: - Lighting, atmosphere and sound design seemed a bar above the usual indie games of this

Thanks Celeritas Games for giving me this game for a review for my curator: However, I don't recommend it. Let me explain why by evaluating each aspect of the game:Atmosphere (5/10). This is a typical jumpscare horror game. I prefer this genre over survival games, but the scares were not effective. I missed half of them because they occurred outside my field of view. The other half were triggered by cutscenes that forced my character to turn around. There was not enough tension and creepiness throughout the game.Narrative (4/10). The story was unrealistic and bizarre from the start. The developers could have made it more interesting, but they chose to go with a vague and mysterious approach that only made it worse.Gameplay (5/10). This is a simple walking simulator where you collect keys and notes. The enemies do not harm you, so you cannot die. There is no save system, so you have to complete the game in one sitting, or you can select levels from the menu. I did not see the point of having night vision goggles, since I could finish the game with just a flashlight. The game design was not very impressive. It was often unclear what I had to do or where I had to go.Graphics (7/10). The assets and lighting looked nice, but there was not enough visual variety and texture quality. Most of the models were decent, but some of them looked very cheap.Sound (7/10). Celeritas Games did a good job of choosing and placing sounds in the game. However, it felt like I was listening to scripted events rather than natural sounds.Originality (6/10). I do not recall many games set in a mining environment, so it could have been a unique setting to explore. But the developers did not use this feature

Pulseball is an Early Access (development hell) PvP only sports FPS which blends FPS PvP arena gameplay with a ball and goal scoring system. The game failed, reaching a tiny peak of just 12 concurrent players, and is now generally unplayable with only 2 players or less logging on every day, not even enough to make a match. While the game is still being updated, it's gone past the developers commitment date to complete the game and laucnh it, and there's no clear sign that it will reach a full release. The game is therefore classified as being in development hell. On a technical basis the game has deep flaws in the engine. One example is that it's impossible to make the game run in 4K as the developer incomprehensibly locks out the ability to change resolution in full screen, and doesn't set the game to the monitor native resolution. I suppose that's something that would happen when developers lack familiarity with the PC as a gaming platform, but it's an inexcusable defect in the product.With no players, it's important to understand why this game failed. The developers made the terrible mistake of launching a multiplayer only game in Early Access. This is almost certain to kill the game. Most gamers will evaluate a game only once. If they do so when the game is incomplete, they will check it out, then abandon it. When (IF) the game eventually does get around to release, there will be no players, because the developers burned the first impressions through their faulty Early Access experience. Players who saw the game and didn't like it because it was incomplete . Multiplayer games must have a large population if they are to go "viral" and succeed, especially without single player content to fall back on.

review: First game on steam that I got 100%. From the beginning, I knew this game was going to be great. It really expresses the way deer are and how they work. But I can say this will show you the general idea on how deer are in daily and old fashioned life. Today, we take for granted what we have now that we don't ever realize how hard it use to be, us deer of course. I am very grateful to this game because it shows what we have to go through and the struggles in our everyday life. Deer are a proud and noble race and we fight for our families and friends until we die. I have realized I have been losing my way a little bit until I played this game cause it reminded me of who I am, who we are. I can honestly say, if you are looking for a fantastic representation of a daily life of a deer, then this is the game for you. Thank you, and stay well my deer brother and sisters and they/them. Honestly, I started the game with very low expectations, knowing it was developed by four people part-time just for fun. But once I entered the game, I could feel and see how efficiently and thoughtfully they utilized their limited time. The simulation aspect is neither so detailed that it overwhelms you with mechanics nor too simple to be called "arcade." This balance ensures that the act of making toast doesn’t overshadow the atmosphere of the mystical environment but also doesn’t get lost beneath it—much like how our emotions align with the flow of life in real life. The interactions in the game aren't as incredibly intuitive as in a mobile game, but it's clear that this design choice was made to nurture the desire to explore and learn within its intriguing world. As I mentioned, the developers’ minds and dreams come together here in a balanced, effective way. I had the best toast I could get for this price and I recommend it to everyone.

Is this City Skylines? No, it's simpler. Sim City? Nope, it's still simpler. Townscaper? Okay, maybe a little bit more complex than that, but not by too much. Is it still fun? Oh gods yes. If you've ever wanted a city planning game you can just zen out while doing, this is it. The tutorial is about 15 minutes, and the next 3-18 hours are just pure city building flow. The graphics are fun, but still simple enough to distinguish most kinds of buildings. Plus the overlays are comprehensive, making figuring out your next step super simple. The controls are a bit simplistic, and I have yet to find a stop-time button (this may be a me problem), but the game is forgiving enough for that not to be too much of an issue, without being so easy or simple as to feel like a formulaic point-and-click. Additionally, every feature in the game is implemented well. Disasters in the game only happen after the end of the tutorial, and you get a quick pop-up explaining them and how to recover, for those new to the genre. Traffic congestion affects happiness, but not so much that you usually have to worry about it unless you're trying to make the perfect city. Every potentially useful stat, such as traffic congestion and happiness, is on some tab of your city stats page too, in a super easy to follow way. Plus there's a racing mini-game, and who doesn't love one of those?So yeah, if you've been looking for a fun planning game to spend your time on, you've come to the right place. And for basically 4 USD, it's a fairly cheap way to spend hours making a little world exactly as perfect as you're willing to put the hours into.

The game play loop of Drift is to adventure out from your destroyed ship to collect resources from the asteroid belt that you spawn near and to rebuild your ship. You'll also need to manage your oxygen and nutrition to stay alive. As you gather resources you'll be able to unlock several work stations that will allow you to progress through the game.The pacing of the game feels pretty good and once you understand where to get the specific resources you need you'll quickly be able to ramp up progress. At the time of this review I have spent 5 hours in game and without spoiling any of the content I've unlocked all but two "things."During my 5 hours I did experience a game breaking bug where I got stuck on terrain and couldn't get free but for the launch the devs have added an unstuck button as a temporary fix for this. When I loaded my save where I was stuck my character was free and able to return to my ship so it appears to be fixed.Overall the foundation is there for a decent game but whether you want to buy it now really depends on two factors. First are you okay with early access? Second are you okay with the current price knowing you'll likely see all the game has to offer in about 5-6 hours? I'm going to give the game a recommend based on what I've seen but if you answered no to one or both of these question I'd recommend wishlisting the game and waiting for a few updates to see how the game progresses.

This is a wonderful VR mech simulator that also can be played without VR. I have only played it in VR, so I can't comment on the non-VR gameplay. You really feel fully immersed and in control of a metal behemoth. You can play in 3 very different game modes and change the parameters for the game in many ways. For instance, you can have up to 4 teams, or no teams (pure deathmatch). The largest game I've played in is 16 and that was bordering on cramped. The AI isn't great but it is functional and you often can't tell the difference between a human player and an AI mech. You can set the max players and start in and play AI until people join, or join a dedicated server (I don't know if they are dedicated through the publisher/developer or if they are independantly owned but lag has never been an issue for me). Mech customization isn't really deep but you can change out the weapons in pre-determined large or small slots. There are 5 mechs that are very different and you can switch when you die. Oh yeah, you do get to respawn after a short delay (15-20 seconds or so). Matches usually run 15 minutes but you can modify that to be shorter or longer and you can also make it so that instead of time, it's based off of who gets to a certain score first.The price is just right in my oppinion. My only complaint at the moment is that there is no story mode. If they added a campaign they could probably charge more, but I've had plenty of fun as is with this game.

Pinball FX is a great game that builds on previous iterations. Some of the biggest improvements you will notice are in the physics department and with the graphics and lighting. I am a seasoned digital pinball player and can tell you this is by far the closestthis game has come to having realistic physics. For me, the physics are what really soldme on this title and I have played it since its first release on the Epic Games Store.When you play digital pinball games, realistic physics can go a long way because it challenges you to make good shots and rewards you when you do but also punishesyou when you don't. In FX3, for example, the physics felt like the ball had a predetermined path(especially on the Zen tables) which is why I played the Williams titles for the majority of my playtime.That is not the case with Pinball FX and because of the physics overhaul, I am finding myself enjoyingtitles from FX3 that I didn't have much interest in before. The second biggest improvement is the lighting and animations that you will notice while you are playing.The Williams tables received a glow update that improved lighting specifically around the flashers which wasvery noticeable.If you are coming from FX3, the physics will feel a lot different at first and it will take getting used to becauseit's a different engine but you will notice how much more "realistic" they feel the more you play.Lastly, the amount of tables Pinball FX offers is actually quite insane. There is something for everyone. For oldtimers like myself, I enjoy playing the Williams recreations the most but because of the renewed physics,I am also enjoying original titles like Crypt of the Necrodancer a lot.

Hopefully we'll be seeing some of the other Bally and Williams classics like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Doctor Who, Black Knight, Centaur, Banzai Run, and PinBot soon.One of big under the hood changes is the move to Unreal as the game engine, replacing their in-house engine. There's some small lighting improvements, but it's similar. 30 days to survive is a zombie survival, side scrolling platformer. It's the first of its kind that I've seen personally. At the very least the devs should be commended for attempting it. The physics are a little wonky, but it fits well with its blocky, Lego-man-esque art style.The controls and game mechanics take some getting used to. Right out of the gate can be pretty unforgiving. With its quick hunger and energy depletion, coupled with zombies that get little to no knockback from attacks. The items are RNG heavy, so you can get very unlucky with starving to death or losing the ability to run and jump. Progression hinges upon using the save function at your house to build up an arsenal of gear to survive with. It can be easily exploited by save scumming, but to some degree you kind of have to in order to live beyond 5 stages away from home. There is a sewer system that you can discover that acts as a sort of checkpoint system. There is a taxi that can appear randomly which you use to fast travel home. For the most part though, the further away from home you go, the further you have to walk back. Items respawn after moving two stages beyond, so you have a chance to find enough food and energy to make the journey back. Enemies respawn as well though, so it isn't an easy decision to risk the journey.The music and sound are pretty good, albeit repetitive, but there is an option to adjust the volume on both.The story is very minimal, but you really don't need one for this type of game.All in all, If you can look past the shortcomings, and are patient enough to learn the game. I think you will enjoy

Hey everyone! Here is my script for my video review. Feel free to keep reading below, or check out my video!Yupitergrad reminds me a lot of Borderlands. The artstyle and the voice acting have direct inspirations from Borderlands, and this is a good thing. Outside of this, Yupitergrad couldn’t be any more unique. Let me try to explain what you actually do in this game…Yupitergrad is a first-person parkour puzzle platformer which has you shooting suction cups so you can swing around like spider-man, or use thrusters to navigate around obstacles. You’re in space, navigating space stations and trying to complete tasks while completing movement puzzles and doing your best to stay alive.On the Index controllers you use the triggers to shoot your suction cups, and squeeze the controller to use your thrusters with each hand. The thumbsticks can rotate you left and right, and reel in your suction cup to pull you forward.You simply shoot suction cups which can only stick to blue surfaces... This reminds me of Portal, which had surfaces where portals could not be created on, and this makes navigating more of a challenge as you quickly think about your next move.Shooting and swinging around felt great once you adjusted to the controls, and the thrusters were fun to make those fine adjustments to get around the next obstacle.The campaign is only around 2 hours long, but there's a time attack mode which you can do to keep things interesting, and this is where the meat of the game is which will keep you busy once you finish the campaign. game_name: Don't Give Up: Not Ready to Die
review: This game is very delightful on the first play through and I hope to change my mind in later releases. The game starts with an interesting narrative involving a girl having a car accident and her soul being released from her body. After a short dialogue with "death" we quickly find ourselves in a forest staring over our characters body and wondering what to do. There were no prompts, hints or any directions given to the player and considering the ridiculously small time frame you have to actually leave the locale of the body before being killed, there is little chance for the player to actually understand what is required without multiple failures and a sprinkle of luck that the items you need are actually nearby. A phone indicates a timer of one hour? Are we expected to sit protecting the girl for this long in one sitting? Perhaps I was confused or missed something.I managed to build all of the items in one attempt to then find myself just sat on the body doing nothing for around 5 minutes. Eventually the things you build collapse and you need to craft them again and so the loop continues endlessly without any indication of progression or if there is any more to the game than this small scene. After an hour of waiting around and eventually being killed by death enough times, I got bored and decided I had enough of not feeling like the game was actually going anywhere.I won't be recomending this game on this occasion.---------------------------------------------------------if I have missed something or perhaps missed something crucial, please leave a comment below and let me know. game_name: Don't Give Up: Not Ready to Die
review: Man, how difficult is to beat this game! I'm amazingly surprised on how this game delivers what I like in survival games, while being an easy experience by a really low price. It's simple, it's fun, with a lot of hidden secrets and an amazing story. It's the perfect entry game for those seeking to adventure themselves in the survival genre, or for those without time to dedicate to the other bigger games of the genre. But besides the fun gameplay, what is amazing about this game is the cute pixel art and the amazing story! It's impossible not being completely involved in the plot. The Death is a lovely character, and I do recommend you to seek for the hidden items and ghosts on the woods, because they deepen the plot even more.

This is a small interactive novel where you choose a clothing set for your character, and it triggers a reminiscence of a painful memory. The story is centered on a love story between two girls, your character and her best friend at a new school.You can choose between two prompts to answer at times, but it makes no difference in the outcome. There are no real choices, and the story is straightforward.The story runs on an awkward note, with your character never truly acknowledging/stating her love for her friend, so the progression left me confused as to whether the love was ever voiced/acted upon. For me it wasn't clear by the end of the story.The story gets increasingly sad, and there is no happy resolution. It felt lacking, with the interactions between the characters meaningless and empty. It has a great theme as a base for creating impacting emotions, but it falls short with the lack of story structure and development.The art is really cute, very pleasant. Unfortunately, there is no UI nor options; this becomes a problem with the very slow text, and the looping background music that quickly becomes tiring.Still, this is a decent free game, which takes you half an hour to complete, so you can always give it a try.

IMPORTANT UPDATE: A patch recently released that reportedly removes the needless racial slurs. I appreciate that the team took responsibility and issued a public apology to go along with the update. I say "reportedly" because I actually refunded the game (though I do plan to purchase it again once it goes on a decent sale), but I assume the update does what it says it does. So, my prior complaint about poorly handled racial prejudice is now invalid.The review will be kept in its original form below.A pretty good Papers Please-esque game with some glaring faults. The gameplay itself is interesting, and the story mode continues to add new wrinkles that increase the difficulty in fun and creative ways. It doesn't outstay its welcome either, only lasting for just as long as it needs to.The story covers some...shall we say, "interesting" topics. I can tell the developers were trying to present an unflinching portrayal of WW2 Germany, but there are moments when it just goes too far and feels more sensationalist than anything. For example, the main character is canonically racist, and there's very frank discussion of sexual assault as well. These don't add anything of value to the story, and end up detracting from it overall. This especially hurts when other aspects of the story feel nuanced and complicated.The translation is pretty bad, but not indecipherable. And it never made the core gameplay feel confusing, which helps make it feel like less of a problem.My recommendation is to skip the cutscenes, where the bulk of the translation errors and mishandled controversial content sits. The gameplay itself is fun and challenging, and I'd say it, along with the solid pixel art, makes it worth playing.Only on a good sale, though. $12 is a whole lot for a game this short.

Good Bones is the first game released by Indie Game Dev RETCON Games.An original story driven point-and-click mystery set in a spooky house in a small town.The game features an inclusive narrative with intention to give a voice to the gamers that are often overlooked by mainstream gaming.The story is tight without a lot of fluff and bloat. It gets you where you need to be without unneeded detours.There are choices to be made and, judging by the tag "Choices Matter" and the fact that I am missing a few achievements, there is opportunity to replay and experience a different outcome.From a technical perspective the game is as one would expect from this genre of game. Almost everything is clickable to get some flavor and most things can be interacted with multiple times at various stages of the game for more flavor as the plot unravels.A few technical upgrades I would like to see from future games would be to have some animation to the world. Things like trees rustling in the wind, clouds floating by, and interactable objects animate when interacting. I think it would help make the game feel more alive.I would also like to see (or hear) material based sound effects applied to the environment. That is, when you click on paper you hear paper, when you click water you hear splashes, soft stuff sounds soft, and hard stuff sounds hard. I think that would help immerse the senses.If you are a fan of the genre, want a tightly packaged story without endless drivel, and are a supporter of Indie Devs and of the underrepresented gamer groups, pick up Good Bones.

Good Bones is the first outing by studio Retcon Games. It swaddles you with vibrant visuals, chill lofi beats, and quirky characters. As you settle in for an evening of cozy exploring the experience begins to unfold. The taught relationship between a Mother and a Daughter. A mysterious house where the clues begin to suggest murder myserious! Buried guilt and trauma? It's got visitors, not all of them welcome. It's got basements, spiders, and ropes. Secret combinations, sneaky hiding spots, and mysterious doodles. Point yourself in the right direction and click your way through 2 ( at least) endings, countless doodads with text that shifts as you progress, and a story with stakes that rise to a fever pitch as the barrier between the realm of the living and dead begins to weaken. A big shoutout to the developer, I never thought I'd see the end of a Point-and-click title. I did NOT get frustrated by opaque sequences and puzzles. I did NOT begin to fall asleep because of lack of progression. I did NOT get frustrated and uninstall. The pace is good, the difficulty is liesurely, and your time as a player is respected like it should be. This title might be my gateway to exploring the genre further, something I did not think possible before I played Good Bones. Additional kudos to a first time developer releasing a finished title that doesn't crash, doesn't have crazy performance issues, and the bugs are so minor you'd miss them if you weren't looking. This is a rare thing in 2023. Finally, this title has my CRT gaming endorsement. Fire your favorite monitor up and run it as low as 800x600 to feast your eyes on that 90s PC look. The game's artwork and scanlines are a match made in heaven.Rob

This action/crafting game gives you a real purpose to your activities – you need to build up your defenses (fences, automatic turrets, food to heal you) during the peaceful daytime so that you can survive the alien attacks at night time. You can also swing your ax during the nighttime to try and protect your farm, but the aliens are pretty tough, so it's much more survivable if you have good defenses. Note that there's almost no hand-holding so expect to die a lot at first while you figure out what you can do, and what actually helps you survive the onslot at night. A nice change of course from the games that constantly tell you want to do every 10 seconds! There also seems to be a fairly large map to explore, 1 hour in I've only seen a small part of it, and there's definitely loot hidden out there. The game kind of reminds me of a simpler, single player Ark Survival Evolved, but with considerably more utility to crafting structures than in ark, and no boring downtime at night. I do wish the controller support was a bit more robust though. The game is definitely playable without mouse and keyboard, but I did have to do some button remapping (and use steam input to invert Y) before all features were accessible.

Serious Fun Football is a 3D football game designed to encapsulate the feeling of playing with your friends on a small pitch. Playing as one of a team of three in solo mode, or controlling all three players in team mode, Serious Fun Football gives you the option to play online or offline in career mode or in friendly matches.Does Serious Fun Football live up to its name?The question I posed in the introduction was does Serious Fun Football live up to its name? I would say it’s almost there. I think with a flourishing online presence and the introduction of more options like a league table, replays, fouls, free kicks, swerving, and general improvements in movement, it could well be seriously fun.The first thing I would do to improve this game is have a proper league table with different teams. Currently, there are just Team North and Team South and each match earns you points. There are six leagues, and a certain points target must be reached to get promotion, or if you fail to achieve enough points, you run the risk of demotion. Half the fun of football is analyzing the league table and watching your team climb and fall in position, pushing for promotion, or perhaps scraping into a playoff spot on the last day of the season. The current system is okay, but I think this would make things more exciting.You play twenty matches a season, so I’d rather see a league table with ten different teams which you play home and away. It would be interesting to have a rough rating for each team, so you know when you are up for a difficult match. There did seem to be some obvious differences in AI team skill within each division. The current version did not recognize my controller, and the only way to use it was bind it to the keyboard keys to it. Not ideal since you end up with only 8 directions. The camera angle resets to default every time there is a break in the game, but the default becomes whatever it was set to before the last game ended.Player switching is either weird or non existent. It's hard to stay in control once the player switches from AI controlled, to player controlled. I will admit that most games of this kind suffer of this, so this might be just the matter of getting used to it.The ugly:AI. It needs work. A lot of work. Biggest issue is the positioning of the entire squad. During action, if you keep possession long enough all of the teammates will go DEEP into the opposing territory without much regard for their actual positions. If you then turn the ball over, the opposing team has a clear path from midfield to your goal while 6-7 of your players are in the opposing box. Throw ins are especially bad. The teams will routinely populate opposing halves with the entire crew. If you get awarded a throw in in front of your corner flag, you will have nobody to pass it to since your entire team is 60 m away

There's no way for gamers to ensure this is running at the native resolution of their displays... there's no guarantee this game will look right on any PC as a result of this hamfisted design decision. There's no way for gamers to try improve the low quality graphics. The game features lazy low-polygon "retro" assets, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the mid 2000s (the footballers don't even have faces! Creepy!). It's unclear why the developers weren't able to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets for the game, and also irrelevant... what matters is that this looks bad as a result of their decisions, a compromise PC gamers shouldn't have to put up with.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers.Because this is a mobile app, it carries a number of deliberate design deficiencies. Compromises were made to cater to the iPhones that the game was designed for. These are unfortunate handicaps and limitations that PC gamers shouldn't be forced to accept, but it's evident that PC was an afterthought for the iPhone developers who are to blame for this. The complaints mentioned in others' reviews about performance are definitely valid, but they are part and parcel with what makes this experience so great, which is the overwhelming level of beautiful detail that makes up the virtual world in Gnomes & Goblins. The other thing that sets Gnomes & Goblins apart is that it isn't quite a game with an explicitly stated goal or point system, nor is it a traditional narrative one passively watches unfold, but rather a combination of the two--this might understandably create frustration for players who want Gnomes & Goblins to firmly stake a claim in one genre or another, but in my opinion being in this fuzzy (maybe even awkward) middle ground is exactly what makes VR as a medium so exciting. And there are very few other experiences trying to strike this balance with such ambition. So, if you have a high-end PC definitely buy the game. And if you don't, buy it anyway as there are performance updates already rolling out. All that said, the highlight of this "game" for me is in simply being able to aimlessly roam and explore the world (floating down a river at twilight most especially), which took me back to how I felt trying to figure out old Nintendo games like Legend of Zelda or even theme park rides like Pirates of the Caribbean at Disneyland. Buy it, and keep coming back to see what else gets added, and I'm sure you'll at least eventually appreciate it if you don't already.

He has been actively involved in the community on his Discord and welcomes feedback and suggestions. As it stands now, there is one very large map and many exercises within this map to go through. The game as it is now merits the cost in my opinion for those who just want to practice although variety of scenery is not that diverse, from a practical exercise perspective it's all there with more than enough variety of challenge to practice pretty much indefinitely without being able to memorize the landscape.Some good stuff here from newbie to expert. -For newbies there will be some required learning of concepts by a combination of watching YouTube videos (the author of this game has a "LandNav game" channel that he continues to add example runs to that you can watch to give you an idea how to apply these concepts to your own sessions. It's one thing learning the concept though and then an entirely different thing applying them in your own session and will take a lot of practice to start to get the hang of.I came in with basic knowledge map orienteering, taking/following a bearing, and some basic map reading skills. I've learned several concepts and continue to improve my terrain association reading skills through this game.

This game is a fantastic land navigation simulator. It’s also the only real one out there. I wish I had a training tool like this when I was in the Army.
