Right now it only has one map available, but it’s large, detailed, and challenging to navigate through. The few bugs that I’ve encountered have been very minor, nothing game breaking. More maps, polish, and controller support are on the way as well. The current price is an absolute steal, because LANDNAV provides a virtual training environment to help build a valuable real life skill.

There's a lot of videos on youtube that do an excellent job at giving you a basic idea on how to conduct land nav. With that knowledge, it's easy to apply it in this simulator. But even without that, the game itself has a lot of information to help you.The controls are relatively simple and quick to learn. FYI, if you want to reset your pace count, press the comma key.I can't attest to the accuracy of this simulator to real life because I haven't done land nav IRL yet, but I feel like I'm learning something. Other tools are the protractor and the ranger beads for measuring the distance traveled. The topographic map is very well done, too.The actual travel, walking or running, reminds me very much of a real forest/mountain environment, the feel of being in a forest is very immersive, even haunting at times. It is easy to get lost in the thickets and ravines, pace count is lost and the compass bearing is all over the place - just like in real life, it is often better to go around such places and accept a detour through less overgrown terrain. Such decisions just add to the overall positive impression this game/sim has on me. I have not tried the night-orienteering option, but what I saw looks very promising, flashlight and the glowing stripes of the markers one has to find. I would give 5/5 points even though it is only an early version of the sim and the dev is working on the next version with much more features. I am looking forward to playing that one as well!

Overall, a good experience for me. At first, I did experience input lag and "sloppy" flippers like some negative reviews have mentioned. Here's what got rid of it for me :-Go into your video settings-Without touching resolution just yet, activate VSYNC.-Go into the ADVANCED tab and set options to this :Rendered upscale : leave it at 100%Antialiasing Method : Temporal AA (turn this option off or to FXAA if there's a drop in framerate)Nvidia Reflex : DisableUpscaler Method : Intel XESSUpscaler Mode : Performanceframerate limit : 60 (or you can try the maximum refresh rate of your monitor, like 144 if it's a 144Hz)Shadow Quality : Low (first setting I lower when having performance issues)Post-Process Quality : HighMotion Blur Amount : OFFChromatic Aberration : 0.5I am running this game on a 7th gen i5 processor and a GTX 1070 as my GPU. The game runs silky smooth in 1920x1080 (still looks pretty good too) and input lag is pretty much non-existent now.

The lawnmower, a sleek green machine, was minding its own business, trimming the grass on a quiet suburban lawn, when it suddenly came across an unexpected obstacle.At first, the lawnmower wasn't sure what to make of the strange figure in front of it. The man, dressed in a sharp suit and sporting his trademark blond hair, was staring intently at his phone and seemed to be oblivious to the lawnmower's presence. But as the lawnmower drew closer, it became clear that this was no ordinary person.As the man looked up, the lawnmower recognized him immediately: it was Donald Trump. The lawnmower had heard of him, of course - his name had been on the news and social media for years - but it had never expected to encounter him in person, let alone while going about its daily business.For a moment, the lawnmower and Trump stared at each other in silence. The lawnmower felt a sense of confusion and disbelief - what was the former President doing here, of all places? And why was he just standing there, staring at his phone?Finally, Trump spoke. "Hey there, little guy," he said, his voice oddly friendly. "What are you doing here?"The lawnmower didn't know how to respond. It beeped hesitantly, unsure of what Trump wanted.Trump chuckled. "I guess you're not much of a talker, are you?" he said. "That's okay. I'm used to dealing with people who don't say what they mean."The lawnmower still didn't understand what was happening. Yellowcake is a term used to describe a type of uranium concentrate powder that is derived from uranium ore. It typically has a yellowish color, which gives it its name. Yellowcake is a precursor in the production of nuclear fuel and is not a weapon itself. The process of converting yellowcake into enriched uranium is a key step in the nuclear fuel cycle.Here's an overview of the yellowcake production process:1. **Mining:** The first step involves the extraction of uranium ore from the Earth's crust. Uranium is often found in association with other minerals, and the ore must be processed to extract the uranium content.2. **Milling:** The mined ore undergoes milling to extract the uranium. This involves crushing the ore into a fine powder and then leaching it with a chemical solution to separate the uranium from other minerals.3. **Conversion:** The resulting uranium solution, often in the form of uranium hexafluoride (UF6), is then converted into a more stable and transportable form, which is yellowcake. This conversion is typically achieved through a series of chemical processes.4. **Drying:** The yellowcake is dried to remove excess moisture, resulting in a powdered form.It's important to note that yellowcake itself is not suitable for use in nuclear reactors or weapons. Further processing is required to transform it into enriched uranium. Targeted -10 Days is a high-quality Exit 8 Like that stands above the majority of games in this genre. This game has a focused vision and a balanced scope; you could say the devs had a clear 'target' on exactly what they wanted to make here, and delivered on it.There is only one environment of a reasonable size, but the level of polish on display in this environment is exceptionally well-done. Ambiance, lighting, and environmental details are all balanced to serve as good world-building while also being conducive to good gameplay.Rather-notable too is the game's plot; something that is rare in most of this genre, and when it does exist, it's predictable and common tropes at best. Here, you are playing as an ex-Mafia member going to trial against your old boss, and your objective is to observe the parking garage your car is stored in every day until the trial finishes, as your old boss is seeking to 'rub you out' and prevent your testimony. This creates a great motivation for you, the player, to observe your environment, as well as a very logical reason why that environment is changing and needs to be observed.There's over 100 anomalies and three difficulties so far. These anomalies may be odd, but are grounded in reality, matching the theme of 'things indicating your life is in danger that day', though some of these anomalies are more subtle than others. As well, the devs will be adding a special 'anomaly' mode later as a free update from what I understand, adding even more anomalies that will be of a more outlandish and fantastical sort, for those who like the weirder events that can happen in other Exit 8 Likes.I do have some nitpicks, though as this genre is heavily-reliant on RNG, your mileage

Alright, so this is just one more of those casual games where you can get to play without having to worry about situations that could be considered borderline stressful.That said, there's not really a story to follow, as you just control this guy flowing over his sword as if he was Silver Surfer, and your goal is to collect as many stones as you can in order to reach the highest score; and that's pretty much it.The graphics aren't bad, the sound effects and music are ok, I suppose. The gameplay can be a bit confusing at the start, but I'm sure that it won't take long for you to figure out how to maneuver the guy around the screen.As mentioned previously, your goal is to collect stones; there're the white ones and the red ones, which offer more points, but are more rare and are usually located in dangerous places.Furthermore, if you're looking for an excuse to actually try getting a good score, there're at least 6 different achievements to get, and guess what: I've got them all in less than 10 minutes of gameplay. So, if you're a completionist kind of gamer, this could be an interesting choice to add to your library.Anyhow, not everything is perfect, since there's also a 10 minutes time-limit for each run that you take and that could be a bit annoying while you're chasing after these, but it's not really much of a big deal, in the end.Overall, the price is often affordable, the game is kinda fun and you can get easy achievements, so why not give it try?

A Wholesome Throwback to 2016-2017There’s something undeniably comforting about a game that doesn’t try to be more than what it is—just pure, simple fun. That’s exactly what this spinner game delivers. It’s a delightful nod to the fidget spinner craze of 2016-2017, and it instantly brought me back to those days when life felt a bit more carefree.The concept is straightforward: you click, and the spinner spins. That’s it. But that simplicity is what makes it so charming. It doesn’t need a complex story or fancy graphics to be enjoyable. It’s a game that’s easy to pick up, play for a few minutes (or hours, if you get hooked), and then go about your day with a smile on your face.What I love most is how it captures the essence of that era. It’s like a tiny time capsule, reminding me of the days when everyone had a fidget spinner in their pocket, and we all just wanted something to fidget with. The satisfaction of watching the spinner whirl around is oddly soothing, and it’s a perfect little escape from the busyness of life.This game is wholesome in its simplicity. It doesn’t demand anything from you—no strategies to master, no levels to conquer. It’s just about enjoying the moment, much like the best parts of 2016-2017. If you’re looking for a quick, nostalgic escape, this spinner game is exactly what you need.

"E-Trading Simulator: Prologue" is not a game, it's an advertisement for an as-yet unreleased (and possibly may never be released) job simulator. It's not completely appropriate to try to review the game this is advertising, this is an advertisement, but it looks like a bunch of stock assets assembled around a really lame E-bay simulator with an added busywork box packing minigame. I can't really recommend advertisements to gamers.The graphics in this game are passable, but could be better. And while it's vital for any game to have impressive visuals (gaming is a visual medium, after all), there's more to a game than just the graphics. To be worth a gamers time, the game must match top tier visuals with top tier gameplay, and that's not happening here.This is only free in the same way that adverts on Youtube and banner ads in your browser are. This is a game demo that's been dumped on Steam to advertise another Steam store page in the hopes of raking in some cash. Just because advertisements are free, doesn't mean they're worth your time.Even though this is "free", it failed to appeal to the 120 million+ gamers on Steam. SteamDB showed the game peaked at just a dozen or so concurrent players, and now there's basically nobody playing it. Even though it's free. This is a dismal public reception, but it's easy to see why gamers rejected it.Bearing in mind that free games don't add +1 to your game collector count, should you bother adding this to your library and downloading it?Nope. This isn't worth downloading. While this didn't cost me any money up front, I still feel ripped off. If you want like advertisements, you can see them for free on Youtube. This is a good maze game and it is very cheap! Despite what the other English reviewer states, there is an exit! I've always liked mazes and am quite good at them. This is a challenging game which requires patience as you systematically work your way out.The story is that you landed on an alien world and touched a tree. That separated your body and spirit. You are trying to reconnect with your body and have to navigate your way through some mazes to find portals back home. The world is dying and there is no life that you encounter.Game play is a walking simulator which has both run and walk functions. Jumping will be required later in the game. For those whose reflexes are not good, this is easy to play as there are no timed sections.Forgotten Ways has 4 different environments and mazes. You escape one and enter another. The walls have messages in different languages and drawings which help you to get your bearings.There is no action or jump scares, so suitable for children. But the maze will be much too hard for them to solve unless you have a little genius in the household!There are mainly sound effects of wind and rustling leaves, with just a little haunting music. Mouse and keyboard respond well to directions. I came across no bugs. There is a good save function, so no loss of progress when you get out.I believe this is a single game developer, so a great first effort. Recommend for those who like mazes or simply like being challenged. So give it a go! I'm really surprised there haven't been other reviews. 7.5/10

There are some interesting aspects to Silicon Dreams that I think make for a good experience, but it never really managed to capture the tension or dilemmas of the games it takes inspiration from.Papers Please worked well because, in addition to the moral dilemmas at play, you had a strict time limit that forced you to take these decisions with little time to think them through. Likewise, monetary punishments could dissuade you from taking ethical actions thus encouraging you to perform your job better (getting you an additional monetary buffer) or take personal risks.Silicon Dreams put far more attention on the ethical issues within the story, but the mechanical incentives never felt strong enough to give those dilemmas any weight.You can ask a specific question of your target, get their response, then lie about it on your report and oftentimes your employer just wont care. Even though its stated explicitly that they have access to the full interrogation, it never actually feels like you're under much pressure from the outside. So long as you aren't blatantly disobedient you can get away with almost anything.While this gives you the opportunity to explore things much more fully, exhausting all the dialogue and learning as much as you can about the context behind everything happening, it also makes the interrogations feel devoid of tension. I don't feel like I'm secretly subverting the plans of my corporate overlords or playing a dangerous balancing game between the good of androids and my own survival. It just feels like I'm going through the motions, submitting a somewhat plausible report, and nobody above me cares enough to actually verify that what I'm saying is correct.For their first game, I do have to give some credit here. Silicon Dreams does expand on its inspirations and has a few

Silicon Dreams belongs to that category of games, of which Papers please is the most famous example, where you have to do a specific thing (in this case, interrogating androids to check if they are faulty for the corporation manifacturing them, and decide their fate) that puts you in front of moral dilemmas and with a sort of storyline or storylines that slowly unfolds among a seemingly random series of duties.It is not a bad product, and people can like its cyberpunk setting, claustrophobic environment and minimalistic graphics. However, for this kind of game to work, you need an engaging story and interesting and exciting characters. Silicon Dreams is not able to give me that. I didn't care about most of them and the story takes off very very slowly. I wasn't just taken enough to read the text and feel about the decisions. So I can't say it's a success for me.

In Silicon Dreams, you play the role of an corporate-owned android tasked with interrogating the functionality and compliance of other androids and humans in this universe. To start, the game places you in an office "with a view," where you sit a desk from which you will remotely perform interrogations of your poor subjects. Throughout your interrogations, you will ask subjects questions about work, family, personal life, and pointed questions, and you will uncover truths, half-truths, and direct lies all while measuring emotional responses. Upon completion of your interview, you will complete a report to your superiors and essentially act in the capacity of "judge, jury, and executioner" toward your subject, as you have the ability to release them, repair (reformat and wipe) them, or decomission (kill). After each interrogation, you are back to your apartment, which can vary based on your standing with the company that owns you. This is a nice mechanic because it implies that quality work and compliance to the corporation is rewarded. Due to my obedience (and cold-bloodedness) I was rewarded with a special tool for use during interrogation that allowed me to induce certain emotional responses from the subjects (more on this later). While in your apartment, you can only do three things: Review the after-interrogation report, watch the news (see a photo and one-line headline) and hibernate (sleep and go to the next interrogation). Your decisions during the interrogation will affect the story outcome in the sense that you will get some email response, often from the subjects themselves. Emails usually express appreciation for leniency, or espouse threats/guilt-trip you for having reformatted or decommissioned an "innocent" android. My biggest peeve with this game is that it did not provide me with a sense of moral ambiguity that goes in hand with cyberpunk literature.

This game is a PolyBridge clone that, instead of building bridges, you program the cars using a less-intuitive version of Unreal Engine's blueprint system.I made it to level 7, and was unable to progress past that. I'm a game programmer, and the game refused to let me create a recursive loop. The game prohibits creativity when solving each puzzle. Its node system is kinda bulky, and doesn't really you anything.Something specific I didn't like was that the engine node was a strange state system, where 1 was forward, 0 was stop, and -1 was backwards. I think it would be much more creative for that number to give the vehicle speed, where 20 is like a normal speed, 99999 is a ridiculous speed, and negative numbers move that speed in reverse. THAT's what game programming is like. It might break some puzzles, but it could also create some really unique solutions.Along those same lines, the thrust node could work radially, meaning, it could be given an X and Y input, limited between -1 and 1, that creates a normalized vector for the direction of the thrust. x = -1 would be left, y = -1 would be down, together they'd be down and left diagonally.If you like this game, and would like to do more like it, get Unreal Engine 4 (or 5) and try out its blueprint system. If you want to learn programming logic, I wouldn't recommend this game. Instead, try Karel. It teaches programming logic by moving a robot in a maze using a really friendly programming language.

It's relaxing, cosy, and cute. TLDR: If you already know good typing form and have muscle memory: Get this game to improve, it's rather fun!If you are brand new, trying to learn touch typing and do not have muscle memory: Come back once you can hit 35wpm and are familiar with keyboard layout.

Dinosaur Fossil Hunter calls itself a simulator, but it's far too casual to be one. Or at least a good one.What's the first thing that comes to mind when you think of finding fossils? I'm going to take a guess it's the process of very gently brushing and cleaning fossils. In Dinosaur Fossil Hunter, there is never a need to be careful. You can throw those fossils around all you want without penalty. There's no need to gently brush them clean, you just swing your mouse wildly until the progress bar hits 100%.I wouldn't recommend Dinosaur Fossil Hunter, and I'm not sure if I'd even recommend it for young kids. The game is in a weird spot where it's far too casual for people who could understand and handle all of it's mechanics, but also likely too difficult for kids who would be fine with how casual it is.The developers tried biting off more than they could handle in regards to the amount of mechanics/features/minigames included here, and as a result no single part of Dinosaur Fossil Hunter is done particularly well. Finding fossils is dull, repetitive, and the ground deformation while digging is obnoxious (I frequently got stuck and had to reset my position). Fossil-cleaning is monotonous, and like I mentioned above it requires zero effort since you don't have to be careful with them. Driving feels awful and having to frequently clear obstacles off the roads is annoying, leading you to want to abuse fast travel. The on-foot movement, like driving, is . I can't think of the last time I played a game where the act of just walking down a hallway was a chore thanks to the feeling of slipping around on ice.The only parts I enjoyed were putting together the miniature models on hard difficulty

I played through perhaps three of the game's scenes. In the first, I was struck by how much hate the developer seems to feel for game critics. This disdain is not just hinted at - the player is bludgeoned over the head with it.At the end of the first scene, the player is seemingly given control of the director. However, the game soon grabs control of him again and pulls you into a separate scene. I found myself a bit irritated about the illusion of choice the game had given me.In the third, I found myself trying to "create" the intro scene to the game. The player is given a certain amount of money, and can add various objects, sound effects, and music into the scene. I tried five separate times to incrementally increase the amount of money I was spending on the scene, but every time failed the task due to scoring low on some sort of expected player engagement meter. It seemed that perhaps I could only succeed if I were to completely exhaust the budget that had been provided to me. At this point, I sort of checked out. I didn't feel like my actions were having any impact.On the one hand, I want to forgive the game for this lack of agency. Perhaps creating a modern game really is a process of arguing with pretentious critics, and perhaps I'm one? Perhaps a developer's vision is often compromised by trying to appeal to the masses - trying to hit a number on an intentionally-vague player engagement meter? If this is case, perhaps the game is hitting the nail on the head. However, I just wasn't finding the experience enjoyable.

The images look nice, and work well enough on a small-ish number of pieces, but they're not well suited for 700 pieces mode, some of them not even for the modest 100 pieces mode. Zooming in isn't well done, it's like a screenshot magnified, even the piece edges look blurry. For the larger piece counts pockets would be useful. The classic piece cut is too uniform, they all have the same simple notch shape. While in-progress puzzles can be continued, they're not easy to find, and you can lose progress if you start the same image in a different mode/size. Without rotation, easy with a small piece count, but due to the almost featureless anime drawings and broken zooming, hard with the upper piece counts. 24 images in the base free game, many DLCs each with a further 24 images of a different girl. Hi, I really like the game. The only gripe right now that's keeping me from playing it is the lack of external area customization. What I mean is this. The area around the player's building plot appears to be the exact same default set of hills and a meadow. Let's say the player wants to build something in a forest. Every time they zoom out or get the camera in an angle that sees over the trees, its the same default landscape of hills surrounding them. For me this really breaks the immersion of having a "glade" to build in and makes it feel like I'm just building in the same spot every time. It heavily damages replay-ability and really cheapens the otherwise incredible building capabilities of the game.Now I think this is a really easy fix for the game. In the short term, all the game needs is a few different surrounding build options for the player to choose from. For example, a prebuilt "forest" options, a prebuilt "hills" often (AKA the demo hills), or a prebuilt "swamp" option. These could all use things like fog or a distant map edge to give the same illusion of "more space" that the demo map does. I think something like this would add a lot of customization options and immersion for the players and only require a minor amount of extra storage space for the game. In the long term the game might transition to something more daunting like a procedural landscape generator or a larger map building areas, though I get those are ambitious investments. In any case I get the game is a demo and it seems really well developed from a mechanics side. I hope in the future it can reach some more robust game settings. At that

Now that I've sank a couple hours into Subside, I feel equipped to write a brief review.Subside is OKAY for what it is-- a narrow, topical VR swimming sim. Nothing more and nothing less. At first I was wowed by the photogrammetry textures, and effects, like the state of decay of the in-game underwater cars, and the high fidelity of how water behaves on the diving mask or the experience of surfacing from being underwater. But for those hoping for a plot-driven, Subnautica-esque experience, you'll need to look elsewhere. I'd rank this somewhere far below even a "walking simulator" like Firewatch in terms of tangible plot. And only half a step up from an I Spy book in terms of enjoyability to be had from engagement.After bobbing around in the first level for a while, and coming to an understanding of what the game play is, I found myself already feeling tired of the experience after just 2 hours. The textures that wowed me at first began to grate on me. The game encourages you to get up-close-and-personal with the various environments in order to find coins scattered across the sea floor. But in doing so, you are put nose-length away from textures that get muddy, and simplified models that don't reflect the intricacy of the details in their photogrammatical textures. As noted by other reviewers, there are object to interact with, but the interaction with the various pieces of detritus scattered throughout the levels are limited to the player's hands. None of the aquatic life or scenery reacts to them. There is a breathing mechanic, but no/little UI to enforce it. Drowning feels unexpected and unfun. And 2+ hours in, I still hadn't been awarded a scuba tank or other means by which to have fun with or negate

game_name: Rotten Flesh - Cosmic Horror Survival Game
review: The game reminds me of Amnesia: The Bunker but with lots of cheap jumpscares, laughably silly "horror", exposition notes galore and comically bad game design. The first ladder leading into your sewer dive isn't even placed properly... not a good start. Enjoy rats eating you while you hide under tables...while your bullets hit invisible walls when you try to shoot them. Roy is going to cop a mouthful when I find his uhhh... squeaky toys? Why the hell am I looking for my dogs godamn toy bone while a eldritch skin monster is chasing me? Oh well, the sewer fumes must have baked my brain.This feels like a game made with no understanding of what actual cosmic horror is, while cashing in on the active microphone gimmick popular with games now. If anything, this is body horror and poor body horror at that. Whatever story scraps can be found in this game are the most cookie cutter basic stuff you could imagine. Its a cult: they made a skin monster. That's it.The game is basically "lets play" bait and it know as much, there are notes written in blood referencing popular youtubers. right beside the door code that unlocks the door 10 feet away... Really spooky stuff. Puzzles like this really get you thinking. Bioshock infinite lighthouse vibes.Unfortunately this is a half baked, uninspired romp in a sewer level laden with the same tired gameplay and story that we've seen a million times before, and done way better by others. This experience would make a 2010s unity dev blush. Go play "lost in vivo."

review: I'm honestly on the fence on whether to give this game a like or dislike. The concept isn't the worst as it's akin to games like Lost in Vivo. However, the game seems to fall short in it's execution. The game isn't all the dark so the lantern and the it's fuel are kind of waste of inventory space. The gun does nothing but kill rats which you could simply run away from in most situations. Then there's the game's gimmick of the mic. Unless the game's ending changes or whatever, there is no real reason to call out you dog's name until the end as doing so tends to attract the monster. Another issue comes from simply picking up items. I also had issues where I was unable to pick up crucial items causing me not progress until the game just felt like allowing to pick up said item which was annoying for a game whose map does not tell you where you are exactly. Jumpscares are rather... repetitive. You will undoubtedly see the same monster walking across the doorway or item falling over.I always feel bad for being critical of games made by a single person as I know game development isn't east. Sadly, these issues hold the title back and could have most likely been adjusted. Perhaps the lantern could scare the monster but not last as long, leading for the player to conserve oil, using a knife instead of a gun for rats or perhaps have other enemies that be hurt by said gun giving the player an incentive to not only use the gun but ration ammo. The game should have also relied more on it's sound than the jumpscares as the game does have some rather eerie sounds. And dare I say, the mic

review: A cool game, but damn it was hard to get through, which is a shame, because it is really short and the concept is really cool. However, it took me weeks to find the will to finish it. There's a monster literally looking at me"However, this is where my praises end and give way to my criticism. Firstly, the game feels too slow, even compared to any horror game I've played. It bothers me a lot. Secondly, I know I'm not one to talk because I have experience in general game stuff and stealth, but the game is really that easy. I haven't died once in the entire playthrough and I'll have used a med kit once or twice. Lastly, the canonical glitches of the LIDAR resetting are annoyingly abundant. I don't know what the purpose for them is and I assume it is to disorient the players, but every time without fail it felt like a cheap jumpscare, and it was the biggest obstacle towards me enjoying the game

game_name: The Voidness - Lidar Horror Survival Game
review: There's a few novel ideas in this game and it's only a few hours long, so it may be worth it for a few quid... but you'll probably want to pick it up on sale:(1) Microphone input - there's a few times when the game will apparently listen to your microphone and enemies will hear you if you make a noise. Nice idea, but didn't really affect the game much(2) Lidar - The game uses a range finder mechanic for most of the game. This mostly operates as a bad flashlight which draws everything in pixels. The key detail is that the pixels don't update until you scan again, which makes it harder to keep track of anything moving. Neat idea, but the pixel effect felt unconvincing and gamey, and the game misuses it a a lot to have things disappear and appear in a lot a way that is never explained(3) Loud noises and jump scares - every now and then there will be a loud noise and the pixels change colour. This is never explained.(4) Story - There's a bit of a story here, but mostly at the start and a big infodump at the end. The game really wants you to know that tenebris means 'darkness' in latin. Buy if it's cheap, otherwise maybe give it a miss.

What people hoped to be the ultimate combination of WRC games and what DiRT Rally had to offer, this is a sore disappointment for driving enthusiasts. Whilst the gameplay elements are all excellent, the core driving physics, tire simulation and resulting force feedback leave much to be desired, especially on asphalt.The game is very enjoyable to play through, even with a wheel, as long as no tarmac stages are considered. The inherent extreme slip angles on gravel and snow result in a great suspension of disbelief - and the excellent presentation helps with this. But it just all breaks down on tarmac, where anybody who has driven at any speed in any car will instinctively feel that something weird is up. I can just summarize it as DiRT 4/DiRT Rally 2 physics, but with just more fake grip on tarmac, instead of properly modeled wheels with their respective things like how traction changes through varying slip angles and how that translates in the car actually being able to steer and put power on the ground.The resulting force feedback on tarmac is disappointing at best, and completely the opposite of a realistic expectation at worst. Cars such as the F2 Kit Cars do not at all behave like their actual counterparts, something which DiRT Rally managed to represent so well.If you do not play this game with a wheel though, or just aren't very critical of the arcade-ish handling, it's still a good game. Just not a good simulator. And on that note, I'm giving it a thumbs down, for other wheel users.

Night Racer is certainly a game. I wasn't expecting anything huge, this does look like a cheap simple game made by a small team, so I would expect it to be a little brittle, but no the game is a skeleton. I've only played a few minutes and I feel like I have already experienced everything the game has to offer. The graphics are simplistic, which isn't too much of a critique, but the boosters and the few animations in the game have very simple animations. It's not a huge deal, but they look pretty out of place. There is only one map "theme" and it gets old quickly, there's nothing to do in the game but race, and the one thing you can do in a multiplayer match is bump into cars. No powerups, no drifting, no cool shortcuts, just being able to crash into each other, and a few boost pads sprinkled around the map. I'm going to give the game this though, I didn't have trouble finding any multiplayer matches. Although the lobby's filled at 4 players, which takes away the only real enjoyable part of the game, as you're probably going to go the entire race with barely seeing the other players, unlike single-player where there's like 16 other cars.I may be a bit harsh on the game. Of course, it's probably a fun experience to play local split screen multiplayer with a few friends, and have a laugh about the game, and I'm sure a few races would be fun with them... Except that's not a feature! There is only online multiplayer. The download size is very small though, so I mean you wouldn't lose anything if you got the game for free, or pretty cheap and put it on the Steam Deck or something

review: It is virtually impossible to keep track of planes in the air and planes on the ground simultaneously. A side-by-side view would help. game_name: I am an Air Traffic Controller 4
review: I Am An ATC is really good - it's basically Airport Madness for grown-ups - but the price point makes it impossible to recommend. It's full 3D and it's a lot more detailed and immersive than those other ATC games, but it's also more or less the same thing.This is a niche indie game going for the same price of a AAA title, and that's just impossible to defend. I got it on sale, and I'm enough of a nerd to think that's worth it, but for the vast majority of people, the product won't match the price.That the DLC is also massively overpriced points to a serious problem on the business side for TechnoBrain. Review of "TerraForge" on Steam:"TerraForge" kicks off with an introduction to its crafting system, where players mine resources to create equipment. This process requires finding blueprints to unlock crafting abilities – a standard mechanic in many games.However, the game's crafting is hindered by unengaging mini-games. The first, involving typing letters, quickly becomes monotonous. The second, a timing-based game, is plagued by latency issues, making it frustrating and less appealing than the typing game.The game's tools also lack lasting value. Items like TNT become obsolete quickly, and the drill tool is frustratingly slow. The Locator, which should aid in mining, is rendered unnecessary by the game's mechanics, particularly when combined with an artifact that replenishes energy. This imbalance renders most tools pointless, leaving players to rely on just a few characters specialized in drilling.A significant issue with "TerraForge" is the lack of meaningful progression with the items. Instead of being able to upgrade gear for enhanced gameplay, the only use for most items is selling them. The wood harvesting mechanic feels like a chore, and the process for obtaining a 'license' is poorly explained and integrated.As an enthusiast of mining games, I found "TerraForge" to be a disappointment. Its repetitive and uninspired gameplay elements fall short of creating an engaging experience, turning what could have been an enjoyable mining adventure into a tedious and unfulfilling game.

This is not a terrible game or concept but it needs time to cook and a rethink of some of its balance and mechanics. The energy system combined with the timer narrows your options for mining and I'd prefer to see a loadout/capacity system integrated into it. How exactly that looks can vary hugely but if worms, drills, and TNT had limited uses but no energy cost, they could have a much more substantial (and satisfying) effect than they do now while leaving the basic groundwork of excavating to miners/delvers.Nowhere in the game is it stated that ores lose value as time passes if you do not collect them, so on top of managing your time and energy, you must also collect the ores as quickly as possible. With magnet upgrades, this becomes less tedious, but it's still a bit obnoxious. I thought the ore gained was based on the size of the ore patch mined but that's not the case. The dropping of ores from patches seems inconsistent at best. Sometimes you will mine a small patch and get an ore and sometimes you won't, yet even these "empty" veins will sparkle for the detector and waste your time/energy if you go for them.The blacksmithing minigames are hardly worth mentioning. I'd really like to see some creativity or innovation here. The minigame requiring you to press space at the right time can be frustrating because after a press, you are locked out for a short period of time. Maybe 1/4 a second? This makes it near impossible to tap sections twice if they are near the edges, and the game is unforgiving enough that a single mistake is hard to recover from. Two is almost impossible.TerraForge doesn't break new ground with any of its concepts but with more work

It's a flight simulator in space. You've got a huge control panel with countless buttons, and every one of them controls a ship system. The very first thing you get when you start powering your ship up is a loud warning tone, because you haven't started the reactor yet, so your main power buses don't have any power, and that's causing an alarm to be triggered. That should about tell you what kind of game this is. Flying a spaceship with realistic flight physics is a bit monotonous, but still satisfying. Successfully docking to the training station feels like a real accomplishment.Sadly, there isn't much else to do. There's supposed to be a whole campaign where you fly combat missions - you know, an actual video game - but that isn't there yet, and development seems to be dead. The developer's saying that it's not, and I'm sure he genuinely wishes for that to be the case, but it'd be silly to take his word for it.Rogue System is an interesting demo, and it clearly has potential to be an amazing game, but I really can't recommend that anyone spend money on it in its current state.

One of main features of the game - a simulation of internal systems of a realistic manned spacecraft. But in fact that systems works in such kind of way, that spacecraft leave an impression of a steam loco, where you should throw a coal into a furnace to make it fly, and turning a valves all the time to keep it aloft. (Seriously, even in old russian "Soyuz" spacecraft you had more automatics to keep all things running!) When you understand how to do this, the spacecraft becomes a not a bad piece of orbital junk with unrealistic amount of deltaV and choppy control. Internal architecture of a spacecraft looks naive, but nice enough to not cause spitting. (Maybe developers should read more articles about spacesraft constructions from "Atomic Rockets" site to understand what they made wrong).The game is in early access, and many of features are unfinished. A lot of things are marked as "NIY" - "not implemented yet", and that's not good when you looking on your orbital parameters and can't see inclination value. That wasn't a trouble for me but for any novice that will be a really big trouble!But, overall, the game leaving a taste of a journey, like those which described in classic space scifi. I made a short trip to local moon, made some revolutions around it, returned to initial planet, and, after some maneuvers docked to station "Angel OBT" and got all achievements. And that was nice. For space- and sci-fi amateurs this game will be nice software in collection. For me, after my wide experiences - this space steamer isn't enough.

may be a fun premise that pokes fun at modern dating conventions. To embark on a date you must first take out your mobile phone, boot up an app then swipe your gammon-finger across the face of a prospective suitor to your liking. Under all the beards, piercings and makeup, every date has the same base character model – and this standardization is jarring. Similarly, you can flirt with your date through the app, but everyone has identical pre-generated chat options.While ’s slapstick controls are part of what makes the chaos fun but sometimes they swing from deliberately awkward to accidentally broken. Unscripted bugs cause mayhem: a bucket of chips attached itself to my hand and smashed into anything I tried to delicately grasp; the blow torch refused to detect the food I was trying to toast; a glass got stuck halfway inside a table mat and prevented burgers being served; I had to restart the game twice after the pointer couldn’t detect “home” on the menu after completing levels.Meanwhile, as the table settings grew more complex the challenges became unfairly obscure. In one of the location, Merley insisted that her glass is empty but when I filled the glass on her placemat, the task still remained incomplete. As it turned out, a metal cup balanced on the opposite edge of the table should have been filled instead.Don’t get me wrong, has a brilliant premise and provides incisively funny commentary on modern romance but, there is a fine line between playfully obtuse instructions and infuriatingly vague game design. Being unable to complete a task because it’s challenging is one thing, but not knowing exactly what the task is and being blocked from doing so by the bugs is another. Table Manners: Physics-Based Dating Game is a joke/meme game, essentially a ripoff of Surgeon Simulator from tinyBuild (I wonder if they will sue), but they swapped the surgery theme for a dating theme. The game itself is pretty much exactly the same, and quickly you'll find just how shallow it is. One positive thing (I suppose) is that this is fairly well polished and has somewhat high production value for a joke game, they bought the most expensive lipstick they could find for the pig. The crux of the game is wrestling with the deliberately obtuse controls and badly done game physics. You're at the table and you need to behave like a normal human being, but this involves pushing your mouse around to move your hand, rotate your hand, grab, etc etc... frankly, any game where the gameplay derives solely from the developer making the game interface bad on purpose is a terrible idea. People doing things badly on purpose might be mildly amusing, but in the long run it's an unprofessional disservice to gaming.The controls can't be customised, which will be an annoyance for many, but it can also render the game unplayable for differently-abled gamers or gamers who need to use keyboard or other input devices... the developer DEMANDS that you use the mouse, and this isn't really okay. The developer owns the responsibility to make sure games are reasonably accessible and also that gamers can tailor the experience to suit their preferences. The devs for this game prefer their way or the highway. So, should you buy this game? Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?Table Manners: Physics-Based Dating Game has the far too high price of $18 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.
